title: (1.1) Vector Algebra
content:
1.1 Vector Algebra# A scalar has only a size (temperature, mass, charge). A vector has a size and a direction (velocity, force, electric field). Strictly, a vector is not just “three numbers”: it is three numbers that change in a particular way when you rotate your axes. The last part of this section explains what that means.
Vector operations# You add vectors component by component; the order doesn't matter. Picture it as placing arrows head to tail. Subtracting \( \vec{B} \) means adding \( \vec{B} \) reversed. Multiplying by a scalar \( a \) stretches the arrow by \( a \) without turning it (it flips round if \( a < 0 \)).
Adding puts arrows head to tail. A minus sign reverses an arrow. The two orders of adding make the two sides of a parallelogram, so A + B = B + A. Subtracting B is adding minus B. Multiplying by 2 doubles the length. Left: the unit vectors, one along each axis. Right: any vector is the sum of three parts, one along each axis. Adding vectors component by component is adding these parts. There are two ways to multiply two vectors, and they answer different questions.
Dot product gives a number, and the order doesn't matter:
\[\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z\] Here \( \theta \) is the angle between the arrows when drawn tail to tail. The dot product asks how much of one vector points along the other. It is zero for perpendicular vectors, and \( \vec{A} \cdot \vec{A} = A^2 \). Work, flux and potential energy are all built from it, because each only cares about the part of a vector along some direction.
Cross product gives a vector, and swapping the order flips its sign:
\[\vec{A} \cross \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \vu{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \vu{x} & \vu{y} & \vu{z} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}\] So \( \vec{A} \cross \vec{B} = -\vec{B} \cross \vec{A} \) and \( \vec{A} \cross \vec{A} = \vec{0} \). The unit vector \( \vu{n} \) sticks out perpendicular to the plane of \( \vec{A} \) and \( \vec{B} \); the right-hand rule picks which way. The size of the cross product is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors make, so it is zero for parallel vectors. It asks how much the two vectors point away from each other.
Left: the dot product uses the part of A that lies along B. Middle: the third side of the triangle is A − B; its length gives the law of cosines. Right: the size of the cross product is the area of the parallelogram. Triple products# The scalar triple product gives a number, and you can cycle the letters round without changing it:
\[\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \cross \vec{C}) = \vec{B} \cdot (\vec{C} \cross \vec{A}) = \vec{C} \cdot (\vec{A} \cross \vec{B})\] It is the volume of the slanted box (parallelepiped) built on the three vectors. That explains the cycling: it's the same box whichever face you call the base. Swapping any two vectors flips the sign. In components it is the determinant with the three vectors as rows.
The slanted box built on A, B and C. Base area times height gives its volume, which is the scalar triple product. The vector triple product simplifies by the “BAC-CAB” rule:
\[\vec{A} \cross (\vec{B} \cross \vec{C}) = \vec{B} (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{C}) - \vec{C} (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B})\] You will use this a lot in radiation (Chapter 11), where the fields of an accelerating charge contain double cross products. The brackets matter, because the cross product is not associative:
\[\vec{A} \cross (\vec{B} \cross \vec{C}) \neq (\vec{A} \cross \vec{B}) \cross \vec{C}\] Any longer product of vectors can be broken down into these two forms.
Position, displacement and separation vectors# The position of a point, measured from the origin, is
\[\vec{r} = x\vu{x} + y\vu{y} + z\vu{z}, \qquad r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}, \qquad \vu{r} = \frac{\vec{r}}{r}\] and a tiny step in any direction is \( \dd{\vec{l}} = \dd{x},\vu{x} + \dd{y},\vu{y} + \dd{z},\vu{z} \).
The position vector r runs from the origin to the point (x, y, z). The unit vector r-hat points the same way with length 1. In electrodynamics there are always two points to keep apart: where the charge is, and where you are measuring the field. The source point \( \vec{r'} \) is where the charge sits. The field point \( \vec{r} \) is where you are. The arrow from the charge to you is the separation vector:
\[\gr \equiv \vec{r} - \vec{r'}, \qquad \gr = |\vec{r} - \vec{r'}|, \qquad \vu{\gr} = \frac{\vec{r} - \vec{r'}}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r'}|}\] The source point (where the charge is), the field point (where you measure), and the separation vector between them. \( \gr \) is not \( \vec{r} \). Also, \( \vu{\gr} \) is not a constant: its direction changes as you move from one bit of charge to the next, so you cannot pull it outside an integral over the charge. Split it into Cartesian components first (\( \vu{x}, \vu{y}, \vu{z} \) are constant and can come out), then integrate.
How vectors transform# If you rotate the coordinate axes, the components of a vector change according to
\[\bar{A}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{3} R_{ij} A_j\] where \( R_{ij} \) is the rotation matrix. For example, rotating by angle \( \phi \) about the \( x \)-axis gives
\[\begin{pmatrix} \bar{A}_y \\ \bar{A}_z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\phi & \sin\phi \\ -\sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A_y \\ A_z \end{pmatrix}\] One arrow, two sets of axes. Turning the axes by φ changes the angle from θ to θ-bar, so the components change, but the arrow itself does not. This rule is what defines a vector. Three numbers that don't change this way are not a vector, even if you write them with arrows. The arrow itself stays the same when you turn your head, so its length \( A^2 = \vec{A} \cdot \vec{A} \) does not change under rotation. That is why quantities built from dot products (energy, work) mean the same thing in every set of axes.
Example# Find the angle between the face diagonals of a cube.
Two face diagonals of a unit cube, both starting at the origin. Solution triple-click to reveal Put one corner of a unit cube at the origin, with its edges along the axes. Two face diagonals starting at the origin are
\[\vec{A} = 1\vu{x} + 0\vu{y} + 1\vu{z}, \qquad \vec{B} = 0\vu{x} + 1\vu{y} + 1\vu{z}\] Work out the dot product from the components:
\[\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = (1)(0) + (0)(1) + (1)(1) = 1\] and from the geometry, using \( A = B = \sqrt{2} \):
\[\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = 2\cos\theta\] Setting the two equal gives \( \cos\theta = 1/2 \), so \( \theta = 60^\circ \).
This is the standard trick for finding angles: work out the dot product both ways and set them equal.
Example# Find the area of the triangle with vertices at \( (1,0,0) \), \( (0,2,0) \) and \( (0,0,3) \), and a unit vector normal to its plane.
The triangle and a unit vector normal to it (seen from the side, so the normal doesn't point straight at you). Solution triple-click to reveal Take two edges of the triangle, both starting from the first vertex:
\[\vec{A} = -\vu{x} + 2\vu{y}, \qquad \vec{B} = -\vu{x} + 3\vu{z}\] Their cross product is
\[\vec{A} \cross \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \vu{x} & \vu{y} & \vu{z} \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6\vu{x} + 3\vu{y} + 2\vu{z}\] Its size is the area of the parallelogram on the two edges. The triangle is half of that parallelogram:
\[|\vec{A} \cross \vec{B}| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7, \qquad \text{area} = \frac{7}{2}\] A cross product is always perpendicular to both vectors, so it is normal to the triangle's plane:
\[\vu{n} = \frac{1}{7}\left( 6\vu{x} + 3\vu{y} + 2\vu{z} \right)\] The negative of this is just as good; taking the edges in the other order gives it.
Full derivation: §1.1.

title: (1.2) Differential Calculus
content:
1.2 Differential Calculus# An ordinary derivative \( df/dx \) tells you how fast \( f \) changes as you move along a line.
A small derivative means f changes slowly; a large one means it changes fast. In three dimensions one number is not enough, because the rate of change depends on which direction you move. The fix is the “del” operator:
\[\grad = \vu{x} \pdv{}{x} + \vu{y} \pdv{}{y} + \vu{z} \pdv{}{z}\] Del is not really a vector. On its own it means nothing; it is an instruction to differentiate whatever comes after it. But it behaves like a vector, so it can act in the same three ways a vector can multiply:
on a scalar → the gradient \( \grad t \) with a dot product on a vector → the divergence \( \div{\vec{v}} \) with a cross product on a vector → the curl \( \curl{\vec{v}} \) Maxwell's equations are four statements about the divergence and curl of \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \). So these three derivatives are all the calculus the subject needs.
Gradient# For a scalar field \( t(x,y,z) \) (say, the temperature at each point in a room),
\[\grad t = \pdv{t}{x}\vu{x} + \pdv{t}{y}\vu{y} + \pdv{t}{z}\vu{z}\] When you take a small step \( \dd{\vec{l}} \), the change in \( t \) is
\[\dd{t} = (\grad t) \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = |\grad t| \, |\dd{\vec{l}}| \cos\theta\] This tells you what the gradient means. The change is biggest when \( \theta = 0 \), that is, when you step along \( \grad t \). So:
the gradient points in the direction in which \( t \) increases fastest, and its size is the slope in that direction. Picture standing on a hillside. The gradient of the height points straight uphill, and its size is how steep that is. If you step at right angles to the gradient, \( \dd{t} = 0 \): you walk along a contour line. So the gradient is always perpendicular to surfaces of constant \( t \).
Where the gradient is zero the ground is flat: a hilltop, a valley bottom or a saddle (a mountain pass).
Divergence# \[\div{\vec{v}} = \pdv{v_x}{x} + \pdv{v_y}{y} + \pdv{v_z}{z}\] A scalar that measures how much the field spreads out from a point. Imagine \( \vec{v} \) is the velocity of water on a pond, and you sprinkle sawdust on it. If the sawdust spreads apart, you are at a point of positive divergence (a source, like a tap). If it bunches together, the divergence is negative (a sink, like a drain). Water that neither spreads nor bunches has zero divergence.
Curl# \[\curl{\vec{v}} = \begin{vmatrix} \vu{x} & \vu{y} & \vu{z} \\ \pdv{}{x} & \pdv{}{y} & \pdv{}{z} \\ v_x & v_y & v_z \end{vmatrix}\] A vector that measures how much the field swirls around a point. Put a small paddle wheel in the water: if it spins, the curl is non-zero there. The curl points along the wheel's axle, in the direction given by the right-hand rule. A whirlpool is a region of large curl.
Left: a field that spreads out (divergence, no curl). Middle: a uniform field (neither). Right: a field that swirls (curl, no divergence). Careful: you can't always see divergence or curl just by looking.
Left: the arrows are parallel but grow as they go, so more flows out than in: positive divergence. Right: nothing goes round, but a paddle wheel would spin, because the water on top moves the other way from the water underneath: non-zero curl. Product rules# As with ordinary derivatives, there are product rules. There are six; these five are the ones used most (the sixth, for \( \curl{(\vec{A} \cross \vec{B})} \), is in the full notes):
\[\grad(fg) = f(\grad g) + g(\grad f)\] \[\grad(\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}) = \vec{A} \cross (\curl{\vec{B}}) + \vec{B} \cross (\curl{\vec{A}}) + (\vec{A} \cdot \grad)\vec{B} + (\vec{B} \cdot \grad)\vec{A}\] \[\div{(f\vec{A})} = f(\div{\vec{A}}) + \vec{A} \cdot (\grad f)\] \[\div{(\vec{A} \cross \vec{B})} = \vec{B} \cdot (\curl{\vec{A}}) - \vec{A} \cdot (\curl{\vec{B}})\] \[\curl{(f\vec{A})} = f(\curl{\vec{A}}) - \vec{A} \cross (\grad f)\] Each one can be proved by writing out the components and using the ordinary product rule.
Second derivatives# Applying \( \grad \) twice gives five possible second derivatives. Two of them are always zero:
\[\div{(\curl{\vec{v}})} = 0, \qquad \curl{(\grad t)} = \vec{0}\] An easy way to remember why: they look like \( \vec{A} \cdot (\vec{A} \cross \vec{B}) \) and \( \vec{A} \cross \vec{A} \), with \( \grad \) in place of \( \vec{A} \), and both of those are zero. (Intuitively: a pure swirl has no source, and walking uphill round a closed loop can't produce any circulation.)
These two facts are the foundation of potentials. In electrostatics \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \), so \( \vec{E} \) can be written as a gradient: that gives the electric potential. And \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) always, so \( \vec{B} \) can be written as a curl: that gives the vector potential. §1.6 makes this precise.
Of the other three, the important one is the Laplacian, the divergence of the gradient:
\[\laplacian t = \div{(\grad t)} = \pdv{^2 t}{x^2} + \pdv{^2 t}{y^2} + \pdv{^2 t}{z^2}\] The second is the gradient of the divergence, \( \grad(\div{\vec{v}}) \). It has no special name and turns up less often. Note that it is not the same as the Laplacian of a vector, \( \laplacian \vec{v} \) (which means the Laplacian of each component).
The third, the curl of the curl, is not new; it breaks down into the other two:
\[\curl{(\curl{\vec{v}})} = \grad(\div{\vec{v}}) - \laplacian \vec{v}\] You will use this identity to get the wave equation out of Maxwell's equations (§9.2).
So there are really just two independent second derivatives: the Laplacian (very important) and the gradient of the divergence (seldom needed).
Example# Compute the divergence of \( \vec{v}_1 = \vu{r} \) and of \( \vec{v}_2 = \vu{r}/r^2 \) at points away from the origin. Both fields point radially outward; account for the difference in the results.
Solution triple-click to reveal In spherical coordinates (§1.4), the divergence of a field that points only radially is
\[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}\left( r^2 v_r \right)\] For \( \vec{v}_1 = \vu{r} \), \( v_r = 1 \):
\[\div{\vec{v}_1} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}(r^2) = \frac{2}{r}\] For \( \vec{v}_2 = \vu{r}/r^2 \), \( v_r = 1/r^2 \), so \( r^2 v_r = 1 \) is a constant and
\[\div{\vec{v}_2} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}(1) = 0 \qquad (r \neq 0)\] A sketch won't show the difference: both sets of arrows point outward. Think of the flow through spheres of growing radius. A sphere's area grows like \( r^2 \). The first field keeps the same strength as the spheres grow, so more and more flows out through bigger spheres: something must be adding to the flow, and the divergence is positive. The second field weakens like \( 1/r^2 \), exactly cancelling the growth in area, so the same amount flows through every sphere: nothing is added between them, and the divergence is zero.
The second field is the field of a point charge. It has zero divergence everywhere except the origin, yet a non-zero flow through any sphere around the origin. That puzzle is solved by the Dirac delta function in §1.5.
Example# Determine the curl of \( \vec{v} = -y\vu{x} + x\vu{y} \) and of \( \vec{w} = x\vu{x} + y\vu{y} \).
Solution triple-click to reveal Both fields lie in the \( xy \) plane and don't depend on \( z \), so only the \( z \) component of the curl is non-zero:
\[(\curl{\vec{v}})_z = \pdv{v_y}{x} - \pdv{v_x}{y}\] For \( \vec{v} = -y\vu{x} + x\vu{y} \):
\[\curl{\vec{v}} = \left[ \pdv{}{x}(x) - \pdv{}{y}(-y) \right]\vu{z} = (1 + 1)\vu{z} = 2\vu{z}\] This field goes round the origin anticlockwise, and the curl points along \( +\vu{z} \), as the right-hand rule says. Its divergence is zero.
For \( \vec{w} = x\vu{x} + y\vu{y} \):
\[\curl{\vec{w}} = \left[ \pdv{}{x}(y) - \pdv{}{y}(x) \right]\vu{z} = \vec{0}\] This field points straight outward and doesn't swirl. Its divergence is \( \div{\vec{w}} = 2 \).
The pair shows that divergence and curl measure different things: the first field swirls but doesn't spread, the second spreads but doesn't swirl.
Full derivation: §1.2.

title: (1.3) Integral Calculus
content:
1.3 Integral Calculus# Line, surface and volume integrals# Line integral of a vector field along a path from \( a \) to \( b \):
\[\int_a^b \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\] Cut the path into small steps dl. At each one take the part of v along the step, then add them all. At each small step along the path, take the part of \( \vec{v} \) that points along the step, and add them all up. The work done by a force is the classic example. Usually the answer depends on which path you take, not just on where you start and finish. Around a closed loop it is written \( \oint \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} \); going round the other way flips the sign.
Two routes between the same two points. For most fields the line integral is different along each. Surface integral, or flux, through a surface \( S \):
\[\int_S \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}}\] Cut the surface into small patches da, each pointing straight out of the surface. Add up v · da over all of them. Here \( \dd{\vec{a}} \) is a small patch of surface, pointing straight out of it. If \( \vec{v} \) were the velocity of flowing water, the flux would be how much water passes through the surface each second. For a closed surface (like a balloon) \( \dd{\vec{a}} \) points outward by convention. For an open surface (like a sheet) you choose a direction to go round its edge, and the right-hand rule then picks the side. Usually the answer depends on the surface itself, not just its edge.
Which way da points. Open surface: curl the fingers of your right hand round the rim, and your thumb gives da. Closed surface: da points outward. Volume integral:
\[\int_V t \dd{\tau}, \qquad \dd{\tau} = \dd{x}\dd{y}\dd{z}\] For example, if \( t \) is a density, this adds up the total amount inside \( V \).
A region V to integrate over: the wedge 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 − x, 0 ≤ z ≤ 3. The fundamental theorems# Each derivative from §1.2 has its own theorem, and all three say the same thing:
Adding up a derivative over a region gives the same answer as looking at the function on the region's boundary.
This is just the fundamental theorem of calculus you already know, \( \int_a^b (df/dx)\dd{x} = f(b) - f(a) \), carried into three dimensions.
The one-dimensional version. The small rises df between a and b add up to f(b) − f(a). Only the two ends matter. Gradient theorem. The boundary of a path is its two endpoints:
\[\int_a^b (\grad t) \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = t(b) - t(a)\] Two consequences: the line integral of a gradient is the same for every path between the same two points, and it is zero around any closed loop. (Walking round a hill and back to your start, your total change in height is zero.)
On a hill, every path from a to b climbs the same total height, t(b) − t(a). Divergence theorem (Gauss's theorem). The boundary of a volume is the closed surface around it:
\[\int_V (\div{\vec{v}}) \dd{\tau} = \oint_S \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}}\] In words: all the “sources” inside the volume, added up, equal the total flow out through the surface.
Curl theorem (Stokes' theorem). The boundary of a surface is its rim:
\[\int_S (\curl{\vec{v}}) \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = \oint_P \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\] In words: all the little swirls on the surface, added up, equal the circulation around its edge. Consequences: the flux of a curl depends only on the rim, so any two surfaces with the same rim give the same answer; and over a closed surface, which has no rim, it is zero.
Why the divergence and curl theorems work: cut the region into tiny cubes. For each cube, divergence × volume is the net flow out through its six faces. Where two cubes touch, what flows out of one flows into the other, so these cancel. Only the faces on the outside surface are left. The curl theorem works the same way with tiny loops on a surface: shared edges cancel and only the outer rim is left.
Why Stokes' theorem works. Where two little squares touch, their circulations run opposite ways and cancel. Only the outer rim is left. These theorems let you switch Gauss's law and Ampère's law between integral form and differential form. You will use them in almost every chapter.
Integration by parts# Combine the product rule \( \div{(f\vec{A})} = f(\div{\vec{A}}) + \vec{A} \cdot (\grad f) \) with the divergence theorem:
\[\int_V f (\div{\vec{A}}) \dd{\tau} = - \int_V \vec{A} \cdot (\grad f) \dd{\tau} + \oint_S f \vec{A} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}}\] This moves the derivative from one factor to the other, at the price of a minus sign and a surface term. If you integrate over all space and the fields die away fast enough far out, the surface term is zero. This trick comes up again and again later.
Example# Compute the flux of the point-charge field \( \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\vu{r} \) through a sphere of radius \( R \) centred on the charge. Determine whether the result depends on \( R \), or on the sphere being spherical.
Solution triple-click to reveal On the sphere, \( \vec{E} \) and \( \dd{\vec{a}} \) both point radially outward, so the dot product is just the product of their sizes. Also \( |\vec{E}| \) is the same everywhere on the sphere, so it comes out of the integral:
\[\oint \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{R^2} \oint \dd{a} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{R^2}\left( 4\pi R^2 \right) = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}\] The \( R^2 \) cancels, so the flux does not depend on the radius.
It doesn't depend on the shape either. Think of a narrow cone coming out of the charge. Further out, the field is weaker by \( 1/r^2 \), but the cone's cross-section is bigger by \( r^2 \). The two cancel, so the flux through the cone is the same wherever you cut it. Any closed surface around the charge is cut by every cone exactly once, so it always gets the full \( q/\epsilon_0 \).
If the charge is outside the surface, the flux is zero: each cone goes in through one part of the surface and out through another, and the two cancel.
This “size and shape don't matter” result is Gauss's law (§2.2).
Example# Verify the divergence theorem for \( \vec{v} = xy,\vu{x} + 2yz,\vu{y} + 3zx,\vu{z} \) over the cube of side 2 occupying the first octant with one corner at the origin.
The six faces of the cube and their outward normals. Dashed arrows point away from you. Solution triple-click to reveal Volume side. The divergence is
\[\div{\vec{v}} = y + 2z + 3x\] Integrate over the cube, with each variable from 0 to 2. The three terms all have the same form, so they give the same integral apart from their coefficients. The first one is
\[\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^2 y \dd{x}\dd{y}\dd{z} = (2)(2)\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^2 = 4 \cdot 2 = 8\] so the three terms give \( 8 \), \( 2(8) = 16 \) and \( 3(8) = 24 \), a total of
\[\int_V (\div{\vec{v}}) \dd{\tau} = 48\] Surface side. The cube has six faces. The three faces through the origin give nothing: on \( x=0 \), for instance, the outward normal is \( -\vu{x} \) but \( v_x = xy = 0 \) there. The same happens on \( y = 0 \) and \( z = 0 \).
On the face \( x = 2 \), \( \dd{\vec{a}} = \dd{y}\dd{z},\vu{x} \) and \( v_x = 2y \):
\[\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^2 2y \dd{y}\dd{z} = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8\] On \( y = 2 \), \( v_y = 4z \): \( \int_0^2!!\int_0^2 4z \dd{x}\dd{z} = 16 \).
On \( z = 2 \), \( v_z = 6x \): \( \int_0^2!!\int_0^2 6x \dd{x}\dd{y} = 24 \).
Adding all six faces: \( 0 + 0 + 0 + 8 + 16 + 24 = 48 \), the same as the volume integral. ✓
Full derivation: §1.3.

title: (1.4) Curvilinear Coordinates
content:
1.4 Curvilinear Coordinates# Choosing coordinates that match the shape of the problem saves a lot of work. A charged ball is a nightmare in \( x, y, z \) and easy in spherical coordinates. Two systems cover almost everything in this course.
Spherical coordinates# \( (r, \theta, \phi) \):
\( r \) is the distance from the origin (\( r \geq 0 \)); \( \theta \) is the angle down from the \( z \)-axis, like latitude measured from the North Pole (\( 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \)); \( \phi \) is the angle round from the \( x \)-axis, like longitude (\( 0 \leq \phi < 2\pi \)). \[x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi, \qquad y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = r\cos\theta\] Spherical coordinates of the point P, and the three unit vectors at P. r-hat points away from the origin, θ-hat points south, φ-hat points east. The three unit vectors are mutually perpendicular and right-handed, \( \vu{r} \cross \vu{\theta} = \vu{\phi} \). In Cartesian terms,
\[\vu{r} = \sin\theta\cos\phi\,\vu{x} + \sin\theta\sin\phi\,\vu{y} + \cos\theta\,\vu{z}\] A small step, and a small volume, are
\[\dd{\vec{l}} = \dd{r}\,\vu{r} + r\dd{\theta}\,\vu{\theta} + r\sin\theta \dd{\phi}\,\vu{\phi}\] \[\dd{\tau} = r^2 \sin\theta \dd{r}\dd{\theta}\dd{\phi}\] On a sphere of radius \( R \), a small patch of area is \( \dd{a} = R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} \). The angular part alone adds up to \( \int \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} = 4\pi \) (the “total solid angle”).
A small patch on a sphere, between two lines of latitude and two of longitude. It points straight out from the centre. Cylindrical coordinates# \( (s, \phi, z) \), where \( s \) is the distance from the \( z \)-axis, \( \phi \) is the same angle as above, and \( z \) is the usual height.
\[x = s\cos\phi, \qquad y = s\sin\phi, \qquad z = z\] Cylindrical coordinates of P. s is the distance from the z-axis, not from the origin. \[\dd{\vec{l}} = \dd{s}\,\vu{s} + s\dd{\phi}\,\vu{\phi} + \dd{z}\,\vu{z}, \qquad \dd{\tau} = s \dd{s}\dd{\phi}\dd{z}\] Griffiths uses \( s \) for distance from the \( z \)-axis and keeps \( r \) for distance from the origin. Other books use \( \rho \) or \( r \) for \( s \). They are different: \( s = r\sin\theta \). Mixing them up is a common mistake when comparing formulas from different books.
Where the extra factors come from# Angles are not lengths. That one fact explains every extra factor above:
changing \( r \) by \( \dd{r} \) moves you a distance \( \dd{r} \); changing \( \theta \) by \( \dd{\theta} \) moves you along an arc of length \( r\dd{\theta} \) (a bigger distance the further you are from the origin); changing \( \phi \) by \( \dd{\phi} \) moves you \( r\sin\theta \dd{\phi} \), because the circles of constant \( \theta \) shrink towards the poles (lines of longitude get closer together near the North Pole). The three small steps. The φ step runs round a circle of latitude, whose radius is r sin θ, not r. Multiply the three lengths to get the volume element.
The same factors show up inside the derivatives. In spherical coordinates,
\[\grad t = \pdv{t}{r}\vu{r} + \frac{1}{r}\pdv{t}{\theta}\vu{\theta} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\pdv{t}{\phi}\vu{\phi}\] \[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}\left( r^2 v_r \right) + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\pdv{}{\theta}\left( \sin\theta\, v_\theta \right) + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\pdv{v_\phi}{\phi}\] and in cylindrical coordinates,
\[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{s}\pdv{}{s}\left( s v_s \right) + \frac{1}{s}\pdv{v_\phi}{\phi} + \pdv{v_z}{z}\] You don't need to memorise these. The full list, including curl and Laplacian, is inside the front cover of Griffiths.
Unit vectors that change direction# \( \vu{x}, \vu{y}, \vu{z} \) point the same way everywhere. \( \vu{r}, \vu{\theta}, \vu{\phi} \) do not: \( \vu{r} \) points “outward”, which is a different direction at every point. This has two consequences:
r-hat points away from the origin, so it points a different way at every point. At A it is +y-hat; at B it is −y-hat. You cannot pull them outside an integral. To integrate a vector, first write it in \( \vu{x}, \vu{y}, \vu{z} \) components. When you differentiate, the unit vectors change too. That is where the extra terms in the formulas above come from. Example# Compute the volume of a sphere of radius \( R \), and the surface area of a hemisphere of the same radius, by direct integration.
Solution triple-click to reveal Volume. Write out the volume element in full:
\[V = \int_0^R \!\! \int_0^\pi \!\! \int_0^{2\pi} r^2 \sin\theta \dd{\phi} \dd{\theta} \dd{r}\] The three integrals are independent:
\[\int_0^{2\pi}\!\dd{\phi} = 2\pi, \qquad \int_0^\pi\!\sin\theta \dd{\theta} = 2, \qquad \int_0^R\! r^2 \dd{r} = \frac{R^3}{3}\] so \( V = 2\pi \cdot 2 \cdot R^3/3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \). The angles together give \( 4\pi \), the total solid angle.
Hemisphere area. On the surface, \( r = R \) is fixed, so \( \dd{a} = R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} \). For the top half, \( \theta \) runs from \( 0 \) to \( \pi/2 \):
\[A = R^2 \int_0^{2\pi} \!\! \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\theta \dd{\theta} \dd{\phi} = R^2 (2\pi)(1) = 2\pi R^2\] The \( \theta \) integral is now 1 instead of 2, so you get half the area of the whole sphere, as expected.
Example# Verify the divergence theorem for \( \vec{v} = r^2 \vu{r} \) over a sphere of radius \( R \) centred on the origin.
Solution triple-click to reveal Volume side. The field only has an \( r \) component, so
\[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}\left( r^2 \cdot r^2 \right) = \frac{1}{r^2}\left( 4r^3 \right) = 4r\] Integrate over the ball:
\[\int (\div{\vec{v}}) \dd{\tau} = \int_0^R (4r)\, r^2 \dd{r} \int \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} = 4\frac{R^4}{4}(4\pi) = 4\pi R^4\] Surface side. On the sphere, \( \dd{\vec{a}} = R^2 \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi},\vu{r} \) and \( \vec{v} = R^2\vu{r} \), so the dot product is \( R^4 \sin\theta \):
\[\oint \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = R^4 \int \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} = 4\pi R^4\] The two sides agree. ✓ It was quick only because the coordinates suit the shape; in \( x, y, z \) the same check takes far more work.
Full derivation: §1.4.

title: (1.5) The Dirac Delta Function
content:
1.5 The Dirac Delta Function# A puzzle: the divergence of \( \vu{r}/r^2 \)# The field \( \vec{v} = \vu{r}/r^2 \) (the shape of a point charge's field) causes a problem. Its divergence, worked out in spherical coordinates, is
\[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}\left( r^2 \cdot \frac{1}{r^2} \right) = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}(1) = 0\] That is zero everywhere the formula makes sense. But the flux through a sphere of radius \( R \) around the origin is
\[\oint \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = \int \left( \frac{1}{R^2}\vu{r} \right) \cdot \left( R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi}\,\vu{r} \right) = 4\pi\] for any \( R \). The divergence theorem says the volume integral of \( \div{\vec{v}} \) must also be \( 4\pi \). How can adding up zeros give \( 4\pi \)?
The field r-hat / r² gets weaker further out, but the spheres get bigger at the same rate. So the flux through every sphere is 4π. The answer: the divergence is not zero at the origin, where the formula breaks down (you'd be dividing by zero). All of the \( 4\pi \) is packed into that one point. No ordinary function is zero everywhere except one point and still has a non-zero integral, so we need a new kind of object.
Definition# \[\delta(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \neq 0 \\ \infty, & x = 0 \end{cases} \qquad \text{with} \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x) \dd{x} = 1\] The delta function: zero everywhere except at 0, where it is an infinitely tall, thin spike with area 1. Think of it as an infinitely tall, infinitely thin spike with area exactly 1. It isn't a true function; it only makes sense inside an integral. You can picture it as the limit of a tall narrow pulse (a rectangle, triangle or Gaussian) with area 1, made narrower and taller without end. The shape of the pulse doesn't matter; only where the spike is and its area of 1 survive.
Narrower and taller pulses, all with area 1. In the limit they all become δ(x). Properties# The key property, from which the rest follow, is the sifting property:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, \delta(x - a)\, \dd{x} = f(a)\] The spike is zero everywhere except \( x = a \), so only the value of \( f \) there matters. That value is a constant, comes outside, and the spike's area of 1 is left. So the delta function “picks out” \( f(a) \). If \( a \) is outside the limits of integration, the answer is zero.
Multiply f(x) by a spike at a and integrate: only the value f(a) survives. Other useful rules:
\[f(x)\delta(x-a) = f(a)\delta(x-a), \qquad \delta(-x) = \delta(x), \qquad \delta(kx) = \frac{1}{|k|}\delta(x)\] The last one comes from substituting \( u = kx \) in the integral. The delta function is also the derivative of the step function (0 for \( x<0 \), 1 for \( x>0 \)): \( \dd{\theta}/\dd{x} = \delta(x) \). The step jumps by 1 at a single point, so its slope is a spike of area 1 there.
When is an equation involving \( \delta \) true? When both sides give the same answer inside any integral. That is the only sense in which delta-function identities hold.
Three dimensions# \[\delta^3(\vec{r}) = \delta(x)\delta(y)\delta(z), \qquad \int_{\text{all space}} f(\vec{r})\, \delta^3(\vec{r} - \vec{a})\, \dd{\tau} = f(\vec{a})\] with \( \int \delta^3(\vec{r}) \dd{\tau} = 1 \). This solves the puzzle we started with:
\[\div{\left( \frac{\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2} \right)} = 4\pi \delta^3(\vec{\gr})\] Zero divergence everywhere except the point, and a total of \( 4\pi \) at the point. This is what lets Gauss's law be written in differential form (§2.2). An equivalent statement is
\[\laplacian \left( \frac{1}{\gr} \right) = -4\pi\delta^3(\vec{\gr})\] which you will meet with Poisson's equation in §2.3.
Point charges as densities# A point charge \( q \) at \( \vec{r'} \) can be written as a charge density:
\[\rho(\vec{r}) = q\, \delta^3(\vec{r} - \vec{r'})\] So every formula written for spread-out charge also works for point charges. There is no need to treat the two cases separately.
Example# Evaluate \( \int_0^5 (x^3 + 2x), \delta(x - 2), \dd{x} \) and \( \int_0^5 (x^3 + 2x), \delta(x - 7), \dd{x} \).
Solution triple-click to reveal In the first, the spike is at \( x = 2 \), which is inside the limits. The sifting property applies, so just put \( x = 2 \) into the rest:
\[\int_0^5 (x^3 + 2x)\, \delta(x - 2)\, \dd{x} = (2)^3 + 2(2) = 12\] In the second, the spike is at \( x = 7 \), outside the limits. Everywhere we actually integrate, the integrand is zero, so
\[\int_0^5 (x^3 + 2x)\, \delta(x - 7)\, \dd{x} = 0\] Always check whether the spike lies inside the limits before using the sifting property.
Example# Evaluate \( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cos(x), \delta(3x - \pi), \dd{x} \).
Solution triple-click to reveal There is a 3 in front of \( x \), so use the scaling rule before sifting. Take the 3 out as a factor:
\[\delta(3x - \pi) = \delta\!\left( 3\left( x - \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{3}\,\delta\!\left( x - \frac{\pi}{3} \right)\] Now you can see the spike is at \( x = \pi/3 \), with a factor \( 1/3 \) in front:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cos(x)\, \delta(3x - \pi)\, \dd{x} = \frac{1}{3}\cos\!\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{6}\] The common mistake is to forget the \( 1/|k| \). Here is why it's there: as \( x \) changes, \( 3x \) sweeps past the spike three times faster, so the spike is three times narrower in \( x \) but no taller. Its area in \( x \) is therefore only \( 1/3 \).
Full derivation: §1.5.

title: (1.6) The Theory of Vector Fields
content:
1.6 The Theory of Vector Fields# The Helmholtz theorem# If you know a vector field's divergence and its curl everywhere, you know the field — as long as it dies away fast enough far from its sources.
This explains the shape of the whole subject. Maxwell's equations don't tell you \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) directly. They tell you the divergence and the curl of each. Two fields, each needing a divergence and a curl: that is why there are four equations.
In detail: if \( \div{\vec{F}} = D \) and \( \curl{\vec{F}} = \vec{C} \) (with \( \div{\vec{C}} = 0 \), which must be true since the divergence of a curl is always zero), then
\[\vec{F} = -\grad U + \curl{\vec{W}}\] with
\[U(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int \frac{D(\vec{r'})}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}, \qquad \vec{W}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{C}(\vec{r'})}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] So any field splits into two pieces: one that only spreads (all the divergence, no curl) and one that only swirls (all the curl, no divergence).
Curl-less fields# For a field \( \vec{F} \) in a region with no holes in it, these four statements all say the same thing. Prove any one and you get the other three:
\( \curl{\vec{F}} = \vec{0} \) everywhere \( \vec{F} = -\grad V \) for some scalar potential \( V \) \( \int \vec{F} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} \) is the same for every path between two given points \( \oint \vec{F} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \) around every closed loop Such fields are called conservative (or irrotational). Gravity near the Earth is an example: the work done lifting a mass depends only on the change in height, not the route.
Why the “no holes” condition? If the region has a hole in it where the curl is not zero (a wire carrying current through the middle, say), a loop around the hole can give a non-zero answer even though the curl is zero everywhere along the loop itself.
Divergence-less fields# Likewise, these all say the same thing:
\( \div{\vec{F}} = 0 \) everywhere \( \vec{F} = \curl{\vec{A}} \) for some vector potential \( \vec{A} \) \( \oint \vec{F} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = 0 \) for every closed surface \( \int \vec{F} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} \) depends only on the boundary line of the surface Such fields are called solenoidal. Whatever flows into any closed surface also flows out.
What this means for the rest of the course# Field Condition Potential Chapters \( \vec{E} \), electrostatic \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) scalar \( V \) 2-4 \( \vec{B} \), always \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) vector \( \vec{A} \) 5-6 \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) is only true when charges are not moving. Once fields change with time, it fails (that is Faraday's law, Chapter 7), and \( V \) alone is no longer enough. The general case needs both \( V \) and \( \vec{A} \) together (Chapter 10).
\( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \), on the other hand, is always true: it says there are no magnetic monopoles (no isolated north or south poles). So the vector potential can always be used.
Potentials are not unique# You can add a constant to \( V \) and \( \grad V \) doesn't change. You can add the gradient of any function to \( \vec{A} \) and \( \curl{\vec{A}} \) doesn't change (because the curl of a gradient is zero). So only differences in potential mean anything physically, and you have to choose where \( V = 0 \). The usual choice is \( V \to 0 \) at infinity.
This freedom is called gauge freedom. Later (Chapter 10) it becomes useful: a clever choice makes the equations for \( V \) and \( \vec{A} \) separate.
Example# Determine whether \( \vec{F} = y\vu{x} + x\vu{y} \) can be written as the gradient of a scalar. If so, construct that scalar.
Solution triple-click to reveal Check the curl first: zero curl is exactly the condition needed. The field lies in the \( xy \) plane and doesn't depend on \( z \), so only one component is left:
\[\curl{\vec{F}} = \left( \pdv{F_y}{x} - \pdv{F_x}{y} \right)\vu{z} = (1 - 1)\vu{z} = \vec{0}\] So a potential exists. To find it, use the maths convention \( \vec{F} = \grad V \) (no minus sign). The \( x \) component says \( \pdv{V}{x} = y \). Integrate with respect to \( x \):
\[V = xy + g(y)\] The “constant” of integration \( g(y) \) can be any function of \( y \), because it disappears when you differentiate with respect to \( x \). Now use the \( y \) component:
\[\pdv{V}{y} = x + g'(y) = F_y = x\] so \( g'(y) = 0 \), meaning \( g \) is just a constant. Therefore
\[V = xy + \text{constant}\] The leftover constant is the non-uniqueness described above. It doesn't affect the field.
Example# Show that \( \vec{F} = yz,\vu{x} + zx,\vu{y} + xy,\vu{z} \) is both curl-less and divergence-less, and comment on what this implies.
Solution triple-click to reveal Divergence. Each term is differentiated by the one variable it doesn't contain:
\[\div{\vec{F}} = \pdv{}{x}(yz) + \pdv{}{y}(zx) + \pdv{}{z}(xy) = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\] Curl. The \( x \) component is
\[(\curl{\vec{F}})_x = \pdv{}{y}(xy) - \pdv{}{z}(zx) = x - x = 0\] The field looks the same if you cycle \( x \to y \to z \to x \), so the \( y \) and \( z \) components are zero too: \( \curl{\vec{F}} = \vec{0} \).
Since the curl is zero, there is a scalar potential. By inspection \( V = xyz \), because \( \grad(xyz) = yz,\vu{x} + zx,\vu{y} + xy,\vu{z} \). Since the divergence is zero, there is also a vector potential.
Put the two together: \( \laplacian V = \div{(\grad V)} = 0 \). So the potential obeys Laplace's equation. Fields with zero curl and zero divergence are exactly those whose potential satisfies Laplace's equation, the subject of Chapter 3.
Full derivation: §1.6.

title: (2.1) The Electric Field
content:
2.1 The Electric Field# The basic question# Electrodynamics asks one question: given some charges (the source charges), what force do they exert on another charge \( Q \) (the test charge)? The answer is given using fields. The source charges don't reach out and push \( Q \) directly. Instead they set up an electric field filling all of space, and \( Q \) feels whatever field there is at its own position.
The source charges make the field; the test charge Q feels it. The separation vector runs from a source charge to Q. Coulomb's law# The force on \( Q \) from a single point charge \( q \), both at rest, is
\[\vec{F} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{qQ}{\gr^2}\vu{\gr}\] where \( \gr \) is the separation vector from \( q \) to \( Q \), and
\[\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \frac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\] is the permittivity of free space. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and the force acts along the line joining them. It gets weaker as \( 1/\gr^2 \): twice as far away, a quarter of the force.
Superposition# With several source charges, work out the force from each one on its own and add them as vectors. One charge being there doesn't change the force from another. This is called the principle of superposition. It isn't obviously true (many forces in nature don't work this way), but it holds exactly in classical electromagnetism, and it is what makes the subject solvable.
Two equal charges. Each makes its own field at P; adding them as vectors, the sideways parts cancel and the total points straight up. The electric field# Divide out the test charge:
\[\vec{E}(\vec{r}) \equiv \frac{\vec{F}}{Q} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{q_i}{\gr_i^2}\vu{\gr}_i\] so \( \vec{F} = Q\vec{E} \). The field depends only on position, and exists at every point whether or not a test charge is there. It is the force per unit charge: put a charge \( Q \) at that point and it feels \( Q\vec{E} \). The units are newtons per coulomb, which is the same as volts per metre.
Is the field “real”, or just a handy way of doing the sums? Electrostatics can't tell. Later chapters settle it: fields carry energy and momentum (Chapter 8), and radiation carries them away from their source for good (Chapter 11).
Continuous distributions# When charge is spread out smoothly, the sum becomes an integral. There are three cases:
Distribution Density Small piece of charge line (e.g. a wire) \( \lambda \) (C/m) \( \dd{q} = \lambda \dd{l'} \) surface (e.g. a sheet) \( \sigma \) (C/m²) \( \dd{q} = \sigma \dd{a'} \) volume (e.g. a ball) \( \rho \) (C/m³) \( \dd{q} = \rho \dd{\tau'} \) Charge spread along a line, over a surface, or through a volume. Cut it into small pieces dq and add up the field of each. The volume version (the others are special cases of it) is
\[\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'})}{\gr^2}\vu{\gr}\, \dd{\tau'}\] \( \vu{\gr} \) points a different way for each piece of charge, so it can't come outside the integral. In practice, work out the \( x \), \( y \) and \( z \) components separately, and use symmetry to spot which components cancel.
Example# Find the electric field a distance \( z \) above the midpoint of a straight line segment of length \( 2L \) carrying uniform line charge \( \lambda \).
Pieces at +x and −x give fields that tilt opposite ways. Their sideways parts cancel, so the total field is straight up. Solution triple-click to reveal Lay the segment along the \( x \)-axis from \( -L \) to \( +L \). The field point is straight above the middle, at height \( z \). A small piece \( \dd{x} \) at position \( x \) has charge \( \lambda \dd{x} \) and is a distance \( \gr = \sqrt{x^2 + z^2} \) away.
For every piece at \( +x \) there is a matching piece at \( -x \). Their sideways pushes cancel, so only the upward parts are left. Each upward part is the full contribution times \( \cos\theta = z/\sqrt{x^2 + z^2} \):
\[E_z = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{-L}^{L} \frac{\lambda \dd{x}}{x^2 + z^2}\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2+z^2}} = \frac{\lambda z}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{\dd{x}}{(x^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\] The integral is a standard one:
\[\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{\dd{x}}{(x^2+z^2)^{3/2}} = \left[ \frac{x}{z^2\sqrt{x^2+z^2}} \right]_{-L}^{L} = \frac{2L}{z^2\sqrt{L^2+z^2}}\] so
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2\lambda L}{z\sqrt{z^2+L^2}}\vu{z}\] Check the limits. Far away (\( z \gg L \)), the segment should look like a point charge \( Q = 2\lambda L \), and indeed the formula becomes \( Q/4\pi\epsilon_0 z^2 \). For an infinitely long wire (\( L \to \infty \)), it becomes \( \lambda/2\pi\epsilon_0 z \), which falls off as \( 1/z \), more slowly than a point charge's \( 1/z^2 \).
Example# Find the electric field a distance \( z \) above the centre of a circular loop of radius \( R \) carrying uniform line charge \( \lambda \).
Solution triple-click to reveal Every piece of the loop is the same distance \( \gr = \sqrt{R^2 + z^2} \) from the field point, which makes this easy.
By symmetry the sideways parts cancel: each piece has a partner on the opposite side of the loop pushing the other way. The upward part of each contribution has a factor \( \cos\theta = z/\sqrt{R^2+z^2} \). Both \( \gr \) and \( \cos\theta \) are the same all round the loop, so they come outside the integral, which then just adds up the charge:
\[E_z = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\cos\theta}{\gr^2}\int \lambda \dd{l'} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{z}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\left( \lambda \, 2\pi R \right)\] With total charge \( Q = 2\pi R\lambda \),
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Qz}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\vu{z}\] Check. At the centre (\( z = 0 \)) the field is zero, because every push is cancelled by an opposite one. Far away (\( z \gg R \)) it becomes \( Q/4\pi\epsilon_0 z^2 \), the field of a point charge, as it should.
Full derivation: §2.1.

title: (2.2) Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic Fields
content:
2.2 Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic Fields# The Helmholtz theorem (§1.6) says a field is fixed once you know its divergence and its curl. This section finds both for \( \vec{E} \).
Field lines and flux# Field lines are drawn so that at every point they run along \( \vec{E} \), and they are packed closer together where the field is stronger. They start on positive charges and end on negative ones. They never cross, because the field can only point one way at any point.
Two ways to draw the same field. Arrows: longer means stronger. Field lines: closer together means stronger. Left: lines leave the positive charge and end on the negative one. Right: two positive charges push their lines apart. The flux through a surface,
\[\Phi_E = \int_S \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}}\] counts how many field lines pass through it (lines going out count positive, lines coming in count negative). For a point charge at the centre of a sphere of radius \( r \),
\[\oint \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = \int \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\left( r^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} \right) = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}\] The radius cancels. That makes sense: every field line leaving the charge must cross the sphere, however big it is. The same is true for any closed surface of any shape around the charge. And by superposition it works for any number of charges.
The flux through a patch counts the field lines that pass through it. Every field line leaving the charge crosses the closed surface, whatever its shape, so the flux is always the charge inside over epsilon-zero. Gauss's law# \[\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\epsilon_0}\] The total flux out of any closed surface equals the charge inside, divided by \( \epsilon_0 \). Charges outside don't count: their field lines go in one side and out the other. Using the divergence theorem on the left side, and writing \( Q_{\text{enc}} = \int \rho \dd{\tau} \), gives the differential form:
\[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}\] This is the first of Maxwell's equations. It says field lines spread out from wherever there is charge.
Only charge inside counts. Left: the net flux out is (2q − q)/ε₀. Right: every line from the outside charge that goes in also comes out, so the net flux is zero. Using Gauss's law# Gauss's law is always true, but it only lets you find \( \vec{E} \) easily when symmetry makes \( \vec{E} \) the same size everywhere on a surface and pointing straight through it. Then \( \oint \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} \) is just \( E \times \text{area} \). This works for three shapes:
Spherical symmetry: use a sphere with the same centre Cylindrical symmetry: use a cylinder with the same axis Plane symmetry: use a flat “pillbox” poking through the plane Pick the Gaussian surface to match the symmetry, so E is the same size all over it and points straight through it. The standard results:
\[\vec{E}_{\text{sphere}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\vu{r}, \qquad \vec{E}_{\text{line}} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 s}\vu{s}, \qquad \vec{E}_{\text{plane}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\vu{n}\] Notice that the field of an infinite plane doesn't get weaker with distance.
The curl of E# Take a single point charge at the origin and work out the line integral between two points. The field is radial, so \( \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = E_r \dd{r} \) (only movement towards or away from the charge counts):
\[\int_a^b \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{r_a}^{r_b}\frac{\dd{r}}{r^2} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left( \frac{1}{r_a} - \frac{1}{r_b} \right)\] The answer depends only on the start and end points, not the path. So around any closed loop \( \oint \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \), and by Stokes' theorem
\[\curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0}\] Along any path from a to b, only the steps towards or away from the charge count. So every path gives the same answer. By superposition this holds for any arrangement of charges that are not moving. So static electric fields never swirl. This stops being true once fields change with time (Chapter 7).
Because the curl is zero, §1.6 says \( \vec{E} \) can be written using a scalar potential. That is §2.3.
Example# Find the field inside and outside a solid sphere of radius \( R \) carrying uniform volume charge density \( \rho \).
Solution triple-click to reveal The charge is spherically symmetric, so the field points radially and its size depends only on \( r \). Use a sphere of radius \( r \) with the same centre as the Gaussian surface. On it, \( \vec{E} \) points straight out and has the same size everywhere, so
\[\oint \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} = E(r)\, 4\pi r^2 = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\epsilon_0}\] Outside (\( r > R \)), the surface encloses all the charge, \( Q_{\text{enc}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho \), so
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2}\vu{r}\] exactly as if all the charge were a point at the centre.
Inside (\( r < R \)), only the charge within radius \( r \) is enclosed, \( Q_{\text{enc}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho \), so
\[E(r)\,4\pi r^2 = \frac{4\pi r^3 \rho}{3\epsilon_0} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{E} = \frac{\rho}{3\epsilon_0} r\,\vu{r}\] So the field rises steadily from zero at the centre, is strongest at the surface, and then falls off as \( 1/r^2 \) outside. The two formulas give the same value at \( r = R \), as they must, since there's no extra charge sitting on the surface.
Example# Two infinite parallel planes carry uniform surface charge densities \( +\sigma \) and \( -\sigma \). Find the field in all three regions.
In each region, the field of the positive plane (top row) and the negative plane (bottom row). They add between the plates and cancel outside. Solution triple-click to reveal Each plane on its own makes a field of size \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), the same at any distance. It points away from the positive plane and towards the negative one. Now add the two.
Between the planes, both fields point from the positive plane towards the negative one, so they add:
\[E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} + \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\] Outside, on either side, the positive plane's field points away from it and the negative plane's field points towards it. They are equal and opposite, so
\[E = 0\] All the field is trapped between the plates. This is how a parallel-plate capacitor works (§2.5). It relies on the planes being infinite; near the edges of real plates some field leaks out.
Full derivation: §2.2.

title: (2.3) Electric Potential
content:
2.3 Electric Potential# Definition# Since \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \), the line integral of \( \vec{E} \) doesn't depend on the path, and so we can define a scalar potential:
\[V(\vec{r}) \equiv -\int_{\mathcal{O}}^{\vec{r}} \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\] Here \( \mathcal{O} \) is a reference point where \( V = 0 \), usually taken at infinity. The difference in potential between two points,
\[V(\vec{b}) - V(\vec{a}) = -\int_{\vec{a}}^{\vec{b}} \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\] doesn't depend on where you put the reference point. Going the other way, the gradient theorem gives
\[\vec{E} = -\grad V\] So the field points “downhill” in potential, in the direction \( V \) drops fastest. The minus sign means a positive charge moves from high potential to low, just as a ball rolls downhill. The unit is the volt: one joule per coulomb.
Because the curl of E is zero, every path from a to b gives the same line integral. That is what lets us define V. Potential is not the same as potential energy. Potential energy is potential times charge. \( V \) exists at every point, whether or not a charge is there.
Why the potential is useful# \( \vec{E} \) needs three functions (its three components). \( V \) needs only one, yet it carries all the same information, because you get \( \vec{E} \) by differentiating. This is possible because the three components of \( \vec{E} \) are not independent: \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) ties them together.
Potentials also add, and since they are just numbers, you add them as plain numbers rather than as vectors.
Poisson's and Laplace's equations# Put \( \vec{E} = -\grad V \) into Gauss's law:
\[\div{\vec{E}} = \div{(-\grad V)} = -\laplacian V = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}\] This is Poisson's equation:
\[\laplacian V = -\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}\] Where there is no charge it becomes Laplace's equation, \( \laplacian V = 0 \), the subject of Chapter 3.
\( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) is automatically true for any \( \vec{E} \) made from a potential. So all of electrostatics boils down to this one equation for one unknown function.
Potential of a localized distribution# For a point charge at the origin, integrating in from infinity gives \( V = q/4\pi\epsilon_0 r \). Adding up many charges,
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'})}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] The same idea three times: add up charge divided by distance. No directions to worry about. This integral is much easier than the one for \( \vec{E} \): there is no direction \( \vu{\gr} \) to keep track of, and the bottom has \( \gr \) rather than \( \gr^2 \). So the usual way to find a field is find \( V \) first, then differentiate.
The whole of electrostatics in one picture. Each arrow is a formula that takes you from one quantity to another. Boundary conditions# What happens to the field as you cross a sheet of charge \( \sigma \)?
Gauss's law, applied to a thin pillbox through the sheet, shows the part of \( \vec{E} \) perpendicular to the sheet jumps. \( \oint \vec{E}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \), applied to a thin loop through the sheet, shows the part parallel to the sheet doesn't change. \[E_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - E_{\text{below}}^{\perp} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \vec{E}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} = \vec{E}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel}\] or in one line, \( \vec{E}{\text{above}} - \vec{E}{\text{below}} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\vu{n} \).
Left: the pillbox shows the part of E across the sheet jumps. Middle: the thin loop shows the part along the sheet does not. Right: V is the same just above and just below. The potential itself does not jump. \( \vec{E} \) stays finite, so integrating it across a sheet of zero thickness gives zero. But the slope of \( V \) does jump:
\[\pdv{V_{\text{above}}}{n} - \pdv{V_{\text{below}}}{n} = -\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\] Example# Find the potential inside and outside a spherical shell of radius \( R \) carrying uniform surface charge \( \sigma \), with total charge \( q \).
Solution triple-click to reveal First the field, from Gauss's law. Outside, the shell acts like a point charge. Inside, a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \).
Outside (\( r > R \)), integrate in from infinity:
\[V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r'^2}\dd{r'} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}\] Inside (\( r < R \)), the path from infinity has two parts. From \( \infty \) to \( R \) it's the same as above. From \( R \) inward the field is zero, so that part adds nothing:
\[V(r) = -\int_\infty^R \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r'^2}\dd{r'} - \int_R^r 0 \dd{r'} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{R}\] So inside, the potential is a constant, equal to its value at the surface. It is not zero. Zero field means the potential is flat, not that it is zero. (Think of a flat plateau high on a mountain: no slope, but plenty of height.) Mixing these up is a very common mistake.
The potential is continuous at \( r = R \), as it must be, while its slope jumps there because of the surface charge.
Example# Find the potential a distance \( z \) above the centre of a uniformly charged disc of radius \( R \) and surface charge \( \sigma \), then obtain the field.
Solution triple-click to reveal Cut the disc into thin rings of radius \( s \) and width \( \dd{s} \). Each ring has charge \( \dd{q} = \sigma, 2\pi s \dd{s} \), and every point of it is the same distance \( \gr = \sqrt{s^2 + z^2} \) from the field point. So each ring's potential is simple, and we just add up the rings:
\[V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_0^R \frac{\sigma\, 2\pi s \dd{s}}{\sqrt{s^2+z^2}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\int_0^R \frac{s \dd{s}}{\sqrt{s^2+z^2}}\] Substituting \( u = s^2 + z^2 \) makes this easy:
\[V = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left[ \sqrt{s^2+z^2} \right]_0^R = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left( \sqrt{R^2+z^2} - z \right)\] (for \( z > 0 \)). Now differentiate to get the field:
\[E_z = -\pdv{V}{z} = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left( 1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}} \right)\] Check the limits. For a huge disc (\( R \to \infty \)) this becomes \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), the infinite-plane field. Far away (\( z \gg R \)), expanding the square root gives \( Q/4\pi\epsilon_0 z^2 \) with \( Q = \sigma\pi R^2 \): a point charge.
Finding \( V \) first and then differentiating avoided all the vector components that a direct calculation of \( \vec{E} \) would need.
Full derivation: §2.3.

title: (2.4) Work and Energy in Electrostatics
content:
2.4 Work and Energy in Electrostatics# Work to move a charge# To move a test charge \( Q \) slowly from \( a \) to \( b \), you must push against the electric force. The work you do is
\[W = -Q\int_a^b \vec{E}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = Q\left[ V(b) - V(a) \right]\] and it's the same for every path, because \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \). To bring a charge in from infinity, where \( V(\infty) = 0 \),
\[W = QV(\vec{r})\] This is what potential means: \( V \) at a point is the work needed per coulomb to bring a charge there from far away.
Moving Q from a to b against the field of the source charges costs Q times the change in V. Energy of a group of point charges# Build up a group of charges one at a time. The first is free, since there is nothing yet to push against. Each new one costs work against the charges already there. Add up all the pairs:
\[W = \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{q_i q_j}{\gr_{ij}} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i V(\vec{r}_i)\] Here \( V(\vec{r}_i) \) is the potential at charge \( i \) from all the other charges. The \( \frac{1}{2} \) is there because the double sum counts every pair twice (\( i,j \) and \( j,i \)). The \( j \neq i \) leaves out each charge's interaction with itself, which would be infinite for a point charge.
Build the group one charge at a time. Each new charge costs work against the ones already there; every pair counts once. Energy of a continuous distribution# For spread-out charge the sum becomes an integral:
\[W = \frac{1}{2}\int \rho V \dd{\tau}\] Replace \( \rho \) by \( \epsilon_0 \div{\vec{E}} \), integrate by parts, and use the divergence theorem. The result is an integral over all space:
\[W = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_{\text{all space}} E^2 \dd{\tau}\] (The surface term disappears because far away \( V \) falls as \( 1/r \) and \( E \) as \( 1/r^2 \), faster than the surface area grows.)
The two formulas give the same number, but they tell different stories about where the energy is. The first puts it on the charges. The second puts it in the field, with energy density \( \epsilon_0 E^2/2 \) (joules per cubic metre). In electrostatics it doesn't matter which story you believe. In Chapter 8 it matters a lot: light carries energy through empty space where there are no charges at all, so the energy really is in the field.
Notice that \( E^2 \) is never negative, so the field formula always gives a positive energy. But \( \frac{1}{2}\sum q_i V_i \) is negative for a pair of opposite charges. The difference is the self-energy of the point charges that the sum left out, which is infinite.
Energies don't simply add# Energy depends on \( E^2 \), so if you combine two charge distributions, the total energy is not just the sum of their separate energies:
\[W_{\text{tot}} = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int |\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2|^2 \dd{\tau} = W_1 + W_2 + \epsilon_0\int \vec{E}_1\cdot\vec{E}_2 \dd{\tau}\] The extra cross term is the interaction energy between the two distributions.
Example# Find the energy of a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius \( R \) and total charge \( q \), by both available methods.
Solution triple-click to reveal Method 1: charge × potential. On the shell the potential is \( V = q/4\pi\epsilon_0 R \), the same everywhere, so it comes out of the integral:
\[W = \frac{1}{2}\int \sigma V \dd{a} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}\int \sigma \dd{a} = \frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{R}\] Method 2: the field. Inside the shell \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \); outside, \( E = q/4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2 \). Only the outside contributes:
\[W = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_R^\infty \left( \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \right)^2 4\pi r^2 \dd{r} = \frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\int_R^\infty \frac{\dd{r}}{r^2} = \frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{R}\] Both methods agree. Notice the energy blows up as \( R \to 0 \): squeezing the charge into a point takes infinite energy. That is the infinite self-energy of a point charge, showing up openly.
Example# Find the energy of a solid sphere of radius \( R \) carrying total charge \( q \) distributed uniformly through its volume.
Solution triple-click to reveal Use the field method. This time the field inside is not zero. From §2.2,
\[E_{\text{in}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q r}{R^3} \quad (r<R), \qquad E_{\text{out}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2} \quad (r>R)\] The outside part is exactly the same as for the shell above: \( q^2/8\pi\epsilon_0 R \). The inside adds
\[\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_0^R \left( \frac{qr}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^3} \right)^2 4\pi r^2 \dd{r} = \frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R^6}\int_0^R r^4 \dd{r} = \frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{1}{5R}\] Adding the two,
\[W = \frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R}\left( 1 + \frac{1}{5} \right) = \frac{3}{5}\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{R}\] The solid sphere stores \( 6/5 \) times as much energy as the shell. The extra comes from the field inside the ball, which the shell doesn't have.
Full derivation: §2.4.

title: (2.5) Conductors
content:
2.5 Conductors# Basic properties# A conductor (such as a metal) has charges that are free to move around. Treat the supply as unlimited. Five properties follow, and they all come from the first.
1. \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \) inside. If there were a field inside, it would push the free charges. They would keep moving until their new arrangement cancelled the field. Once everything has settled, no field is left.
Put a conductor in a field and its charges move: minus to one side, plus to the other. Their own field cancels the outside field inside the metal. 2. \( \rho = 0 \) inside. Gauss's law gives \( \rho = \epsilon_0 \div{\vec{E}} = 0 \).
3. Any net charge sits on the surface. There's nowhere else for it to go.
4. The whole conductor is at one potential. With \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \) inside, \( V(b) - V(a) = -\int \vec{E}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \) between any two points in it.
5. Just outside, \( \vec{E} \) is perpendicular to the surface. If it had a part along the surface, that part would push the surface charges along until it was gone.
Just outside a conductor, E points straight out of the surface. Induced charges# Bring a positive charge near an uncharged conductor. Negative charge is pulled to the near side and positive charge pushed to the far side. The conductor is still neutral overall, but its charges have separated. The nearby negative charge is closer than the far positive charge, so the net force is attractive. That's why a charged comb picks up bits of paper.
The near side becomes negative and the far side positive. The near charges are closer, so the pull wins. Put a charge \( q \) inside a hollow in a conductor. Then \( -q \) collects on the hollow's wall and \( +q \) on the outer surface. Why: draw a Gaussian surface inside the metal around the hollow. \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \) there, so the charge enclosed must be zero, and the wall must carry \( -q \) to cancel \( q \).
An empty hollow has zero field inside, whatever is going on outside. So a conductor shields its inside from outside fields. This is the Faraday cage, and it's why your phone loses signal in a lift. It doesn't work the other way round: a charge inside the hollow still produces a field outside (unless the conductor is connected to ground).
Left: a charge q in a hollow pulls −q onto the hollow's wall and leaves +q on the outside. The dashed Gaussian surface lies in the metal, where E = 0. Right: an empty hollow has no field inside. Surface charge and the force on a conductor# Just outside the surface the field points straight out, and (using the boundary condition of §2.3 with zero field inside)
\[\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\vu{n}\] The force per unit area on the surface charge is not simply \( \sigma E \). A patch of charge can't push on itself, and part of that field is its own. The right field to use is the average of the fields just inside (zero) and just outside:
\[\vec{f} = \sigma \vec{E}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\epsilon_0}\vu{n}\] This electrostatic pressure always pulls the surface outward, whatever the sign of the charge. It can also be written \( P = \epsilon_0 E^2 / 2 \).
The patch's own field points away on both sides and can't push the patch. Only the field of all the other charges pushes it. Capacitors# Put \( +Q \) on one conductor and \( -Q \) on another. Double \( Q \) and the field doubles everywhere, so the voltage between them doubles too. So \( V \) is proportional to \( Q \), and the ratio is the capacitance:
\[C \equiv \frac{Q}{V}\] measured in farads. It depends only on the shapes, sizes and spacing of the conductors. Standard results:
\[C_{\text{parallel plate}} = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}, \qquad C_{\text{sphere}} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R, \qquad C_{\text{coaxial}} = \frac{2\pi\epsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}\] Any two conductors with +Q and −Q make a capacitor. Two standard capacitors: a coaxial cable (inner wire radius a, outer tube radius b), and two concentric spherical shells. To charge a capacitor you move charge \( \dd{q} \) across a voltage \( q/C \) that grows as you go. The total work is
\[W = \int_0^Q \frac{q}{C}\dd{q} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{C} = \frac{1}{2}CV^2\] Example# A point charge \( q \) sits at the centre of a spherical conducting shell with inner radius \( a \) and outer radius \( b \), carrying no net charge. Find the field in all regions and the induced surface charges.
Solution triple-click to reveal Region \( r < a \). Only \( q \) is enclosed, so Gauss's law gives
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\vu{r}\] Region \( a < r < b \) (inside the metal): \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \). A Gaussian sphere here must enclose zero charge. The point charge gives \( q \), so the inner surface must carry
\[q_{\text{inner}} = -q, \qquad \sigma_{\text{inner}} = \frac{-q}{4\pi a^2}\] Region \( r > b \). The shell has no net charge, so the outer surface carries \( +q \) to balance the \( -q \) on the inner surface:
\[q_{\text{outer}} = +q, \qquad \sigma_{\text{outer}} = \frac{q}{4\pi b^2}\] The total enclosed is \( q - q + q = q \), so
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\vu{r}\] That's the same as if the shell weren't there. From outside, you can't tell the shell exists. Even if the point charge were off-centre, the inner surface charge would be lopsided, but the outer charge would still spread out evenly, and the outside field would be unchanged.
Example# Find the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area \( A \) and separation \( d \), and the energy stored at potential difference \( V \).
Solution triple-click to reveal Put \( +Q \) on one plate and \( -Q \) on the other, and ignore the edges. The surface charge is \( \sigma = Q/A \). From §2.2 the field between the plates is uniform:
\[E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A}\] The field is constant, so the voltage is just field × distance:
\[V = Ed = \frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0 A}\] So
\[C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}\] It depends only on the geometry, as expected. Bigger plates or a smaller gap give a bigger capacitance. The stored energy is \( W = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \epsilon_0 A V^2 / 2d \).
Check with the field energy (§2.4). The energy density is \( \epsilon_0 E^2/2 \) and the field fills a volume \( Ad \), giving \( \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}(V/d)^2 Ad = \epsilon_0 A V^2/2d \). It agrees. ✓
Full derivation: §2.5.
