title: (3.1) Laplace's Equation
content:
3.1 Laplace's Equation# The problem# To find \( V \) by integrating over the charge, you need to know where the charge is. Usually you don't. On a conductor, the charge moves around in response to everything nearby, so where it ends up is part of the answer, not part of the question.
So instead we solve the differential equation directly. Where there is no charge, Poisson's equation becomes Laplace's equation:
\[\laplacian V = \pdv{^2 V}{x^2} + \pdv{^2 V}{y^2} + \pdv{^2 V}{z^2} = 0\] together with conditions on the boundary (for example, “this conductor is at 10 V”). Solutions of Laplace's equation are called harmonic functions.
One dimension# If \( V \) depends only on \( x \), then \( \dd{^2 V}/\dd{x^2} = 0 \), so
\[V(x) = mx + b\] a straight line, pinned down by the values at the two ends. Even this simple case has two features that carry over to three dimensions:
\( V(x) \) is the average of the values an equal distance either side: \( V(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left[ V(x+a) + V(x-a) \right] \). There are no bumps or dips in the middle. The largest and smallest values are at the ends. In one dimension a solution of Laplace's equation is a straight line. The value at any point is the average of the values an equal distance either side. Three dimensions# Both features survive.
Average value property. The potential at any point equals its average over any sphere centred on that point:
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi R^2}\oint_{\text{sphere}} V \dd{a}\] No bumps or dips. \( V \) takes its highest and lowest values on the boundary, never inside. A peak inside would be higher than everything around it, so higher than its own average, which the property above forbids.
That second fact is Earnshaw's theorem, and it has a real consequence: you cannot trap a charge in a stable position using electrostatic forces alone. A stable trap needs a dip in potential energy, and there are no dips in empty space.
A good picture: a soap film stretched across a bent wire frame. The film takes the smoothest shape that fits the frame, with no bumps of its own. Solutions of Laplace's equation behave the same way.
A soap film on a bent frame. The frame sets the boundary values. The film has no bumps of its own, and the height at the centre of any circle is the average round the circle. Boundary conditions and uniqueness# First uniqueness theorem. If you know \( V \) everywhere on the boundary of a region, there is only one solution of Laplace's equation inside.
Proof idea: suppose there were two solutions, \( V_1 \) and \( V_2 \). Their difference \( V_3 = V_1 - V_2 \) also satisfies Laplace's equation, and it is zero all over the boundary. It can't have a peak or dip inside, so it must be zero everywhere. The two solutions are the same.
The theorem also works for Poisson's equation (with charge inside), and for regions with inner as well as outer boundaries.
First uniqueness theorem: fix V all over the boundary surface S, and there is only one possible V inside. Why this matters: you are allowed to guess. If you find a solution by any method at all (inspection, symmetry, a clever trick like images in §3.2), and it satisfies the equation and the boundary conditions, then it is the answer.
Second uniqueness theorem. In a region surrounded by conductors, with known charge density inside, the field is fixed if you know the total charge on each conductor. You don't need to know their potentials.
Second uniqueness theorem: give the charge density in the region and the total charge on each conductor, and the field is fixed. Four charged pieces (left) are joined by wires in two pairs (middle), so each pair has total charge zero. No charge anywhere meets every condition, so by the theorem that is the answer (right). Example# Show that the average potential over a spherical surface of radius \( R \) due to a point charge \( q \) lying outside the sphere equals the potential at the centre.
A patch \( \dd{a} \) on the sphere, a distance \( \gr \) from the charge. Average \( V \) over all such patches. Solution triple-click to reveal Put the sphere's centre at the origin and the charge on the \( z \)-axis at distance \( z > R \). By the cosine rule, a point on the sphere at angle \( \theta \) is a distance
\[\gr = \sqrt{R^2 + z^2 - 2Rz\cos\theta}\] from the charge. The average over the sphere is
\[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4\pi R^2}\oint \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{\gr}\dd{a} = \frac{q}{16\pi^2\epsilon_0 R^2}\int \frac{R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi}}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2-2Rz\cos\theta}}\] The \( \phi \) integral gives \( 2\pi \). For \( \theta \), substitute \( u = \cos\theta \):
\[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{q}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\dd{u}}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2-2Rzu}} = \frac{q}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\left[ \frac{-\sqrt{R^2+z^2-2Rzu}}{Rz} \right]_{-1}^{1}\] At the limits the square roots are \( |z - R| = z-R \) and \( z+R \):
\[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{q}{8\pi\epsilon_0 Rz}\left[ (z+R) - (z-R) \right] = \frac{q}{8\pi\epsilon_0 Rz}(2R) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{z}\] That is exactly the potential at the centre, a distance \( z \) from the charge. Any charge outside the sphere is a sum of point charges, so the result holds for all of them. This proves the average value property.
Example# A region contains no charge and is bounded by a surface held entirely at potential \( V_0 \). Determine the potential and field inside.
Solution triple-click to reveal Try the simplest guess: \( V = V_0 \) everywhere inside. A constant has all second derivatives zero, so it satisfies Laplace's equation. And it matches the boundary, where \( V = V_0 \).
By the first uniqueness theorem, that guess is the only solution. So \( V = V_0 \) everywhere inside, and
\[\vec{E} = -\grad V = \vec{0}\] This is the shielding result of §2.5 again: an empty hollow inside a conductor has no field, because the conductor's surface is all at one potential. No calculation was needed, just a guess plus the uniqueness theorem. That is typical of how the theorem is used.
Full derivation: §3.1.

title: (3.2) The Method of Images
content:
3.2 The Method of Images# The idea# The uniqueness theorem (§3.1) says any method of finding a solution is fine. If your potential satisfies Poisson's equation in the region you care about, and matches the boundary conditions, it is the right answer.
The method of images uses this. You remove the awkward conductor and replace it with a pretend charge, the image charge, placed where it gives the right boundary condition. The image isn't real. It is a trick that produces the correct potential in the region you care about. It must sit outside that region, so it doesn't change the charge inside.
The classic problem# A point charge \( q \) is a distance \( d \) above a large, flat, grounded (\( V = 0 \)) metal plate lying in the \( xy \) plane. We don't know how the induced charge spreads over the plate, so we can't just integrate.
Instead, forget the plate. Imagine two charges in empty space: \( +q \) at \( z = d \) and \( -q \) at \( z = -d \), like a mirror image. Every point on the plane \( z = 0 \) is equally far from both, so \( V = 0 \) there, just as for the grounded plate. And above the plane the only charge is the real \( +q \). Both conditions of the uniqueness theorem are met, so for \( z > 0 \)
\[V(x,y,z) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[ \frac{q}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-d)^2}} - \frac{q}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z+d)^2}} \right]\] Left: the real problem, where field lines end on the grounded plate. Right: charge plus image. Above the plane the two field patterns are identical. This only holds above the plate. Below it (inside the metal) the field is really zero.
Induced surface charge# Differentiate and use \( \sigma = -\epsilon_0 \pdv{V}{n} \) at the surface:
\[\sigma(x,y) = \frac{-qd}{2\pi (x^2+y^2+d^2)^{3/2}}\] The induced charge is negative and bunched up right under \( q \). Adding it all up gives exactly \( -q \): every field line leaving \( q \) ends on the plate.
Force and energy# The force on \( q \) is the pull from its image:
\[\vec{F} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{(2d)^2}\vu{z}\] So the charge is attracted towards the plate.
But be careful: the energy is not that of the two-charge system. The pretend two-charge setup has field below the plane too; the real setup doesn't. Working out the energy directly from the force gives
\[W = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{4d}\] which is exactly half the two-charge answer. Rule: you can get forces from the image picture, but not energies.
The grounded sphere# A point charge \( q \) is a distance \( a \) from the centre of a grounded metal sphere of radius \( R \) (with \( a > R \)). The image is
\[q' = -\frac{R}{a}q \qquad \text{placed at} \qquad b = \frac{R^2}{a}\] from the centre, on the line towards \( q \). The image is smaller than \( q \) and sits inside the sphere, which is outside the region we care about. The total induced charge on the sphere is \( q' \). If instead the sphere is isolated and uncharged (not grounded), add a second image \( -q' \) at the centre to keep its total charge zero.
Left: the real problem, where field lines end on the grounded sphere. Right: the image \( q' = -(R/a)q \) at \( b = R^2/a \) makes the dashed sphere \( V = 0 \). Example# Verify that the image construction for the grounded sphere places the surface at zero potential.
Solution triple-click to reveal Put the sphere's centre at the origin, \( q \) on the \( z \)-axis at distance \( a \), and the image \( q' = -Rq/a \) at \( b = R^2/a \).
By the cosine rule, a point on the sphere at angle \( \theta \) is these distances from the two charges:
\[\gr = \sqrt{R^2 + a^2 - 2Ra\cos\theta}, \qquad \gr' = \sqrt{R^2 + b^2 - 2Rb\cos\theta}\] Put \( b = R^2/a \) into the second and take out a factor \( R/a \):
\[\gr' = \sqrt{R^2 + \frac{R^4}{a^2} - \frac{2R^3\cos\theta}{a}} = \frac{R}{a}\sqrt{a^2 + R^2 - 2Ra\cos\theta} = \frac{R}{a}\gr\] So at every point on the sphere, the distance to the image is \( R/a \) times the distance to \( q \). The potential is
\[V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left( \frac{q}{\gr} + \frac{q'}{\gr'} \right) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left( \frac{q}{\gr} + \frac{-Rq/a}{(R/a)\gr} \right) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left( \frac{q}{\gr} - \frac{q}{\gr} \right) = 0\] The two terms cancel exactly, for every \( \theta \), so the whole sphere is at zero potential. ✓ The values of \( q' \) and \( b \) are exactly the ones that keep the ratio \( \gr'/\gr \) the same all over the sphere.
Example# A point charge \( q \) is held at distance \( d \) above an infinite grounded plane. Find the work required to remove it to infinity, and reconcile the result with the energy of the equivalent two-charge system.
Solution triple-click to reveal At height \( z \), the image (at \( -z \)) pulls the charge down with force \( q^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 (2z)^2 \). The work needed to pull it from \( d \) out to infinity is
\[W = \int_d^\infty \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{4z^2}\dd{z} = \frac{q^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0}\left[ -\frac{1}{z} \right]_d^\infty = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{4d}\] So the energy of the setup is \( W = -q^2/16\pi\epsilon_0 d \).
Two real charges \( +q \) and \( -q \) a distance \( 2d \) apart would have energy \( -q^2/8\pi\epsilon_0 d \): twice as much.
Why the difference? The energy is stored in the field. With two real charges, the field fills all of space. With the real plate, the field fills only the half above it; below, it's zero. By symmetry that's exactly half the field energy, hence the factor of two.
Another way to see it: with two real charges, pulling them apart moves both charges, and both movements cost work. With the plate, only the real charge is moved by you; the image just follows along for free.
Full derivation: §3.2.

title: (3.S) Green's Functions
content:
3.S Green's Functions# Supplement: beyond Griffiths, but built on him. Read it after §3.1–3.2. It uses Griffiths' SI units and notation throughout (\( \gr \), \( \mathscr{V} \), \( \mathscr{S} \), \( \dd{\tau} \), \( \dd{\vec{a}} \)), and every step points back to the equation in Griffiths it comes from (5th edition numbering). The only new idea is the Green's function \( G \) itself. For further reading: Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, §1.8–1.10, and Zangwill, Modern Electrodynamics, §8.4–8.5. Jackson uses Gaussian units, so his \( G \) is \( 4\pi\epsilon_0 \) times ours.
The idea# You have already met a Green's function without the name. Griffiths Eq. 2.29,
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'})}{\gr}\dd{\tau'},\] builds the potential of any charge out of the potential of a unit point charge, \( 1/4\pi\epsilon_0\gr \). That is the Green's function for empty space. But Eq. 2.29 only works when there are no conductors. With conductors, the induced charge is unknown (the whole problem of Chapter 3).
The uniqueness theorem (Griffiths §3.1.5) says the potential in a region \( \mathscr{V} \) is fixed once you know the charge inside and the potential on the boundary \( \mathscr{S} \). A Green's function turns that into a recipe:
Solve the problem once, for a single unit point charge, with the boundary grounded. That answer is the Green's function \( G \). Every other problem with the same boundary is then just a sum (integral) of these unit answers, exactly as in Eq. 2.29. For planes and spheres, the method of images (Griffiths §3.2) gives you step 1 for free: \( G \) is Eq. 3.9 or Eq. 3.17 with \( q = 1 \).
One dimension# For grounded plates at \( x = 0 \) and \( x = L \), the potential of a sheet of unit surface charge at \( x' \) satisfies Poisson's equation (Eq. 2.24) in one dimension, \( d^2G/dx^2 = -\delta(x - x')/\epsilon_0 \), and vanishes at both plates. With no charge on either side of the sheet, it is a straight line on each side (Eq. 3.6). It is continuous at the sheet, and its slope jumps by \( -1/\epsilon_0 \) there (Eq. 2.36 with \( \sigma = 1 \)):
\[G(x, x') = \frac{x_<\,(L - x_>)}{\epsilon_0 L}\] where \( x_< \) and \( x_> \) denote the smaller and larger of \( x \) and \( x' \). The graph is a tent that peaks at the sheet. Swapping \( x \) and \( x' \) doesn't change it. Any charge density is just many thin sheets added together, so
\[V(x) = \int_0^L \rho(x')\,G(x, x')\dd{x'}\] This is the set-up of Griffiths Prob. 3.55(a): a charge between two grounded plates.
Green's second identity# This is Griffiths Prob. 1.61. Put \( \vec{v} = T\grad U \) into the divergence theorem (Eq. 1.56) and use product rule (iii), \( \div{(T\grad U)} = T\laplacian U + \grad T\cdot\grad U \). That gives Green's identity (Prob. 1.61c). Write it again with \( T \) and \( U \) swapped and subtract, and you get Green's second identity (Prob. 1.61d):
\[\int_{\mathscr{V}} \left( T \laplacian U - U \laplacian T \right) \dd{\tau} = \oint_{\mathscr{S}} \left( T \grad U - U \grad T \right) \cdot \dd{\vec{a}}\] On the surface, \( \dd{\vec{a}} = \vu{n}\dd{a} \) with \( \vu{n} \) the outward normal, and \( \grad U\cdot\vu{n} = \partial U/\partial n \) is the normal derivative of Eq. 2.36. So the right-hand side can also be written
\[\oint_{\mathscr{S}} \left( T \pdv{U}{n} - U \pdv{T}{n} \right) \dd{a}\] which is the form we use below. Griffiths himself uses Green's identity to prove the second uniqueness theorem (Prob. 3.6). (Careful with names: Griffiths also calls the divergence theorem itself “Green's theorem”, §1.3.4. The identity is a different result.)
The integral formula# Define \( G \) by Poisson's equation for a unit point charge at \( \vec{r} \):
\[\nabla'^2 G(\vec{r}, \vec{r'}) = -\frac{1}{\epsilon_0}\,\delta^3(\gr)\] By Eq. 1.102, \( \laplacian(1/\gr) = -4\pi\delta^3(\gr) \), so the Coulomb potential \( 1/4\pi\epsilon_0\gr \) is one solution. The general one is
\[G = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0\gr} + F\] where \( F \) satisfies Laplace's equation (Eq. 2.25) inside \( \mathscr{V} \). Think of \( F \) as the potential of charges outside the region, such as image charges. The prime on \( \nabla' \) means we differentiate with respect to \( \vec{r'} \), the integration variable.
Now set \( T = V \) and \( U = G \) in Green's second identity, integrating over \( \vec{r'} \). Poisson's equation gives \( \nabla'^2 V = -\rho/\epsilon_0 \), and the delta function picks out \( V(\vec{r}) \):
\[V(\vec{r}) = \int_{\mathscr{V}} \rho\, G \dd{\tau'} + \epsilon_0 \oint_{\mathscr{S}} \left[ G \pdv{V}{n'} - V \pdv{G}{n'} \right] \dd{a'}\] Check: with no boundary at all (all space), the surface term vanishes, \( F = 0 \), and this is Eq. 2.29 again.
This is not a solution yet. It needs both \( V \) and its slope \( \partial V/\partial n \) on the boundary, but you can't choose both freely: by uniqueness (§3.1.5), fixing one fixes the other. So we use our freedom to choose \( F \) to make one of the two terms disappear.
Dirichlet and Neumann Green's functions# These are the two kinds of boundary data allowed by uniqueness: \( V \) itself (the first uniqueness theorem, §3.1.5) or its normal derivative \( \partial V/\partial n \) (Griffiths Prob. 3.5).
Dirichlet (\( V \) given on \( \mathscr{S} \)). Choose \( G_D = 0 \) on \( \mathscr{S} \):
\[V(\vec{r}) = \int_{\mathscr{V}} \rho\, G_D \dd{\tau'} - \epsilon_0 \oint_{\mathscr{S}} V \pdv{G_D}{n'} \dd{a'}\] \( G_D \) is the potential of a unit charge with the boundary grounded. The factor \( \epsilon_0, \partial G_D/\partial n' \) in the surface term has a physical meaning: it is the charge that a unit charge at \( \vec{r} \) induces on the grounded boundary. Compare Griffiths Eq. 2.49, \( \sigma = -\epsilon_0,\partial V/\partial n \). The minus sign is gone because our normal points out of the region, which means into the conductor, the opposite way to Griffiths' \( \vu{n} \) in Eq. 2.49.
Neumann (\( \partial V/\partial n \) given on \( \mathscr{S} \)). The obvious choice \( \partial G/\partial n' = 0 \) is not allowed: by Gauss's law, a unit charge must send a total flux of \( 1/\epsilon_0 \) through \( \mathscr{S} \). (Griffiths warns about the same thing in his comment on Prob. 3.5: any \( \partial V/\partial n \) you specify must agree with Gauss's law.) The simplest allowed choice is \( \partial G_N/\partial n' = -1/\epsilon_0 A \), where \( A \) is the area of \( \mathscr{S} \):
\[V(\vec{r}) = \langle V \rangle_{\mathscr{S}} + \int_{\mathscr{V}} \rho\, G_N \dd{\tau'} + \epsilon_0 \oint_{\mathscr{S}} G_N \pdv{V}{n'} \dd{a'}\] The average \( \langle V \rangle_{\mathscr{S}} \) is just a constant you can't determine, which is fine, since adding a constant to \( V \) doesn't change \( \vec{E} \).
Reciprocity. \( G_D(\vec{r_1}, \vec{r_2}) = G_D(\vec{r_2}, \vec{r_1}) \): a unit charge at A produces the same potential at B as a unit charge at B produces at A, whatever the shape of the grounded conductors. This is a special case of Green's reciprocity theorem, Griffiths Prob. 3.54 (Eq. 3.107), \( \int \rho_1 V_2 \dd{\tau} = \int \rho_2 V_1 \dd{\tau} \). Prob. 3.55 shows how useful it is.
Plane and sphere# Half-space \( z > 0 \) above a plane held at \( V(x', y', 0) \), with no charge in the region. Here \( G_D \) is the image potential Eq. 3.9 with \( q = 1 \), and the Dirichlet formula gives
\[V(x, y, z) = \frac{z}{2\pi}\iint \frac{V(x', y', 0)}{[(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + z^2]^{3/2}}\dd{x'}\dd{y'}\] Sphere of radius \( R \) held at \( V(\theta', \phi') \), with no charge in the region. Here \( G_D \) comes from the sphere image, Eqs. 3.16–3.17. With \( \alpha \) the angle between \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{r'} \) (the same angle as in the multipole expansion, Eq. 3.94):
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\oint V(\theta', \phi')\, \frac{R\,\lvert r^2 - R^2\rvert}{(r^2 + R^2 - 2rR\cos\alpha)^{3/2}} \dd{\Omega'}\] The same formula holds outside (\( r > R \)) and inside (\( r < R \)). At the centre (\( r = 0 \)) it reduces to the average value property of §3.1.4.
Boundary data Condition on \( G \) Griffiths \( V \) (Dirichlet) \( G_D = 0 \) on \( \mathscr{S} \) first uniqueness theorem \( \partial V/\partial n \) (Neumann) \( \partial G_N/\partial n' = -1/\epsilon_0 A \) Prob. 3.5 Both on the same surface (Cauchy) Too many conditions: usually no solution uniqueness: fixing one fixes the other The normal points out of the region \( \mathscr{V} \), not out of the conductor. For a problem outside a conductor, that means it points into the conductor: the opposite way to \( \vu{n} \) in Griffiths Eqs. 2.36 and 2.49.
Example# A disc of radius \( a \), set flush in an infinite grounded plane and insulated from it, is held at \( V_0 \). Find the potential on its axis.
Solution triple-click to reveal The potential on the plane is \( V_0 \) on the disc and zero elsewhere, so only the disc contributes. On the axis, the half-space formula in polar coordinates \( (s, \phi) \) gives
\[V(z) = \frac{zV_0}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a \frac{s\dd{s}\dd{\phi}}{(s^2 + z^2)^{3/2}} = V_0\left[ 1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2 + a^2}} \right]\] As \( z \to 0 \), \( V \to V_0 \). Far away (\( z \gg a \)), \( V \approx V_0 a^2/2z^2 \), falling off like a dipole. No arrangement of image charges gives this boundary condition, but the Green's function handles it directly.
Example# Use the one-dimensional Green's function to find the potential of a uniform charge density \( \rho_0 \) between grounded plates at \( x = 0 \) and \( x = L \).
Solution triple-click to reveal Split the integral at \( x' = x \), since \( G \) has a different formula on each side:
\[V(x) = \frac{\rho_0}{\epsilon_0 L}\left[ (L - x)\int_0^x x'\dd{x'} + x\int_x^L (L - x')\dd{x'} \right] = \frac{\rho_0}{\epsilon_0 L}\left[ \frac{(L - x)x^2}{2} + \frac{x(L - x)^2}{2} \right] = \frac{\rho_0}{2\epsilon_0}\,x(L - x)\] Check: this is zero at both plates and satisfies \( V'' = -\rho_0/\epsilon_0 \) (Eq. 2.24 in one dimension), the same answer you get by integrating Poisson's equation twice. ✓
Full derivation: the online full notes don't cover this section yet. See Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics §1.8–1.10, or Zangwill, Modern Electrodynamics §8.4–8.5.

title: (3.3) Separation of Variables
content:
3.3 Separation of Variables# The method# Separation of variables is the standard way to solve Laplace's equation when the boundaries lie along coordinate lines or surfaces (flat plates for \( x, y, z \), spheres for \( r, \theta, \phi \)). You guess that the potential is a product of functions that each depend on only one variable:
\[V(x,y) = X(x)Y(y)\] This turns one hard partial differential equation into two easy ordinary ones. The guess looks too restrictive, since most functions are not products like this. But you can add up as many product solutions as you like, and sums of them can match any boundary condition. The uniqueness theorem then guarantees the answer is right.
Cartesian coordinates# Put the product into \( \laplacian V = 0 \) and divide by \( XY \):
\[\frac{1}{X}\dv{^2 X}{x^2} + \frac{1}{Y}\dv{^2 Y}{y^2} = 0\] The key step: the first term depends only on \( x \), the second only on \( y \). Yet they add to zero for every \( x \) and \( y \). Change \( x \) alone and the first term would change, unless it is a constant. So both terms must be constants:
\[\frac{1}{X}\dv{^2 X}{x^2} = C_1, \qquad \frac{1}{Y}\dv{^2 Y}{y^2} = -C_1\] Writing \( C_1 = k^2 \), the solutions are exponentials in \( x \) and sines and cosines in \( y \):
\[X = Ae^{kx} + Be^{-kx}, \qquad Y = C\sin ky + D\cos ky\] Which variable gets the sines and which gets the exponentials? Let the boundary conditions decide. Use sines where the potential has to be zero at two places (sines can do that; exponentials can't). Use exponentials where it has to die away.
Adding up all the allowed values of \( k \) gives, for a strip of width \( a \) with grounded edges,
\[V(x,y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} C_n e^{-n\pi x/a}\sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\] Fourier's trick# To find the coefficients \( C_n \), use the fact that different sine waves are orthogonal: multiply two of them and integrate across the strip, and you get zero unless they are the same wave:
\[\int_0^a \sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\sin\left( \frac{n'\pi y}{a} \right)\dd{y} = \begin{cases} 0, & n' \neq n \\ a/2, & n' = n \end{cases}\] So multiply the boundary condition by \( \sin(n'\pi y/a) \) and integrate. Every term in the infinite sum vanishes except one, which leaves
\[C_n = \frac{2}{a}\int_0^a V_0(y)\sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\dd{y}\] The same method works in more complicated boxes. Left: a pipe with two sides at \( V_0 \). Middle: its potential across the pipe. Right: a long pipe with its end held at a given \( V_0(y,z) \), which needs a double sum of sines. Spherical coordinates# If nothing depends on \( \phi \) (the problem looks the same when rotated about the \( z \)-axis), then \( V = V(r,\theta) \). The same method gives radial solutions \( r^l \) and \( r^{-(l+1)} \), and angular solutions called Legendre polynomials \( P_l(\cos\theta) \). The general solution is
\[V(r,\theta) = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}\left( A_l r^l + \frac{B_l}{r^{l+1}} \right) P_l(\cos\theta)\] The first few Legendre polynomials are
\[P_0 = 1, \quad P_1 = \cos\theta, \quad P_2 = \frac{1}{2}(3\cos^2\theta - 1)\] Inside a sphere, set \( B_l = 0 \): \( r^{-(l+1)} \) blows up at the centre. Outside a sphere, set \( A_l = 0 \) (except for any term you are told about at infinity): \( r^l \) blows up far away. Legendre polynomials are orthogonal too,
\[\int_0^\pi P_l(\cos\theta)P_{l'}(\cos\theta)\sin\theta \dd{\theta} = \frac{2}{2l+1}\delta_{ll'}\] so you find the coefficients with the same trick as for sines.
Example# Two grounded metal plates lie parallel to the \( xz \) plane at \( y=0 \) and \( y=a \), extending to \( x = \infty \). The end at \( x=0 \) is closed by a strip held at constant potential \( V_0 \). Find the potential in the slot.
The slot: grounded plates at \( y = 0 \) and \( y = a \), closed at \( x = 0 \) by a strip at \( V_0 \). Solution triple-click to reveal The boundary conditions: \( V=0 \) at \( y=0 \) and \( y=a \); \( V=V_0 \) at \( x=0 \); and \( V \to 0 \) as \( x \to \infty \).
\( V \) must be zero at two values of \( y \), so \( Y \) gets the sines and \( X \) the exponentials. Throw away the growing exponential (it would blow up far down the slot). For the sine to be zero at \( y = a \), \( \sin ka = 0 \), so \( k = n\pi/a \):
\[V(x,y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} C_n e^{-n\pi x/a}\sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\] At \( x=0 \) this must equal \( V_0 \). Fourier's trick gives
\[C_n = \frac{2}{a}\int_0^a V_0 \sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\dd{y} = \frac{2V_0}{n\pi}\left( 1 - \cos n\pi \right)\] This is zero for even \( n \) and \( 4V_0/n\pi \) for odd \( n \). So
\[V(x,y) = \frac{4V_0}{\pi}\sum_{n=1,3,5,\ldots}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}e^{-n\pi x/a}\sin\left( \frac{n\pi y}{a} \right)\] The series at the entrance, \( x = 0 \). One term is a single hump. With more terms the sum gets flatter and closer to \( V_0 \), apart from a small wiggle at the corners. Equipotentials in the slot. Near the strip they bunch up; further along \( V \) dies away and the lines become half-sine humps. The higher terms die away fastest. Far down the slot only the \( n=1 \) term is left, so the potential becomes a smooth half-sine hump, whatever the details at the entrance.
Example# An uncharged conducting sphere of radius \( R \) is placed in a uniform field \( \vec{E}_0 = E_0\vu{z} \). Find the potential outside.
Solution triple-click to reveal The sphere is one equipotential. By symmetry, the plane \( z = 0 \) through its middle is at the same potential, so call that \( V=0 \). Far away the sphere makes no difference, and the uniform field has potential \( V \to -E_0 z = -E_0 r\cos\theta \) as \( r \to \infty \).
Nothing depends on \( \phi \), so use the general solution. The condition far away is \( r P_1(\cos\theta) \) times \( -E_0 \), which fixes \( A_1 = -E_0 \) and all other \( A_l = 0 \):
\[V(r,\theta) = -E_0 r\cos\theta + \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}\frac{B_l}{r^{l+1}}P_l(\cos\theta)\] Now require \( V=0 \) on the sphere, \( r=R \), for every \( \theta \). By orthogonality, each \( P_l \) must cancel separately. Only \( l=1 \) has anything to cancel, so every \( B_l \) is zero except
\[-E_0 R + \frac{B_1}{R^2} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad B_1 = E_0 R^3\] Therefore
\[V(r,\theta) = -E_0\left( r - \frac{R^3}{r^2} \right)\cos\theta\] The first term is the uniform field. The second is exactly the potential of a dipole with moment \( p = 4\pi\epsilon_0 E_0 R^3 \) at the centre: the sphere's charges shift to make a dipole. The induced surface charge is
\[\sigma = -\epsilon_0 \left. \pdv{V}{r} \right|_{r=R} = 3\epsilon_0 E_0 \cos\theta\] It is positive on the side the field points towards (\( \theta < 90° \)) and negative on the other side, and it adds up to zero, as it must for an uncharged sphere.
The field lines bend to meet the sphere at right angles. Positive charge gathers on top, where the field points, and negative charge underneath. Full derivation: §3.3.

title: (3.4) Multipole Expansion
content:
3.4 Multipole Expansion# Approximate potentials far away# From far enough away, any small blob of charge looks like a point charge. The multipole expansion turns that into a precise series: a point-charge term, then smaller and smaller corrections in powers of \( 1/r \).
Start from \( V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \rho(\vec{r'})/\gr, \dd{\tau'} \). With \( \alpha \) the angle between \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{r'} \), the cosine rule gives
\[\gr = r\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{r'}{r} \right)^2 - 2\frac{r'}{r}\cos\alpha}\] The set-up: a piece of charge at \( \vec{r'} \), the far point P at \( \vec{r} \), and the angle \( \alpha \) between them. Far away, \( r'/r \) is small, so expand \( 1/\gr \) in powers of it. The coefficients turn out to be Legendre polynomials:
\[\frac{1}{\gr} = \frac{1}{r}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left( \frac{r'}{r} \right)^n P_n(\cos\alpha)\] This gives the multipole expansion of the potential:
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{r^{n+1}}\int (r')^n P_n(\cos\alpha)\rho(\vec{r'})\dd{\tau'}\] The first few terms# The first three terms are called monopole, dipole and quadrupole:
\[V_{\text{mon}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r}, \qquad V_{\text{dip}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\vu{r}}{r^2}, \qquad V_{\text{quad}} \sim \frac{1}{r^3}\] Here \( Q = \int \rho \dd{\tau} \) is the total charge and
\[\vec{p} = \int \vec{r'}\rho(\vec{r'})\dd{\tau'}\] is the dipole moment. For point charges, \( \vec{p} = \sum q_i \vec{r}_i \). For a pair \( +q \) and \( -q \) separated by \( \vec{d} \), it is \( \vec{p} = q\vec{d} \), pointing from the negative charge to the positive one.
Left: a physical dipole seen from a far point. Right: the dipole moment \( \vec{p} = q\vec{r'}+ - q\vec{r'}- = q\vec{d} \) points from \( -q \) to \( +q \). Far away, the first term that isn't zero wins. If the total charge isn't zero, the object looks like a point charge. If it is neutral, the dipole term takes over, falling as \( 1/r^2 \). If the dipole moment is zero too, the quadrupole term leads, and so on.
Monopole, dipole, quadrupole, octopole. Each one is two copies of the one before, with opposite signs, and falls off one power of \( r \) faster. Which term wins? Add up the charge first. If it is not zero, the monopole leads. If it is zero, work out \( \vec{p} \). Does the origin matter?# The total charge \( Q \) doesn't depend on where you put the origin. The dipole moment usually does: moving the origin by \( \vec{a} \) gives
\[\vec{p}_{\text{new}} = \vec{p} - Q\vec{a}\] So \( \vec{p} \) is the same for every origin exactly when the total charge is zero. In general, the first moment that isn't zero never depends on the origin.
Left: a lone charge has \( p = qd \) measured from O, so its dipole moment depends on the origin. Right: moving the origin by \( \vec{a} \) gives \( \vec{p}_{\text{new}} = \vec{p} - Q\vec{a} \). The field of a dipole# With \( \vec{p} \) along the \( z \)-axis, take the gradient of the dipole potential in spherical coordinates:
The dipole sits at the origin and points along \( z \). The field point is at \( (r, \theta, \phi) \). \[E_r = \frac{2p\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}, \qquad E_\theta = \frac{p\sin\theta}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}, \qquad E_\phi = 0\] or all together,
\[\vec{E}_{\text{dip}}(\vec{r}) = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\left( 2\cos\theta\,\vu{r} + \sin\theta\,\vu{\theta} \right)\] A dipole's field falls as \( 1/r^3 \), one power faster than a point charge's. The \( + \) and \( - \) charges almost cancel from far away. In general the \( n \)th term's field falls as \( 1/r^{n+2} \).
Left: a pure dipole, shrunk to a point. Right: a real dipole. Far away the two look the same. Close in they differ, because the real one has its charges apart. Example# Four charges sit in the \( xy \) plane: \( +q \) at \( (a,0) \) and \( (-a,0) \), and \( -q \) at \( (0,a) \) and \( (0,-a) \). Find the leading term in the multipole expansion.
The four charges: \( +q \) on the \( x \)-axis, \( -q \) on the \( y \)-axis. Solution triple-click to reveal Monopole. The total charge is \( q + q - q - q = 0 \), so there is no monopole term, and the potential falls faster than \( 1/r \).
Dipole. Add up \( \vec{p} = \sum q_i \vec{r}_i \):
\[\vec{p} = q(a\vu{x}) + q(-a\vu{x}) + (-q)(a\vu{y}) + (-q)(-a\vu{y}) = \vec{0}\] Each pair cancels, so the dipole moment is zero too. The total charge is zero, so this is true wherever you put the origin.
Quadrupole. With the first two terms gone, the quadrupole term leads. The potential falls as \( 1/r^3 \) and the field as \( 1/r^4 \).
You can think of this arrangement as two dipoles pointing in opposite directions, side by side. Their dipole moments cancel, but because they are not in the same place, their fields don't cancel completely. What's left is a quadrupole.
Example# A sphere of radius \( R \) carries surface charge \( \sigma(\theta) = k\cos\theta \), with \( k \) constant. Find the potential outside.
Solution triple-click to reveal Monopole. The total charge is
\[Q = \int \sigma \dd{a} = k R^2 \int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi \cos\theta \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi} = 2\pi k R^2 \int_0^\pi \cos\theta\sin\theta \dd{\theta} = 0\] The top half is positive and the bottom half negative, and they cancel.
Dipole. By symmetry \( \vec{p} \) points along \( \vu{z} \). Use \( z' = R\cos\theta \):
\[p_z = \int z' \sigma \dd{a} = \int (R\cos\theta)(k\cos\theta)R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta}\dd{\phi}\] \[= 2\pi k R^3 \int_0^\pi \cos^2\theta \sin\theta \dd{\theta} = 2\pi k R^3 \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4\pi k R^3}{3}\] So the dipole term leads:
\[V(r,\theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2} = \frac{kR^3\cos\theta}{3\epsilon_0 r^2}\] In fact this is the exact answer, not just an approximation. The charge goes as \( \cos\theta = P_1(\cos\theta) \), so in the method of §3.3 only the \( l=1 \) term appears. All the higher terms are exactly zero.
Full derivation: §3.4.
Chapter 3 recap# You have reached the end of Chapter 3. To recap, watch this short summary of the whole chapter by Dot Physics, and check that you have the main ideas.

title: (4.1) Polarization
content:
4.1 Polarization# Dielectrics# Chapters 2 and 3 were about conductors, where charge moves freely. This chapter is about dielectrics: insulators such as glass, plastic or water, where every electron stays attached to its own atom. These bound charges can't travel through the material. But they can shift a tiny bit inside each atom or molecule, and those tiny shifts are enough to change the field a lot.
This happens in two ways.
1. Stretched atoms (induced dipoles)# Put a neutral atom in an electric field. The field pushes the nucleus one way and the electron cloud the other, until the attraction between them balances the push. The atom is now slightly stretched, with a little \( + \) end and a little \( - \) end: an induced dipole. For any field you can make in a lab, the stretch is proportional to the field:
\[\vec{p} = \alpha \vec{E}\] \( \alpha \) is the atomic polarizability, a number that describes how easily that kind of atom stretches.
No field: the nucleus sits at the centre of its cloud. In a field the nucleus is pushed one way and the cloud the other, leaving a small dipole. Molecules may stretch more easily in some directions than others. Then \( \alpha \) becomes a matrix (the polarizability tensor), and \( \vec{p} \) need not point exactly along \( \vec{E} \).
CO₂ stretches more easily along its axis, so the induced dipole is pulled towards the axis and does not point along the field. 2. Turning molecules (polar molecules)# Some molecules, such as water, have a built-in dipole moment even with no field. In a uniform field the pushes on the two ends are equal and opposite, so there's no net force. But there is a twist (torque):
\[\vec{N} = \vec{p} \cross \vec{E}\] which turns the molecule to line up with the field, like a compass needle. Random thermal jiggling fights against this, so the molecules only partly line up, and less so when the material is hotter.
Water: the electrons crowd round the oxygen, and the molecule is bent at 105°, so it has a built-in dipole moment. If the field is not uniform, the two ends feel different fields, so there is also a net force:
\[\vec{F} = (\vec{p}\cdot\grad)\vec{E}\] This is why a charged rod picks up uncharged bits of paper. The rod's field polarizes the paper, and since the field is stronger nearer the rod, the dipoles get pulled towards it.
Left: in a uniform field the two forces cancel but make a torque. Right: near a charged rod the field is stronger on the near end, so there is a net pull. Polarization# Either way, the material ends up full of tiny dipoles lined up with the field. We describe this with the polarization:
\[\vec{P} \equiv \text{dipole moment per unit volume}\] with units C/m². From here on we only need \( \vec{P} \); the details of the atoms don't matter any more. §4.2 works out the field that a polarized object produces.
With no field the tiny dipoles point every way and cancel. In a field they line up on average, and \( \vec{P} \) measures how much. Example# A point charge \( q \) is a distance \( r \) from a neutral atom of polarizability \( \alpha \). Find the force between them and its dependence on \( r \).
Solution triple-click to reveal The charge's field at the atom has size
\[E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\] This stretches the atom into a dipole \( p = \alpha E \), pointing along the line between them (away from \( q \) if \( q \) is positive).
A point charge's field is not uniform, so we need the non-uniform force formula. With the dipole along the radial direction,
\[F = p \left| \dv{E}{r} \right| = \alpha E \left| \dv{}{r}\left( \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \right) \right| = \alpha E \frac{2q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\] Put in \( E \):
\[F = 2\alpha \left( \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \right)^2 \frac{1}{r^5}\] The force is always attractive, whatever the sign of \( q \). Flip the charge and the induced dipole flips too, so the two sign changes cancel. It falls off as \( 1/r^5 \), far faster than the \( 1/r^2 \) between two charges. That's why forces from polarization only matter at short range.
Example# An ideal dipole \( \vec{p} \) is placed in a uniform field \( \vec{E} \) at angle \( \theta \) to it. Find the energy of the configuration and the stable orientation.
Solution triple-click to reveal The torque is \( N = pE\sin\theta \), trying to make \( \theta \) smaller. The work needed to turn the dipole against it, from \( \theta_0 \) to \( \theta \), is
\[W = \int_{\theta_0}^{\theta} pE\sin\theta' \dd{\theta'} = -pE\left( \cos\theta - \cos\theta_0 \right)\] Choose zero energy at \( \theta_0 = 90^\circ \), where \( \cos\theta_0 = 0 \). Then
\[U = -pE\cos\theta = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E}\] The energy is lowest at \( \theta = 0 \), dipole along the field: this is the stable position. It is highest at \( \theta = 180^\circ \), pointing against the field. That is also a balance point, but an unstable one, like a pencil standing on its tip.
The energy difference between the two is \( 2pE \). Molecules only line up fully if this is much bigger than the thermal energy \( k_B T \). At room temperature, with ordinary lab fields, it isn't: thermal motion keeps the alignment small. That's why the polarization of materials like water stays proportional to the field.
\( U = -pE\cos\theta \). The energy is lowest (stable) with the dipole along the field and highest (unstable) pointing against it. Full derivation: §4.1.

title: (4.2) The Field of a Polarized Object
content:
4.2 The Field of a Polarized Object# Bound charges# If you know the polarization \( \vec{P} \), you can find the potential by adding up the potentials of all the tiny dipoles:
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_V \frac{\vec{P}(\vec{r'})\cdot\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{\tau'}\] Each small piece \( \dd{\tau'} \) is a dipole \( \vec{p} = \vec{P}\dd{\tau'} \). Add up the potentials of all the pieces. Using \( \grad'(1/\gr) = \vu{\gr}/\gr^2 \) and integrating by parts turns this into two terms, each with a clear meaning:
\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\oint_S \frac{\vec{P}\cdot\vu{n}}{\gr}\dd{a'} + \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_V \frac{-\div{\vec{P}}}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] The first term is the potential of a surface charge, and the second of a volume charge, with
\[\sigma_b \equiv \vec{P}\cdot\vu{n}, \qquad \rho_b \equiv -\div{\vec{P}}\] These are the bound charges. The big payoff: a polarized object produces exactly the same field as these two ordinary charge distributions. So everything from Chapters 2 and 3 applies directly.
What the bound charges really are# Bound charges are real charge, not a mathematical trick.
Surface charge. Picture a bar polarized evenly along its length, like a row of people each holding \( + \) in their right hand and \( - \) in their left. Inside, each person's \( + \) hand is next to their neighbour's \( - \) hand, and they cancel. Only the two people at the ends have an unpaired hand. So charge shows up on the end surfaces. If \( \vec{P} \) is at angle \( \theta \) to the surface, the charge per unit area is \( P\cos\theta = \vec{P}\cdot\vu{n} \).
Left: inside the bar the charges pair off; only the end faces keep unpaired charge. Right: on a slanted face the charge per unit area is \( P\cos\theta \). Volume charge. If the polarization is uneven, the cancellation inside isn't perfect. More charge gets pushed out of some region than pushed in, and a net charge is left behind. The divergence measures exactly this mismatch. The minus sign is there because positive divergence means positive charge is pushed out, leaving negative charge behind.
An uneven polarization (here \( \vec{P} = k\vec{r} \), as in the second example) pushes positive charge outwards: negative bound charge is left inside and positive charge collects on the surface. The object is neutral overall, so the bound charges always add up to zero:
\[\oint_S \sigma_b \dd{a} + \int_V \rho_b \dd{\tau} = \oint \vec{P}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} - \int (\div{\vec{P}})\dd{\tau} = 0\] by the divergence theorem.
Microscopic and macroscopic fields# Zoom right in to a dielectric and the true field is wild: enormous near each nucleus, pointing every which way between atoms. The \( \vec{E} \) we use is the average field, taken over a region big enough to contain many atoms but small compared with the object.
Does averaging change the answer? No. Average the field over a small sphere holding many atoms. The charges outside the sphere contribute their field at its centre. The charges inside contribute \( -\vec{p}/4\pi\epsilon_0 R^3 \), which depends only on their total dipole moment. Put together, the average field is exactly the field of the bound charges above. The exact size of the averaging region doesn't matter.
The macroscopic field at a point is the true field averaged over a small sphere that still holds many atoms. Example# Find the field of a uniformly polarized sphere of radius \( R \), with \( \vec{P} = P\vu{z} \), both inside and outside.
Solution triple-click to reveal The polarization is uniform, so \( \div{\vec{P}} = 0 \): no bound volume charge. The bound surface charge is
\[\sigma_b = \vec{P}\cdot\vu{n} = P\cos\theta\] using \( \vu{n} = \vu{r} \) on the sphere. Positive on top, negative on the bottom.
Why the charge is on the surface: uniform polarization shifts all the + charge up and all the − charge down a little. They cancel everywhere except in thin crescents at the top and bottom. This is exactly the charge from Example 3.4-b, with \( k = P \). That problem gave a pure dipole potential outside, and (by the same method) a uniform field inside:
\[V_{\text{in}} = \frac{P}{3\epsilon_0}r\cos\theta = \frac{P}{3\epsilon_0}z, \qquad V_{\text{out}} = \frac{PR^3}{3\epsilon_0}\frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\] Take the gradient of the inside potential:
\[\vec{E}_{\text{in}} = -\grad V_{\text{in}} = -\frac{P}{3\epsilon_0}\vu{z} = -\frac{\vec{P}}{3\epsilon_0}\] The field inside is uniform and points against the polarization. That makes sense: it runs from the positive charge on top to the negative charge on the bottom. It is called a depolarizing field, because it works against the polarization that created it.
Outside, the field is that of a single dipole with moment
\[\vec{p} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \vec{P}\] which is just polarization × volume, as you'd expect.
The field of the uniformly polarized sphere. Inside it is uniform and points against P. Outside it is a pure dipole field. Example# A sphere of radius \( R \) carries polarization \( \vec{P} = k\vec{r} \), with \( k \) constant. Find the bound charges and the field inside.
Solution triple-click to reveal Volume charge. The polarization is uneven, so
\[\rho_b = -\div{\vec{P}} = -k\,\div{\vec{r}} = -3k\] using \( \div{\vec{r}} = 3 \). So there is a uniform bound charge throughout the sphere.
Surface charge. On the surface \( \vec{r} = R\vu{r} \), so
\[\sigma_b = \vec{P}\cdot\vu{n} = kR\] Check: the total bound charge should be zero:
\[(-3k)\left( \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \right) + (kR)\left( 4\pi R^2 \right) = -4\pi k R^3 + 4\pi k R^3 = 0\] ✓
Field inside. Use Gauss's law on a sphere of radius \( r < R \). It encloses only volume charge, \( Q_{\text{enc}} = -3k \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \):
\[E(r)\,4\pi r^2 = \frac{-4\pi k r^3}{\epsilon_0} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{E} = -\frac{k\vec{r}}{\epsilon_0} = -\frac{\vec{P}}{\epsilon_0}\] Outside, a Gaussian sphere encloses zero total charge, so the field outside is zero.
Full derivation: §4.2.

title: (4.3) The Electric Displacement
content:
4.3 The Electric Displacement# Gauss's law in a dielectric# In a dielectric there are two kinds of charge. Bound charge comes from the polarization. Free charge is everything else: charge you put there on purpose and control, such as the charge on a capacitor plate.
\[\rho = \rho_b + \rho_f\] Gauss's law counts all of it. Put in \( \rho_b = -\div{\vec{P}} \):
\[\epsilon_0 \div{\vec{E}} = \rho_f - \div{\vec{P}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \div{\left( \epsilon_0\vec{E} + \vec{P} \right)} = \rho_f\] Now define the electric displacement
\[\vec{D} \equiv \epsilon_0 \vec{E} + \vec{P}\] and Gauss's law becomes
\[\div{\vec{D}} = \rho_f, \qquad \oint \vec{D}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} = Q_{f,\text{enc}}\] Why bother? You know the free charge, because you put it there. You don't know the bound charge: it depends on the field, which is what you're trying to find. Using \( \vec{D} \) lets you ignore the bound charge and work only with what you know.
A trap: D is not just like E# It is tempting to think of \( \vec{D} \) as “\( \epsilon_0\vec{E} \) with the bound charge hidden”. That is only half true. Take the curl:
\[\curl{\vec{D}} = \epsilon_0(\curl{\vec{E}}) + \curl{\vec{P}} = \curl{\vec{P}}\] This is not zero in general. So:
There is no potential for \( \vec{D} \): it isn't the gradient of anything. Knowing the free charge is not enough to find \( \vec{D} \) in general. The symmetry trick used for \( \vec{E} \) in §2.2 only works for \( \vec{D} \) when \( \curl{\vec{P}} = 0 \) as well.
At the edge of a polarized dielectric, P runs up one side of this loop but is zero on the other, so the loop integral of P is not zero. There \( \curl{\vec{P}} \neq 0 \), and so \( \curl{\vec{D}} \neq 0 \). Boundary conditions# The pillbox and loop arguments, applied to \( \vec{D} \), give
\[D_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - D_{\text{below}}^{\perp} = \sigma_f, \qquad \vec{D}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{D}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel} = \vec{P}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{P}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel}\] The perpendicular part jumps by the free surface charge. The parallel part jumps by the change in polarization. Compare \( \vec{E} \), whose parallel part never jumps.
A subtlety in crystals# “Dipole moment per unit volume” is clear for a finite object. For an endless repeating crystal it isn't. The answer depends on how you choose the repeating unit (the unit cell). Different, equally valid choices give different dipole moments per cell, and so different values of \( \vec{P} \).
The same crystal, paired up two ways. Pair each + with the − below and every dipole points up; pair with the − to the left and they point right. P depends on the choice. What is well defined is the change in polarization when you squeeze the crystal or apply a field, and that change is what experiments measure. The absolute value of \( \vec{P} \) in a bulk crystal is a convention; changes in it are physical.
Example# A long straight wire carrying uniform line charge \( \lambda \) is surrounded by rubber insulation out to radius \( a \). Find the electric displacement.
End view: the wire, the rubber out to radius \( a \), and a Gaussian cylinder of radius \( s \). Solution triple-click to reveal Everything has cylindrical symmetry, and the rubber's polarization points radially, so \( \curl{\vec{P}} = 0 \). That means the symmetry trick for \( \vec{D} \) is allowed.
Use a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius \( s \) and length \( L \) around the wire. The free charge inside is the wire's, \( \lambda L \). The rubber's bound charge isn't free, so it doesn't count:
\[\oint \vec{D}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} = D(s)\,2\pi s L = \lambda L\] so
\[\vec{D} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi s}\vu{s}\] This is true both inside and outside the rubber, since the free charge enclosed is the same.
Notice what just happened: we found \( \vec{D} \) without knowing anything about how the rubber polarizes. To get \( \vec{E} \) you do need that. Outside the rubber \( \vec{P} = 0 \), so \( \vec{E} = \vec{D}/\epsilon_0 \). Inside the rubber you need the extra relation given in §4.4.
Example# A uniformly polarized sphere carries \( \vec{P} = P\vu{z} \) and no free charge. Find \( \vec{D} \) inside and outside, and comment on whether Gauss's law alone could have produced the answer.
Solution triple-click to reveal From §4.2, the field inside is \( \vec{E}_{\text{in}} = -\vec{P}/3\epsilon_0 \). So inside,
\[\vec{D} = \epsilon_0\vec{E} + \vec{P} = \epsilon_0\left( -\frac{\vec{P}}{3\epsilon_0} \right) + \vec{P} = \frac{2}{3}\vec{P}\] Outside, \( \vec{P} = 0 \) and the field is a dipole field, so \( \vec{D} = \epsilon_0\vec{E}_{\text{dip}} \), which is not zero.
Could Gauss's law alone have told us this? No. There is no free charge anywhere, so \( \div{\vec{D}} = 0 \) everywhere and the flux of \( \vec{D} \) through every closed surface is zero. Yet \( \vec{D} \) itself is not zero.
The reason: at the sphere's surface the polarization suddenly drops to zero, so \( \curl{\vec{D}} = \curl{\vec{P}} \neq 0 \) there. A field with zero divergence but non-zero curl is not fixed by Gauss's law. Concluding “no free charge, so \( \vec{D} = 0 \)” is a common and tempting mistake. This example is exactly the warning above in action.
The same sphere. \( \vec{E} \) lines start and end on the bound charge. \( \vec{D} \) lines have no ends at all, because there is no free charge, yet \( \vec{D} \neq 0 \). Full derivation: §4.3.

title: (4.4) Linear Dielectrics
content:
4.4 Linear Dielectrics# Susceptibility, permittivity, dielectric constant# In most materials, as long as the field isn't too strong, the polarization is proportional to the field:
\[\vec{P} = \epsilon_0 \chi_e \vec{E}\] \( \chi_e \) is the electric susceptibility: a pure number that says how easily the material polarizes. Materials that behave like this are called linear dielectrics.
\( \vec{E} \) here is the total field, including the field made by the polarization itself, not just the field you applied from outside.
Put this into the definition of \( \vec{D} \):
\[\vec{D} = \epsilon_0\vec{E} + \vec{P} = \epsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)\vec{E} \equiv \epsilon \vec{E}\] \( \epsilon = \epsilon_0(1+\chi_e) \) is the permittivity of the material. The relative permittivity, or dielectric constant, is
\[\epsilon_r = 1 + \chi_e = \frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon_0}\] For vacuum \( \epsilon_r = 1 \); for water it is about 80.
In a linear dielectric, \( \vec{D} \) is just a multiple of \( \vec{E} \), which makes life much easier. But if the material is not the same throughout (for example, two different materials side by side), the curl of \( \vec{D} \) can still be non-zero at the joins.
Consequences# In a uniform linear dielectric, the bound volume charge is tied to the free charge:
\[\rho_b = -\left( \frac{\chi_e}{1+\chi_e} \right)\rho_f\] So if there is no free charge inside (\( \rho_f = 0 \)), there is no bound volume charge either. All the bound charge is on the surfaces.
A charge inside a dielectric turns the nearby molecules so their − ends face it. The bound charge next to it partly cancels it, so its field is weaker by a factor ε_r. Fill the gap in a capacitor with a linear dielectric and the capacitance goes up by a factor \( \epsilon_r \):
\[C = \epsilon_r C_{\text{vac}}\] Why: bound charge appears on the dielectric's surfaces, opposite in sign to the charge on the nearby plate. It partly cancels the plate's charge, so the field is weaker. A weaker field means a smaller voltage for the same charge, so \( C = Q/V \) is bigger.
Bound charge on each face of the dielectric is opposite to the charge on the plate next to it, so it cancels part of the plate's field. Boundary value problems# At a boundary between linear dielectrics, \( V \) is continuous, and
\[\epsilon_{\text{above}} \pdv{V_{\text{above}}}{n} - \epsilon_{\text{below}}\pdv{V_{\text{below}}}{n} = -\sigma_f\] Inside each uniform region Laplace's equation still holds. So the methods of Chapter 3 work as before; you just match the solutions at the boundaries using these conditions.
With no free charge on the boundary, field lines bend there: \( \tan\theta_2/\tan\theta_1 = \epsilon_2/\epsilon_1 \). Energy in dielectric systems# The energy stored is
\[W = \frac{1}{2}\int \vec{D}\cdot\vec{E}\,\dd{\tau} = \frac{\epsilon}{2}\int E^2 \dd{\tau}\] This is bigger than \( \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int E^2 \dd{\tau} \). The difference is the energy that went into polarizing the material: stretching the atoms and turning the molecules, a bit like stretching tiny springs. \( \frac{1}{2}\int \vec{D}\cdot\vec{E} \) is the total work you do bringing in the free charge, and it includes that spring energy.
Forces on dielectrics# Push a slab of dielectric part-way between the plates of a charged capacitor, and it gets pulled in. The uniform field between the plates can't do this (uniform fields give no net force on dipoles). The pull comes from the uneven “fringing” field that bulges out at the edges of the plates, which attracts the induced dipoles.
Working out that fringing field is hard, so use energy instead:
\[F = -\dv{W}{x}\] where \( x \) is how far the slab is in, and the charge on the plates is kept fixed.
The slab is pulled in by the fringing field at the edge of the plates. It is easier to find the force from the energy than from this field. Example# A parallel-plate capacitor is filled with a linear dielectric of susceptibility \( \chi_e \). Find the field, the bound surface charge, and the capacitance in terms of the vacuum value.
Solution triple-click to reveal Let the free charge on the plates be \( \pm\sigma_f \) per unit area. Use Gauss's law for \( \vec{D} \) on a pillbox through the positive plate. \( \vec{D} \) is zero inside the metal, so
\[D = \sigma_f\] The dielectric is linear, so \( \vec{E} = \vec{D}/\epsilon \):
\[E = \frac{\sigma_f}{\epsilon} = \frac{\sigma_f}{\epsilon_0(1+\chi_e)}\] That is smaller than the vacuum value \( \sigma_f/\epsilon_0 \) by a factor \( \epsilon_r \).
The polarization is \( P = \epsilon_0\chi_e E = \sigma_f \chi_e/(1+\chi_e) \), so the bound surface charge has size
\[\sigma_b = P = \frac{\chi_e}{1+\chi_e}\sigma_f\] with the opposite sign to the charge on the plate next to it. That's what weakens the field.
The voltage is \( V = Ed \), so
\[C = \frac{\sigma_f A}{Ed} = \frac{\epsilon A}{d} = \epsilon_r \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}\] The capacitance goes up by \( \epsilon_r \), so the capacitor holds more charge at the same voltage. This is why real capacitors are filled with dielectric.
Example# A sphere of linear dielectric material with susceptibility \( \chi_e \) is placed in an otherwise uniform field \( \vec{E}_0 \). Find the field inside.
Solution triple-click to reveal Guess that the field inside is uniform, and call it \( \vec{E}_{\text{in}} \). (If the guess leads to a consistent answer, uniqueness says it's right.)
Then the sphere is uniformly polarized, with \( \vec{P} = \epsilon_0\chi_e\vec{E}_{\text{in}} \). From §4.2, a uniformly polarized sphere makes a field \( -\vec{P}/3\epsilon_0 \) inside itself.
The total field inside is the applied field plus this opposing field:
\[\vec{E}_{\text{in}} = \vec{E}_0 - \frac{\vec{P}}{3\epsilon_0} = \vec{E}_0 - \frac{\chi_e}{3}\vec{E}_{\text{in}}\] Notice the loop: the polarization depends on the field, and the field depends on the polarization. Just solve for \( \vec{E}_{\text{in}} \):
\[\vec{E}_{\text{in}}\left( 1 + \frac{\chi_e}{3} \right) = \vec{E}_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{E}_{\text{in}} = \frac{3}{3+\chi_e}\vec{E}_0 = \frac{3}{2+\epsilon_r}\vec{E}_0\] The field inside is uniform, points along \( \vec{E}_0 \), and is weakened by the polarization.
Check the limits. With no material (\( \chi_e \to 0 \)) the field is just \( \vec{E}_0 \). For an extremely polarizable material (\( \chi_e \to \infty \)) the field inside goes to zero, just like a conductor (§3.3).
With \( \epsilon_r = 3 \): some lines end on the − bound charge at the bottom and start again from the + charge at the top, so the field inside is uniform but weaker (\( 0.6,E_0 \)). Full derivation: §4.4.
