Review of Chapters 1–4# That completes electrostatics. Before starting magnetism, this longer Dot Physics video reviews Chapters 1 to 4 together.

title: (5.1) The Lorentz Force Law
content:
5.1 The Lorentz Force Law# Magnetic fields# Magnetic fields are made by moving charges, and they push only on moving charges. Two parallel wires carrying current the same way attract; carrying current opposite ways, they repel. Electrostatics can't explain this, because both wires are electrically neutral. Something new is going on: magnetism.
The force law# The magnetic force on a charge \( Q \) moving with velocity \( \vec{v} \) is
\[\vec{F}_{\text{mag}} = Q\left( \vec{v} \cross \vec{B} \right)\] The magnetic force is at right angles to both \( \vec{v} \) and \( \vec{B} \) (right-hand rule). Add the electric force to get the Lorentz force law:
\[\vec{F} = Q\left[ \vec{E} + \left( \vec{v} \cross \vec{B} \right) \right]\] The magnetic field \( \vec{B} \) is measured in teslas (T). One tesla is one newton per ampere-metre. (A fridge magnet is about 0.01 T; an MRI scanner is 1.5–3 T.)
Magnetic forces do no work# The cross product makes the magnetic force always perpendicular to the velocity. So
\[\dd{W} = \vec{F}_{\text{mag}}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = Q(\vec{v}\cross\vec{B})\cdot\vec{v}\dd{t} = 0\] always. A magnetic force can change the direction a charge moves, but never its speed, so it never changes its kinetic energy. It's like a ball on a string being whirled round: the string turns the ball but doesn't speed it up.
This is a real rule, not a technicality, and it raises an obvious question: magnets do lift paper clips, so who does the work? The answer is subtle and comes in §8.3. In short: something else supplies the energy, and the magnetic force only redirects it.
Cyclotron motion# A charge moving at right angles to a uniform field feels a force of constant size, always sideways to its motion. So it moves in a circle. Set the magnetic force equal to the force needed for circular motion:
\[QvB = \frac{mv^2}{R} \quad \Rightarrow \quad R = \frac{mv}{QB}\] The angular frequency, called the cyclotron frequency, is
\[\omega = \frac{v}{R} = \frac{QB}{m}\] It doesn't depend on the speed. A faster particle goes round a bigger circle but takes the same time per lap. That fact is how a cyclotron (a particle accelerator) works.
If the charge also has some velocity along \( \vec{B} \), that part is unaffected, so the circle gets stretched into a helix (a corkscrew).
Left: with B out of the page, a positive charge goes round clockwise; the force always points to the centre. Right: add some velocity along B and the circle becomes a helix. Currents# A line charge \( \lambda \) moving at speed \( v \) is a current \( I = \lambda v \), measured in amperes. The force on a wire carrying current is
\[\vec{F}_{\text{mag}} = \int I\left( \dd{\vec{l}} \cross \vec{B} \right)\] \( I \) is the same all along the wire, so it can come outside the integral.
In a time \( dt \) all the charge in a length \( v,dt \) passes P. That is \( \lambda v,dt \), so the current is \( I = \lambda v \). Current can also spread over a surface or through a volume:
Type Density Relation surface \( \vec{K} = \sigma\vec{v} \) (A/m) \( \dd{I} = K \dd{l_\perp} \) volume \( \vec{J} = \rho\vec{v} \) (A/m²) \( I = \int \vec{J}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} \) \( \vec{K} \) is current per unit width; \( \vec{J} \) is current per unit cross-sectional area.
\( \vec{K} \) is current per unit width across the flow; \( \vec{J} \) is current per unit area across the flow. The continuity equation# Charge can't be created or destroyed. So if current flows out of a region, the charge inside must go down:
\[\div{\vec{J}} = -\pdv{\rho}{t}\] This is local conservation of charge: charge can't disappear here and reappear somewhere else. It has to flow through the space in between.
Magnetostatics is about steady currents: charges moving, but nothing changing with time (like water flowing steadily through a pipe). Then \( \pdv{\rho}{t} = 0 \) and
\[\div{\vec{J}} = 0\] This condition holds throughout Chapters 5 and 6.
Example# A charge \( Q \) moves in a region with uniform \( \vec{E} = E\vu{z} \) and \( \vec{B} = B\vu{x} \), perpendicular to one another. Determine the velocity for which the particle travels in a straight line at constant speed.
The velocity selector. At exactly v = E/B the two forces cancel. Faster charges are bent one way, slower ones the other. Solution triple-click to reveal The particle goes straight if the total force is zero, meaning the electric and magnetic forces cancel:
\[Q\left[ \vec{E} + (\vec{v}\cross\vec{B}) \right] = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} = -\vec{E}\] \( \vec{B} \) is along \( \vu{x} \) and \( \vec{E} \) along \( \vu{z} \), so we need \( \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \) along \( -\vu{z} \). Try \( \vec{v} = v\vu{y} \):
\[\vec{v}\cross\vec{B} = v\vu{y}\cross B\vu{x} = -vB\,\vu{z}\] That works if \( vB = E \), so
\[v = \frac{E}{B}\] along \( \vu{y} \), at right angles to both fields.
This setup is a velocity selector. Only particles with exactly this speed go straight through, whatever their charge or mass; all others are bent aside. The speed it picks depends only on the two field strengths.
Example# A current \( I \) flows along a wire bent into a semicircle of radius \( R \) lying in the \( xy \) plane, in a uniform field \( \vec{B} = B\vu{z} \). Find the net force on the semicircle.
All the little steps \( d\vec{l} \) add up to the straight arrow joining the ends, so the semicircle feels the same force as that straight wire. Solution triple-click to reveal The force is
\[\vec{F} = I\int \left( \dd{\vec{l}} \cross \vec{B} \right) = I\left( \int \dd{\vec{l}} \right) \cross \vec{B}\] \( \vec{B} \) came outside the integral because it is uniform. Now the useful observation: \( \int \dd{\vec{l}} \) is just all the little steps along the wire added up, which is the straight arrow from one end of the wire to the other.
For a semicircle from \( (-R,0) \) to \( (R,0) \), that arrow is \( 2R\vu{x} \), however curved the path. So
\[\vec{F} = I\left( 2R\vu{x} \right)\cross\left( B\vu{z} \right) = 2IRB\left( \vu{x}\cross\vu{z} \right) = -2IRB\,\vu{y}\] The semicircle feels the same force as a straight wire of length \( 2R \) joining its ends.
It follows straight away that a closed loop in a uniform field has \( \oint \dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \) (you end where you started), so the net force is zero. A current loop in a uniform field gets twisted (a torque) but not pushed. That idea leads to magnetic dipoles in §6.1.
Full derivation: §5.1.

title: (5.2) The Biot-Savart Law
content:
5.2 The Biot-Savart Law# Steady currents# A steady current is a flow that has been going forever at the same rate and never changes. Charges are moving, but the amount of charge at each point stays the same, so \( \div{\vec{J}} = 0 \).
No real current is perfectly steady, but it's a very good approximation. Steady currents are to magnetostatics what charges at rest are to electrostatics.
The law# The magnetic field of a steady current in a wire is
\[\vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{I}\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{l'} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int \frac{\dd{\vec{l'}}\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\] where the permeability of free space is
\[\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{A}^2}\] It looks a lot like Coulomb's law: a \( 1/\gr^2 \) law added up over the source. The difference is the cross product. Because of it, the magnetic field wraps around the current instead of pointing away from it.
Each piece \( d\vec{l'} \) of the wire gives a field \( d\vec{B} \) at right angles to both \( d\vec{l'} \) and \( \boldsymbol{\mathscr{r}} \). For currents on surfaces and in volumes,
\[\vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{K}(\vec{r'})\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{a'}, \qquad \vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r'})\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{\tau'}\] There is nothing like a magnetic “point charge” here. The basic source is a small piece of current, and steady currents always flow round closed circuits.
The straight wire# For a very long straight wire carrying current \( I \), the integral gives
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}\] at distance \( s \) from the wire. The field lines are circles around the wire. Use the right-hand rule: point your right thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way \( \vec{B} \) goes. The field falls as \( 1/s \), just like the electric field of a long line of charge.
The field lines are circles round the wire. Thumb along the current, fingers curl the way B goes. So two parallel wires a distance \( d \) apart, with currents \( I_1 \) and \( I_2 \), push or pull on each other with force per unit length
\[\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\] Currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel. (The opposite of charges, where “same” repels.)
End view. The field of wire 1 at wire 2, times the current in wire 2, gives the force. Same direction: attract. Opposite: repel. Example# Find the magnetic field a distance \( s \) from a long straight wire carrying steady current \( I \), by direct integration.
The piece \( dz \) at height \( z \), the field point P a distance \( s \) away, and the angle \( \alpha \) between the wire and \( \boldsymbol{\mathscr{r}} \). Solution triple-click to reveal Put the wire along the \( z \)-axis and the field point in the \( xy \) plane, a distance \( s \) away. A small piece \( \dd{\vec{l'}} = \dd{z},\vu{z} \) at height \( z \) is a distance \( \gr = \sqrt{s^2+z^2} \) from the field point.
For every piece, \( \dd{\vec{l'}}\cross\vu{\gr} \) points the same way: around the wire. So all the contributions add up; none cancel. Its size is \( \dd{z}\sin\alpha \), where \( \alpha \) is the angle between the wire and \( \vu{\gr} \), and from the geometry \( \sin\alpha = s/\sqrt{s^2+z^2} \). So
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{s^2+z^2}\frac{s}{\sqrt{s^2+z^2}}\dd{z} = \frac{\mu_0 I s}{4\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\dd{z}}{(s^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\] This is the same integral as in §2.1, now over the whole line:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\dd{z}}{(s^2+z^2)^{3/2}} = \left[ \frac{z}{s^2\sqrt{s^2+z^2}} \right]_{-\infty}^{\infty} = \frac{2}{s^2}\] Therefore
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I s}{4\pi}\frac{2}{s^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}\] circling the wire. Ampère's law (§5.3) gets this in one line, which is why it's usually preferred.
Example# Find the magnetic field a distance \( z \) above the centre of a circular loop of radius \( R \) carrying steady current \( I \).
Opposite pieces of the loop give fields tilted opposite ways. The sideways parts cancel; the parts along the axis add. Solution triple-click to reveal Every piece of the loop is the same distance \( \gr = \sqrt{R^2+z^2} \) from the field point. Also, each \( \dd{\vec{l'}} \) is at right angles to its \( \vu{\gr} \), so \( |\dd{\vec{l'}}\cross\vu{\gr}| = \dd{l'} \).
Each piece's contribution \( \dd{\vec{B}} \) is tilted away from the axis. Pieces on opposite sides of the loop cancel each other's sideways tilt, leaving only the part along the axis. That part has a factor \( \cos\theta = R/\sqrt{R^2+z^2} \):
\[B_z = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\frac{\cos\theta}{\gr^2}\oint \dd{l'} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\frac{R}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\left( 2\pi R \right)\] so
\[\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2}\frac{R^2}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\vu{z}\] At the centre (\( z=0 \)), \( B = \mu_0 I/2R \). Far away (\( z \gg R \)),
\[B \approx \frac{\mu_0}{2}\frac{IR^2}{z^3} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{z^3}\] with \( m = I\pi R^2 \) (current × area), the magnetic dipole moment. This is the field along the axis of a dipole, falling as \( 1/z^3 \), exactly like the electric dipole of §3.4. From far away, a small current loop behaves like a tiny bar magnet. §5.4 takes this further.
Full derivation: §5.2.

title: (5.3) The Divergence and Curl of B
content:
5.3 The Divergence and Curl of B# The Helmholtz theorem says a field is fixed by its divergence and curl. Both can be worked out from the Biot-Savart law.
The divergence# \[\div{\vec{B}} = 0\] everywhere, always, not just for steady currents. This is one of Maxwell's equations. It says there are no magnetic monopoles: no isolated north or south poles. Cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles. Magnetic field lines never start or stop; they always form closed loops.
Magnetic field lines have no ends: outside the magnet they run from N round to S, and inside back from S to N. Cut the magnet and each piece has both poles. Compare \( \div{\vec{E}} = \rho/\epsilon_0 \): electric field lines start and end on charges. There is no magnetic charge, so there's nothing on the right-hand side.
The curl: Ampère's law# \[\curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0 \vec{J}\] or, using Stokes' theorem, in integral form:
\[\oint \vec{B}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}\] Going round any closed loop, adding up \( \vec{B} \) along the loop gives \( \mu_0 \) times the current passing through the loop. \( I_{\text{enc}} \) is the current through any surface whose edge is the loop. It doesn't matter which surface you pick: for steady currents the same current passes through all of them.
Only currents through the loop count, with a sign from the right-hand rule (fingers along the loop, thumb gives +). Here \( I_{\text{enc}} = I_1 - I_2 \). This form of Ampère's law only works for steady currents. If \( \div{\vec{J}} \neq 0 \) (charge piling up somewhere, as on a charging capacitor), it contradicts itself: the divergence of a curl must be zero, but \( \div{(\mu_0\vec{J})} \neq 0 \). Maxwell's fix is in §7.3.
Using Ampère's law# Ampère's law always holds, but it only gives you \( \vec{B} \) easily when symmetry makes \( \vec{B} \) the same size along parts of a loop, and either along the loop or at right angles to it. That happens for:
long straight wires: use a circle around the wire flat sheets of current: use a rectangle poking through the sheet long solenoids (coils): use a rectangle with one side inside and one outside toroids (doughnut-shaped coils): use a circle inside the doughnut Standard results:
\[B_{\text{wire}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}, \qquad B_{\text{sheet}} = \frac{\mu_0 K}{2}, \qquad B_{\text{solenoid}} = \mu_0 n I\] where \( n \) is the number of turns per unit length. A solenoid's field is uniform inside and zero outside. A sheet's field doesn't weaken with distance, just like the electric field of a charged plane.
Cut through a long solenoid. The field inside is uniform and along the axis; outside it is zero. The dashed rectangle is the Amperian loop used in Example 5.3-a. A sheet of current. B is parallel to the sheet, opposite ways above and below, and the same size at any distance. The dashed rectangle is the Amperian loop. A toroid seen from above. B circles round inside the doughnut and is zero in the hole and outside. Comparison with electrostatics# Electrostatics Magnetostatics Source charge \( \rho \) current \( \vec{J} \) Divergence \( \div{\vec{E}} = \rho/\epsilon_0 \) \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) Curl \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) \( \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} \) Integral law Gauss Ampère Potential scalar \( V \) vector \( \vec{A} \) The two are mirror images. \( \vec{E} \) spreads out but doesn't swirl; \( \vec{B} \) swirls but doesn't spread out. That's why \( \vec{E} \) gets a scalar potential and \( \vec{B} \) gets a vector potential (§5.4).
E spreads out from charges but doesn't swirl. B swirls round currents but doesn't spread out. Example# Find the magnetic field inside and outside a long solenoid of \( n \) turns per unit length carrying current \( I \).
Solution triple-click to reveal First, which way does \( \vec{B} \) point? Along the axis. It can't point outward from the axis: then field lines would leave a cylinder around the axis without coming back, breaking \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \). And it can't circle the axis, because no current flows along the axis.
Outside. Draw a rectangular loop with both long sides outside the solenoid, at different distances from it. No current passes through the loop, so the field along the two long sides must be equal. So the field outside is the same at all distances. Very far away it must be zero, so it is zero everywhere outside:
\[\vec{B}_{\text{out}} = \vec{0}\] Inside. Draw a rectangular loop of length \( L \) with one long side inside the solenoid (along the axis) and the other outside. Only the inside edge contributes: the outside edge is in zero field, and the short sides are at right angles to \( \vec{B} \). The loop is crossed by \( nL \) turns of wire, each carrying \( I \):
\[BL = \mu_0 n L I \quad \Rightarrow \quad B = \mu_0 n I\] It didn't matter how far inside we put the edge, so the field is uniform inside. The solenoid is the magnetic version of a parallel-plate capacitor: a strong, uniform field neatly trapped inside.
Example# A thick wire of radius \( a \) carries a total current \( I \) distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Find the field inside and outside.
Solution triple-click to reveal The current density is \( J = I/\pi a^2 \), the same across the wire. By symmetry, \( \vec{B} \) circles the axis and its size depends only on the distance \( s \). Use a circular loop of radius \( s \) around the axis. On it, \( \vec{B} \) runs along the loop and has the same size everywhere:
\[\oint \vec{B}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = B(s)\,2\pi s = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}\] Outside (\( s > a \)), all the current passes through the loop:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}\] the same as a thin wire. From outside you can't tell how thick the wire is.
Inside (\( s < a \)), only the current within radius \( s \) passes through:
\[I_{\text{enc}} = J\pi s^2 = I\frac{s^2}{a^2}\] so
\[B(s)\,2\pi s = \mu_0 I \frac{s^2}{a^2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad B = \frac{\mu_0 I s}{2\pi a^2}\] The field rises steadily from zero at the centre to its largest value at the surface, then falls as \( 1/s \) outside. Compare the uniformly charged ball in §2.2: same shape of graph, for the same reason. Inside, the enclosed source grows faster than the loop does; outside, it stops growing.
B rises linearly inside the wire and falls as 1/s outside, with the peak at the surface. Full derivation: §5.3.

title: (5.4) Magnetic Vector Potential
content:
5.4 Magnetic Vector Potential# The vector potential# \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) always, so by §1.6 we can write \( \vec{B} \) as the curl of something:
\[\vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}}\] \( \vec{A} \) is the magnetic vector potential. It plays the role that \( V \) plays for \( \vec{E} = -\grad V \). The saving is smaller, though: \( V \) replaced three components with one number, but \( \vec{A} \) still has three components.
Gauge freedom and the Coulomb gauge# \( \vec{A} \) is not unique. Add the gradient of any function and \( \vec{B} \) doesn't change, because the curl of a gradient is zero:
\[\vec{A}' = \vec{A} + \grad \lambda \quad \Rightarrow \quad \curl{\vec{A}'} = \curl{\vec{A}}\] We can use this freedom to make \( \vec{A} \) as convenient as possible. The usual choice in magnetostatics is the Coulomb gauge:
\[\div{\vec{A}} = 0\] You can always arrange this. Starting from any \( \vec{A} \), pick \( \lambda \) to solve \( \laplacian\lambda = -\div{\vec{A}} \). That is just Poisson's equation, which always has a solution.
Poisson's equation for A# Put \( \vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}} \) into Ampère's law and use \( \curl{(\curl{\vec{A}})} = \grad(\div{\vec{A}}) - \laplacian\vec{A} \). In the Coulomb gauge the first term is zero, leaving
\[\laplacian \vec{A} = -\mu_0 \vec{J}\] That's three copies of Poisson's equation, one for each component. We already know how to solve Poisson's equation from electrostatics (\( \laplacian V = -\rho/\epsilon_0 \) gives \( V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \rho/\gr \)), so just copy the answer:
\[\vec{A}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r'})}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] or \( \vec{A} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int \dd{\vec{l'}}/\gr \) for a wire. There's no cross product, and \( \gr \) instead of \( \gr^2 \), so this is usually much easier than Biot-Savart. Handy picture: \( \vec{A} \) tends to point the same way as the current that makes it.
Boundary conditions# Crossing a sheet of surface current \( \vec{K} \):
\[\vec{B}_{\text{above}}^{\perp} = \vec{B}_{\text{below}}^{\perp}, \qquad \vec{B}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{B}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel} = \mu_0 \vec{K}\cross\vu{n}\] The perpendicular part doesn't jump (because \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \)). The parallel part does (because of Ampère's law). This is the opposite of \( \vec{E} \), where the perpendicular part jumps and the parallel part doesn't.
\( \vec{A} \) itself doesn't jump, but its slope does:
\[\vec{A}_{\text{above}} = \vec{A}_{\text{below}}, \qquad \pdv{\vec{A}_{\text{above}}}{n} - \pdv{\vec{A}_{\text{below}}}{n} = -\mu_0\vec{K}\] Multipole expansion and the magnetic dipole# Expanding \( 1/\gr \) as in §3.4 gives a multipole expansion for \( \vec{A} \). The monopole term is always zero for a closed current loop, because \( \oint \dd{\vec{l'}} = 0 \). That's the “no magnetic monopoles” rule showing up again.
So the first term is the dipole:
\[\vec{A}_{\text{dip}}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\vec{m}\cross\vu{r}}{r^2}\] with the magnetic dipole moment
\[\vec{m} \equiv I\int \dd{\vec{a}} = I\vec{a}\] which is current × area of the loop, pointing perpendicular to the loop (right-hand rule: fingers along the current, thumb along \( \vec{m} \)). Taking the curl gives a field with exactly the same shape as the electric dipole field of §3.4:
\[\vec{B}_{\text{dip}} = \frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}\left( 2\cos\theta\,\vu{r} + \sin\theta\,\vu{\theta} \right)\] There is never a monopole term, so far from any small current distribution the dipole term wins. (In electrostatics, any net charge would drown out the dipole.)
Left: the dipole moment of a current loop, by the right-hand rule. Right: its field lines pass up through the loop and close round outside. From far away this is a dipole field. Example# Find the vector potential of an infinite solenoid with \( n \) turns per unit length, radius \( R \), carrying current \( I \).
Solution triple-click to reveal The integral is awkward here, so use a trick. Apply Stokes' theorem to \( \vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}} \), over a disc of radius \( s \) centred on the solenoid's axis:
\[\oint \vec{A}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = \int (\curl{\vec{A}})\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} = \int \vec{B}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} = \Phi\] The line integral of \( \vec{A} \) round a loop equals the magnetic flux through the loop. It's just like Ampère's law, with \( \vec{A} \) in place of \( \vec{B} \) and flux in place of current.
By symmetry \( \vec{A} \) circles the axis and depends only on \( s \), so the left side is \( A(s),2\pi s \).
Inside (\( s < R \)), the field is uniform, \( \mu_0 n I \), so the flux is \( \mu_0 n I \pi s^2 \):
\[A(s)\,2\pi s = \mu_0 n I \pi s^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{A} = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2}s\,\vu{\phi}\] Outside (\( s > R \)), there's no field beyond \( R \), so the flux stops growing at \( \mu_0 n I \pi R^2 \):
\[\vec{A} = \frac{\mu_0 n I R^2}{2s}\vu{\phi}\] Notice: \( \vec{A} \) is not zero outside the solenoid, even though \( \vec{B} \) is. This is more than a mathematical curiosity. In the Aharonov-Bohm effect (a quantum effect), electrons that travel only through the field-free region outside a solenoid are still affected by \( \vec{A} \).
End view of the solenoid. A circles the axis: it grows like s inside and falls like 1/s outside, where B is zero but A is not. Example# A spherical shell of radius \( R \) carries uniform surface charge \( \sigma \) and rotates about the \( z \)-axis at angular velocity \( \omega \). Find its magnetic dipole moment.
Slice the spinning shell into rings. The ring at angle \( \theta \) is a current loop of radius \( R\sin\theta \). Solution triple-click to reveal Slice the shell into thin rings at angle \( \theta \), each of angular width \( \dd{\theta} \). A ring has radius \( R\sin\theta \), area \( \dd{a} = 2\pi R^2\sin\theta \dd{\theta} \), and so charge \( \dd{q} = \sigma 2\pi R^2 \sin\theta \dd{\theta} \).
Each ring goes round once every \( T = 2\pi/\omega \), so it is a current
\[\dd{I} = \frac{\dd{q}}{T} = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}\sigma 2\pi R^2 \sin\theta \dd{\theta} = \sigma \omega R^2 \sin\theta \dd{\theta}\] Its dipole moment is current × the area it encloses, \( \pi (R\sin\theta)^2 \):
\[\dd{m} = \pi R^2 \sin^2\theta \cdot \sigma\omega R^2 \sin\theta \dd{\theta} = \pi \sigma \omega R^4 \sin^3\theta \dd{\theta}\] Add up all the rings, using \( \int_0^\pi \sin^3\theta \dd{\theta} = 4/3 \):
\[m = \pi\sigma\omega R^4 \cdot \frac{4}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3}\sigma\omega R^4\] pointing along \( \vu{z} \). Every ring spins the same way, so all the contributions add; none cancel.
Full derivation: §5.4.
Chapter 5 recap# You have reached the end of Chapter 5. To recap, watch this short summary of the whole chapter by Dot Physics, and check that you have the main ideas.

title: (6.1) Magnetization
content:
6.1 Magnetization# Three kinds of magnetic material# Every material responds a little to a magnetic field by becoming magnetized. There are three types of response:
Paramagnets (e.g. aluminium, oxygen) become magnetized along the field, and are weakly pulled towards a magnet. Diamagnets (e.g. water, copper, bismuth) become magnetized against the field, and are weakly pushed away. In fact every material is diamagnetic; it just goes unnoticed when a stronger effect is also present. Ferromagnets (e.g. iron, nickel) stay magnetized after the field is removed. The effect is far stronger than the other two. This is what fridge magnets are. A paramagnet magnetizes along the field; a diamagnet (weakly) against it. In every case the cause is the tiny magnetic dipoles of atoms, which come from the electrons' orbits and from electron spin.
Twists and forces on magnetic dipoles# A current loop in a uniform field feels no net force (§5.1), but it does get twisted:
\[\vec{N} = \vec{m}\cross\vec{B}\] A loop seen edge-on. The forces on the two far sides are equal and opposite but not in line, so they twist the loop until \( \vec{m} \) lines up with \( \vec{B} \). This turns \( \vec{m} \) to line up with \( \vec{B} \), like a compass needle. That is how paramagnetism works, exactly like polar molecules lining up in §4.1. In most atoms, electrons pair up with opposite spins and their moments cancel. So paramagnetism usually needs an unpaired electron, typically from an odd number of electrons.
In a non-uniform field there is also a net force:
\[\vec{F} = \grad\left( \vec{m}\cdot\vec{B} \right)\] Above the end of a solenoid the field spreads out. Its outward part pushes every piece of the ring the same way, so there is a net force. Where diamagnetism comes from# Diamagnetism works differently, and happens even in atoms with no magnetic moment of their own. Picture an electron orbiting in a circle, which is a tiny current loop. Now switch on a field at right angles to the orbit. By Faraday's law (Chapter 7), a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, and that nudges the electron's speed up or down.
Changing the speed changes the loop's dipole moment. Working it through, the change in \( \vec{m} \) always points against the applied field, whichever way the electron was going round:
\[\Delta\vec{m} = -\frac{e^2 R^2}{4m_e}\vec{B}\] So the material is pushed away from the magnet. Because this needs no existing moment, it happens in every material. But it's much weaker than paramagnetism, so you only notice it when paramagnetism is absent.
Left: an orbiting electron is a tiny current loop; being negative, its \( \vec{m} \) is opposite to \( \vec{L} \) (the second example). Right: switching on B changes its speed so that \( \Delta\vec{m} \) always points against B. Magnetization# The large-scale description works just like §4.1. The magnetization is
\[\vec{M} \equiv \text{magnetic dipole moment per unit volume}\] with units A/m. Whatever happens inside the atoms, \( \vec{M} \) is all we need from now on. §6.2 works out the field a magnetized object produces.
Electric Magnetic Dipole moment \( \vec{p} \) \( \vec{m} \) Torque \( \vec{p}\cross\vec{E} \) \( \vec{m}\cross\vec{B} \) Density \( \vec{P} \) \( \vec{M} \) Lines up with field polar molecules paramagnets Opposes field — diamagnets Example# A square current loop of side \( a \) carrying current \( I \) is free to rotate about an axis in its plane, in a uniform field \( \vec{B} \) at angle \( \theta \) to the loop's normal. Find the torque and the energy.
Solution triple-click to reveal The dipole moment is \( m = Ia^2 \), pointing along the loop's normal (right-hand rule). The torque is
\[N = mB\sin\theta = Ia^2 B\sin\theta\] and it acts to make \( \theta \) smaller.
You can check this from the forces on the four sides. The field is perpendicular to the rotation axis. The two sides parallel to the axis each feel a force \( F = IaB \), in opposite directions. These forces are offset by a lever arm \( a\sin\theta \), giving \( N = IaB \cdot a\sin\theta \), as above. The other two sides feel equal and opposite forces along the same line (along the axis), so they cancel completely and give no twist.
The energy comes from integrating the torque, just as for the electric dipole in §4.1:
\[U = -\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B} = -Ia^2 B\cos\theta\] It is lowest at \( \theta = 0 \), with the loop's normal along \( \vec{B} \). That is the stable position. Atomic “loops” settling into this position is paramagnetism.
Example# Estimate the magnetic dipole moment of an electron in a circular orbit of radius \( R \) at speed \( v \), and express it in terms of the orbital angular momentum.
Solution triple-click to reveal The electron goes round once in time \( T = 2\pi R/v \), so it acts as a current
\[I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{ev}{2\pi R}\] The dipole moment is current × area:
\[m = I\pi R^2 = \frac{ev}{2\pi R}\pi R^2 = \frac{evR}{2}\] The orbital angular momentum is \( L = m_e v R \), so
\[m = \frac{e}{2m_e}L\] Magnetic moment is proportional to angular momentum. The constant \( e/2m_e \) is called the gyromagnetic ratio. The electron is negative, so \( \vec{m} \) points opposite to \( \vec{L} \).
This link explains why magnetism always goes with spinning or orbiting charge, and why electron spin (angular momentum without any actual orbit) gives a magnetic moment. The classical picture gets the right size, but spin is really a quantum effect, so treating it classically, as we do for materials, is a bit of a fudge (Griffiths admits as much).
Full derivation: §6.1.

title: (6.2) The Field of a Magnetized Object
content:
6.2 The Field of a Magnetized Object# Bound currents# If you know the magnetization \( \vec{M} \), you can get the vector potential by adding up all the tiny dipoles:
\[\vec{A}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{M}(\vec{r'})\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{\tau'}\] Each small piece \( \dd{\tau'} \) is a magnetic dipole \( \vec{m} = \vec{M}\dd{\tau'} \). Add up the vector potentials of all the pieces. Integrating by parts, just as in §4.2, splits this into a volume term and a surface term:
\[\vec{A}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_V \frac{\curl{\vec{M}}}{\gr}\dd{\tau'} + \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\oint_S \frac{\vec{M}\cross\vu{n}}{\gr}\dd{a'}\] These are the potentials of a volume current and a surface current:
\[\vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}}, \qquad \vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n}\] called the bound currents. So a magnetized object makes exactly the same field as these two ordinary currents, and everything from Chapter 5 applies.
What the bound currents really are# Bound currents are real flows of charge.
Surface current. Think of the magnetized material as a tightly packed grid of tiny current loops, all circulating the same way. Where two neighbouring loops touch, their currents run in opposite directions and cancel. At the outer edge there is no neighbour to cancel with, so a current is left flowing round the surface. (Like a crowd of people all walking in small clockwise circles: in the middle they cancel out, but round the edge there's a net flow.) Its size is \( |\vec{M}\cross\vu{n}| \). It's zero where \( \vec{M} \) points straight out of the surface, because then the loops lie flat in the surface and no current crosses the edge.
Tiny current loops, all circulating the same way. Inside, the sides of neighbouring loops cancel; round the edge a current is left over. Volume current. If the magnetization is uneven, neighbouring loops don't quite cancel: a stronger loop next to a weaker one leaves a bit of current over. The curl measures exactly this leftover.
Where M is uneven, a stronger loop beside a weaker one leaves a net current on their shared side. Bound currents always have \( \div{\vec{J}_b} = 0 \) (the divergence of a curl is zero). That has to be so: they flow in closed loops and charge never piles up anywhere.
Comparison with bound charges# Electric Magnetic Volume \( \rho_b = -\div{\vec{P}} \) \( \vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}} \) Surface \( \sigma_b = \vec{P}\cdot\vu{n} \) \( \vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n} \) The same pattern as before: divergence and dot product for electric, curl and cross product for magnetic.
Example# Find the field of a uniformly magnetized sphere of radius \( R \), with \( \vec{M} = M\vu{z} \).
Solution triple-click to reveal The magnetization is uniform, so \( \curl{\vec{M}} = \vec{0} \): no bound volume current. The bound surface current is
\[\vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n} = M\vu{z}\cross\vu{r} = M\sin\theta\,\vu{\phi}\] It flows round the sphere like lines of latitude, strongest at the equator and zero at the poles.
That is exactly the current on a spinning charged spherical shell. From §5.4, a shell with charge \( \sigma \) spinning at \( \omega \) has \( K = \sigma\omega R\sin\theta \). So we can reuse that answer with \( \sigma\omega R \) replaced by \( M \).
The field of a spinning shell is uniform inside and a pure dipole outside:
\[\vec{B}_{\text{in}} = \frac{2}{3}\mu_0 \vec{M}\] and outside, the field of a dipole with total moment
\[\vec{m} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \vec{M}\] which is magnetization × volume.
The uniformly magnetized sphere. The bound current runs round it like lines of latitude (out of the page on the left, into it on the right). B is uniform inside and makes closed loops. Notice that \( \vec{B} \) inside points along \( \vec{M} \). The electrically polarized sphere of §4.2 had \( \vec{E} = -\vec{P}/3\epsilon_0 \) inside, pointing against \( \vec{P} \). The electric and magnetic cases are very similar, but not identical, and this sign is where they differ. (§6.3 explains why.)
Between the charges of an electric dipole the field points against p. Through a current loop the magnetic field points along m. Example# An infinite cylinder of radius \( R \) carries magnetization \( \vec{M} = k s^2 \vu{\phi} \), where \( s \) is the distance from the axis. Find the bound currents and the resulting field.
End view. \( \vec{J}_b \) flows out of the page inside, and \( \vec{K}_b \) flows back into it round the rim. Solution triple-click to reveal Volume current. \( \vec{M} \) only circles the axis and only depends on \( s \), so the curl in cylindrical coordinates is
\[\vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}} = \frac{1}{s}\pdv{}{s}\left( s M_\phi \right)\vu{z} = \frac{1}{s}\pdv{}{s}\left( k s^3 \right)\vu{z} = 3ks\,\vu{z}\] This flows along the cylinder, more strongly further from the axis.
Surface current. On the curved surface \( \vu{n} = \vu{s} \), so
\[\vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n} = kR^2\left( \vu{\phi}\cross\vu{s} \right) = -kR^2\,\vu{z}\] flowing the opposite way, back down the outside.
Check: bound currents form closed loops, so the total should be zero:
\[\int \vec{J}_b \cdot \dd{\vec{a}} + \oint K_b \dd{l} = \int_0^R (3ks)2\pi s\dd{s} - kR^2(2\pi R) = 2\pi k R^3 - 2\pi k R^3 = 0\] ✓
Field. Use Ampère's law on a circle of radius \( s < R \) around the axis. The current through it is \( \int_0^s 3ks',2\pi s' \dd{s'} = 2\pi k s^3 \):
\[B(s)\,2\pi s = \mu_0 2\pi k s^3 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{B} = \mu_0 k s^2 \vu{\phi} = \mu_0\vec{M}\] Outside, the total current through the loop is zero, so \( \vec{B} = \vec{0} \), which fits with \( \vec{M} \) being zero there too.
Full derivation: §6.2.

title: (6.3) The Auxiliary Field H
content:
6.3 The Auxiliary Field H# Ampère's law in magnetized materials# In magnetized matter there are two kinds of current. Bound current comes from the magnetization. Free current is charge actually flowing, the current you drive through wires with a battery and control:
\[\vec{J} = \vec{J}_b + \vec{J}_f\] Ampère's law counts all of it. Put in \( \vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}} \):
\[\frac{1}{\mu_0}\curl{\vec{B}} = \vec{J}_f + \curl{\vec{M}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \curl{\left( \frac{\vec{B}}{\mu_0} - \vec{M} \right)} = \vec{J}_f\] Now define the auxiliary field
\[\vec{H} \equiv \frac{\vec{B}}{\mu_0} - \vec{M}\] and Ampère's law becomes
\[\curl{\vec{H}} = \vec{J}_f, \qquad \oint \vec{H}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = I_{f,\text{enc}}\] The reason is the same as for \( \vec{D} \) in §4.3. You know the free current, because you set it. You don't know the bound current, since it depends on the magnetization, which depends on the field you're trying to find. With \( \vec{H} \) you only need what you know.
\( \vec{H} \) is measured in amperes per metre, like \( \vec{M} \). In the lab, \( \vec{H} \) is what you control directly (by setting the current in a coil). So engineers often call \( \vec{H} \) “the magnetic field” and \( \vec{B} \) the “flux density”. Physicists usually reserve “magnetic field” for \( \vec{B} \). Watch out for this when reading other books.
A trap: H is not just like B# It's tempting to think of \( \vec{H} \) as “\( \vec{B}/\mu_0 \) with the bound current hidden”. As with \( \vec{D} \), that's only half true. Take the divergence:
\[\div{\vec{H}} = -\div{\vec{M}}\] This is not zero in general.
Even though there are no magnetic charges, \( \div{\vec{H}} \) can be non-zero. So knowing the free current is not enough to find \( \vec{H} \) in general. The symmetry trick of §5.3 works for \( \vec{H} \) only when \( \div{\vec{M}} = 0 \) too. Example: a bar magnet has no free current at all, so \( \curl{\vec{H}} = \vec{0} \) everywhere, yet \( \vec{H} \neq \vec{0} \).
At the end of a magnetized rod M stops suddenly. A pillbox across the end has a net outflow of M, so \( \div{\vec{H}} = -\div{\vec{M}} \neq 0 \) there. This is the mirror image of §4.3: \( \vec{D} \) had the right divergence but the wrong curl; \( \vec{H} \) has the right curl but the wrong divergence. Neither can be found from its own law alone. You also need to know how the material responds.
Boundary conditions# \[H_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - H_{\text{below}}^{\perp} = -\left( M_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - M_{\text{below}}^{\perp} \right)\] \[\vec{H}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{H}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel} = \vec{K}_f \cross \vu{n}\] The parallel part jumps by the free surface current. The perpendicular part jumps by the change in magnetization.
Example# A long copper rod of radius \( R \) carries uniformly distributed free current \( I \). Find \( \vec{H} \) inside and outside the rod.
End view. H circles the axis; the dashed circle is the Amperian loop. Solution triple-click to reveal The setup has cylindrical symmetry, and the copper's magnetization circles the axis, so \( \div{\vec{M}} = 0 \). The symmetry trick for \( \vec{H} \) is allowed.
Use a circle of radius \( s \) around the axis. On it \( \vec{H} \) runs along the circle with constant size, so
\[\oint \vec{H}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = H(s)\,2\pi s = I_{f,\text{enc}}\] Inside (\( s<R \)), the free current through the circle is \( I s^2/R^2 \):
\[\vec{H} = \frac{I s}{2\pi R^2}\vu{\phi}\] Outside (\( s>R \)), all the current goes through:
\[\vec{H} = \frac{I}{2\pi s}\vu{\phi}\] We never needed to know how the copper is magnetized. Outside the rod, \( \vec{M} = 0 \), so \( \vec{B} = \mu_0\vec{H} \). Inside, getting \( \vec{B} \) needs \( \vec{M} \), which §6.4 provides. For copper the difference is tiny (its susceptibility is about \( 10^{-5} \)), so \( \vec{B} \approx \mu_0\vec{H} \) is an excellent approximation.
Example# A uniformly magnetized sphere carries \( \vec{M} = M\vu{z} \) and no free current. Find \( \vec{H} \) inside, and account for the sign.
Solution triple-click to reveal From §6.2, the field inside is \( \vec{B}_{\text{in}} = \frac{2}{3}\mu_0\vec{M} \). By definition,
\[\vec{H} = \frac{\vec{B}}{\mu_0} - \vec{M} = \frac{2}{3}\vec{M} - \vec{M} = -\frac{1}{3}\vec{M}\] So inside the sphere \( \vec{H} \) points opposite to both \( \vec{M} \) and \( \vec{B} \).
Think about this. There's no free current anywhere, so \( \curl{\vec{H}} = \vec{0} \) everywhere, and \( \oint \vec{H}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = 0 \) round every loop. Yet \( \vec{H} \) is not zero. “No free current, so \( \vec{H} = 0 \)” is a tempting but wrong conclusion.
The reason: at the surface, \( \vec{M} \) suddenly drops to zero, so \( \div{\vec{H}} = -\div{\vec{M}} \neq 0 \) there. A field with zero curl but non-zero divergence is not fixed by Ampère's law.
Also notice that \( \vec{H} = -\vec{M}/3 \) looks exactly like the electric result \( \vec{E} = -\vec{P}/3\epsilon_0 \) for the polarized sphere. So in the electric–magnetic comparison, it is really \( \vec{H} \) (not \( \vec{B} \)) that behaves like \( \vec{E} \) here. That explains the sign difference noted in §6.2, and it's a good reason for introducing \( \vec{H} \) at all.
The same sphere. B makes closed loops. H runs from the north face to the south face and points against M inside, exactly like E for the polarized sphere of §4.2. Full derivation: §6.3.

title: (6.4) Linear and Nonlinear Media
content:
6.4 Linear and Nonlinear Media# Magnetic susceptibility and permeability# For paramagnets and diamagnets, as long as the field isn't too strong, the magnetization is proportional to the field. By convention it's written using \( \vec{H} \), not \( \vec{B} \):
\[\vec{M} = \chi_m \vec{H}\] \( \chi_m \) is the magnetic susceptibility, a pure number. Materials like this are called linear media.
Using \( \vec{H} \) here is a bit odd. The electric version, \( \vec{P} = \epsilon_0\chi_e\vec{E} \), uses \( \vec{E} \), not \( \vec{D} \). But the convention is too well established to change, and it makes the link between \( \vec{B} \) and \( \vec{H} \) simple:
\[\vec{B} = \mu_0\left( \vec{H} + \vec{M} \right) = \mu_0(1+\chi_m)\vec{H} \equiv \mu\vec{H}\] \( \mu = \mu_0(1+\chi_m) \) is the permeability, and \( \mu_r = \mu/\mu_0 \) the relative permeability.
The sign of \( \chi_m \) tells you the type:
Type \( \chi_m \) Typical size Behaviour Paramagnetic positive \( \sim 10^{-5} \) weakly attracted Diamagnetic negative \( \sim 10^{-5} \) weakly repelled Both are tiny. That's why most everyday materials seem non-magnetic. In a uniform linear material, the bound volume current is tied to the free current:
\[\vec{J}_b = \chi_m \vec{J}_f\] So if no free current flows through the material, the only bound current is on its surface.
Ferromagnetism# Ferromagnets are not linear, and \( \chi_m \) doesn't make sense for them. Their magnetization doesn't just depend on the field now; it depends on what has happened to the sample before. It has a memory.
The cause is a quantum-mechanical effect that makes neighbouring atomic dipoles line up with each other, whether or not there is an outside field. The whole piece doesn't line up in one direction, because that would cost too much energy. Instead it splits into small regions called domains. Each domain is strongly magnetized, but different domains point in random directions, so an ordinary lump of iron looks unmagnetized overall.
Left: domains pointing every way, so the lump is unmagnetized overall. Right: in a field, the domains along it grow at the expense of the others. Apply a field, and domains pointing along it grow while the others shrink. This is largely irreversible: remove the field and much of the alignment stays, leaving a permanent magnet. If you plot \( \vec{M} \) against \( \vec{H} \) while sweeping the field up and down, you don't get a single curve but a loop, called a hysteresis loop. The area inside the loop is energy lost as heat each cycle (that's why transformer cores get warm).
A hysteresis loop. The dashed curve is the first magnetization. Coming back from saturation, B is still large at H = 0 (the remanent field) and only drops to zero at the coercive field. Heat destroys ferromagnetism. Above the Curie temperature (770 °C for iron), thermal jiggling beats the aligning effect, the domains break up, and the material becomes an ordinary paramagnet. The change is sudden: a true phase transition, like ice melting.
Example# An infinite solenoid with \( n \) turns per unit length carrying current \( I \) is filled with a linear magnetic material of susceptibility \( \chi_m \). Find \( \vec{H} \), \( \vec{B} \), and the bound surface current.
Solution triple-click to reveal Use Ampère's law for \( \vec{H} \) with the usual rectangular loop. Only the free current in the windings counts:
\[\vec{H} = nI\,\vu{z}\] That's the same as for an empty solenoid, since \( \vec{H} \) only cares about free current. Then
\[\vec{B} = \mu\vec{H} = \mu_0(1+\chi_m)nI\,\vu{z}\] so the field is \( \mu_r \) times what it would be with the solenoid empty. The magnetization is
\[\vec{M} = \chi_m\vec{H} = \chi_m n I \,\vu{z}\] It's uniform, so there's no bound volume current. The bound surface current is
\[\vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n} = \chi_m n I\,\vu{\phi}\] For a paramagnet (\( \chi_m > 0 \)) it flows the same way as the current in the windings, adding to it and strengthening \( \vec{B} \). For a diamagnet it flows the opposite way and weakens \( \vec{B} \). That's how the material changes the field.
An iron core can boost the field by a factor of thousands. But iron isn't linear, so this calculation doesn't apply to it directly.
End view, paramagnetic core. The bound surface current flows the same way as the winding current, so B is stronger. Example# A current \( I \) flows down a long straight wire of radius \( a \), which is made of a linear material with susceptibility \( \chi_m \). Find the field inside the wire and the bound currents.
Solution triple-click to reveal Take the free current to be spread evenly across the wire. Ampère's law for \( \vec{H} \) on a circle of radius \( s < a \) gives, as in §6.3,
\[\vec{H} = \frac{Is}{2\pi a^2}\vu{\phi}\] Then
\[\vec{B} = \mu\vec{H} = \frac{\mu I s}{2\pi a^2}\vu{\phi}, \qquad \vec{M} = \chi_m\vec{H} = \frac{\chi_m I s}{2\pi a^2}\vu{\phi}\] The magnetization is uneven, so there is a bound volume current:
\[\vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}} = \frac{1}{s}\pdv{}{s}\left( s M_\phi \right)\vu{z} = \frac{\chi_m I}{\pi a^2}\vu{z}\] That is \( \chi_m \) times the free current density \( J_f = I/\pi a^2 \), as the general rule says.
The bound surface current is
\[\vec{K}_b = \vec{M}\cross\vu{n} = \frac{\chi_m I}{2\pi a}\left( \vu{\phi}\cross\vu{s} \right) = -\frac{\chi_m I}{2\pi a}\vu{z}\] The total bound current is \( \chi_m I - \chi_m I = 0 \), as it must be. The volume current carries \( \chi_m I \) down the wire and the surface current brings the same amount back.
For \( \chi_m > 0 \): the bound volume current runs with the free current, and the bound surface current brings the same amount back. Full derivation: §6.4.
Chapter 6 recap# You have reached the end of Chapter 6. To recap, watch this short summary of the whole chapter by Dot Physics, and check that you have the main ideas.

title: (7.1) Electromotive Force
content:
7.1 Electromotive Force# Ohm's law# To keep a current flowing, you have to keep pushing the charges. In most materials the current density is proportional to the push (force per unit charge):
\[\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{f} = \sigma\left( \vec{E} + \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \right)\] \( \sigma \) is the conductivity of the material (big for copper, tiny for glass), and \( \rho = 1/\sigma \) is its resistivity. (Don't confuse these with surface charge and charge density, which use the same letters.) Usually the magnetic part is negligible, leaving
\[\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E}\] A uniform \( \vec{E} \) inside the resistor drives a current density \( \vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E} \). This isn't a law of nature. It's a description of how ordinary materials happen to behave. Charges in a metal don't speed up forever; they keep bumping into atoms, so they drift along at a steady average speed. That's why the current is proportional to the force, not to how long it has been pushing.
For a wire of uniform cross-section this becomes the familiar
\[V = IR\] and energy turns into heat at the rate
\[P = VI = I^2 R\] This is Joule heating: the work done against those collisions. It's what makes a kettle element or a light-bulb filament hot.
Inside a wire carrying a steady current, \( \vec{E} \) is not zero. The rule “\( \vec{E} = 0 \) inside a conductor” is only for charges at rest (§2.5). Here the field is exactly what pushes the current along.
Electromotive force# Something has to drive the charges round a circuit and keep them going despite the losses: a battery, a generator, a solar cell. The electromotive force (emf) is the total push per unit charge, added up all the way round the circuit:
\[\mathcal{E} = \oint \vec{f}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}}\] The name is misleading: emf is not a force. It's energy per unit charge, measured in volts. For an ideal battery (no internal resistance) it equals the voltage between the terminals.
The battery's force \( \vec{f}_s \) pushes charge round the circuit. The emf is the push per unit charge added up all the way round. Motional emf# The most common source of emf is moving a wire through a magnetic field. When a loop of wire moves through a field, the magnetic force on the charges inside it has a part along the wire, which pushes them round the circuit. This is how power-station generators work.
Working this out for a loop gives the flux rule:
\[\mathcal{E} = -\dv{\Phi}{t}, \qquad \Phi \equiv \int \vec{B}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}}\] The emf round a loop equals minus the rate of change of the magnetic flux through it.
The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current always flows in the direction that fights the change that caused it. It has to be this way, or energy wouldn't be conserved. A current that helped its own cause would grow forever, giving free energy.
Lenz's law. As the magnet falls, the downward flux through the ring grows, so the induced current makes an upward field to fight it. There's a puzzle here: this emf comes from the magnetic force, yet magnetic forces do no work (§5.1). The answer (§8.3) is that the magnetic force only redirects energy; the energy itself comes from whoever is moving the loop.
Example# A rectangular loop of width \( w \) is pulled at constant speed \( v \) out of a region of uniform field \( B \) directed into the page. Find the emf, the induced current if the loop has resistance \( R \), and the force required.
The loop is pulled out at speed v. The current flows clockwise, and the force on the end still in the field pulls back against you. Solution triple-click to reveal Let \( x \) be how much of the loop is still in the field. The flux is
\[\Phi = Bwx\] and it shrinks as the loop comes out, since \( \dd{x}/\dd{t} = -v \). By the flux rule,
\[\mathcal{E} = -\dv{\Phi}{t} = -Bw\dv{x}{t} = Bwv\] The current is \( I = \mathcal{E}/R = Bwv/R \). By Lenz's law it flows so as to fight the loss of flux, which means it makes its own field into the page inside the loop.
This current flows through the end of the loop that's still in the field, so that piece of wire feels a magnetic force \( F = IwB \), pulling back against the motion:
\[F = \frac{B^2 w^2 v}{R}\] To keep the speed constant you must pull with an equal force. Your power is
\[P = Fv = \frac{B^2w^2v^2}{R} = I^2 R\] That is exactly the rate at which heat is produced in the loop. All the heat comes from you, the one pulling. The magnetic field supplies none of it, which fits with magnetic forces doing no work.
Example# A metal disc of radius \( a \) rotates at angular velocity \( \omega \) about its axis in a uniform field \( \vec{B} \) parallel to that axis. Sliding contacts connect the centre to the rim. Find the emf.
The Faraday disc. \( \vec{v}\times\vec{B} \) points straight out along every radius, driving current from the axle to the rim. Solution triple-click to reveal This is the Faraday disc. The flux rule is awkward here, because it's not clear which loop's flux is changing. So work directly from the force on the charges.
A charge at radius \( s \) moves round at speed \( v = \omega s \). The magnetic force per unit charge is
\[\vec{f} = \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} = \omega s B \left( \vu{\phi}\cross\vu{z} \right) = \omega s B\,\vu{s}\] pointing straight outward. Add it up along a radius from centre to rim:
\[\mathcal{E} = \int_0^a \vec{f}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = \int_0^a \omega s B \dd{s} = \frac{\omega B a^2}{2}\] The emf is steady, not alternating, so this is a direct-current (DC) generator. It was the first electric generator ever built.
Faraday used this same setup in the experiments described in §7.4, spinning the disc and the magnet in different combinations to test whether a spinning magnet drags its field lines round with it.
Full derivation: §7.1.

title: (7.2) Electromagnetic Induction
content:
7.2 Electromagnetic Induction# Faraday's law# Faraday found that an emf appears in a loop whenever the flux through it changes, and it doesn't matter how the change happens:
move the loop through a steady field (motional emf, explained in §7.1 by the magnetic force on the charges); keep the loop still and move the magnet; keep everything still and change the field's strength (e.g. turn up the current in an electromagnet). Faraday's three experiments. In all three a current flows in the loop. The Lorentz force explains case 1. It can't explain cases 2 and 3: the charges in the loop aren't moving, so there's no magnetic force on them. Something else is pushing the current, and the only candidate is an electric field.
Faraday's conclusion: a changing magnetic field creates an electric field.
\[\mathcal{E} = \oint \vec{E}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = -\dv{\Phi}{t} = -\int \pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}}\] Using Stokes' theorem gives the differential form:
\[\curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\] This is another of Maxwell's equations. It replaces the electrostatic rule \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \), which turns out to be just the special case where nothing changes with time.
This matters: the induced electric field swirls. It is not conservative. It can't be written as the gradient of a potential, and its line integral round a closed loop is not zero. (That's the whole point: it pushes charge round the loop.) So the potential methods of Chapters 2–3 don't work for it.
A shortcut: copy magnetostatics# \( \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t} \) has exactly the same form as Ampère's law \( \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} \), with \( -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t} \) in place of \( \mu_0\vec{J} \). So every magnetostatics answer can be reused: wherever a current would make a certain \( \vec{B} \), a changing field \( -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t} \) of the same shape makes an \( \vec{E} \) of the same shape.
For symmetric problems, this is the fastest method: use the integral form just like an Ampère's-law loop.
A growing field out of the page makes an electric field that circles it clockwise. The pattern is the same as B round a current: it grows like s inside and falls like 1/s outside. Inductance# A current \( I_1 \) in one loop sends flux through a second loop:
\[\Phi_2 = M_{21}I_1\] \( M_{21} \) is the mutual inductance, and it depends only on the shapes and positions of the loops. A surprising fact is that
\[M_{12} = M_{21} \equiv M\] Current \( I \) in loop 1 sends the same flux through loop 2 as current \( I \) in loop 2 sends through loop 1, however different the loops are. This is often the easiest way to find \( M \): work it out whichever way round is simpler.
Some of the field of loop 1 passes through loop 2. The flux is proportional to the current: Φ₂ = M I₁. A changing current also creates an emf in its own loop:
\[\Phi = LI, \qquad \mathcal{E} = -L\dv{I}{t}\] \( L \) is the self-inductance, measured in henries (H). By Lenz's law, this “back emf” fights any change in the current. So inductance acts like inertia for current: the current in an inductor can't change suddenly, just as a heavy object can't suddenly change speed.
Close the switch and the current doesn't jump: it rises smoothly to \( \mathcal{E}_0/R \), with time constant \( L/R \). Energy in magnetic fields# Starting a current takes work against the back emf. Adding it up,
\[W = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\] (compare kinetic energy \( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \), with \( L \) like mass). Written in terms of the field instead of the circuit,
\[W = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}\int_{\text{all space}} B^2 \dd{\tau}\] which matches the electric \( W = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int E^2 \dd{\tau} \) of §2.4. Put them together to get the total energy per unit volume stored in an electromagnetic field:
\[u = \frac{1}{2}\left( \epsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2 \right)\] You will use this throughout Chapter 8.
Example# Find the self-inductance of a long solenoid of length \( l \), radius \( R \), with \( n \) turns per unit length. Verify the stored energy two ways.
Solution triple-click to reveal The field inside is \( B = \mu_0 n I \), uniform, and zero outside. The flux through one turn is \( B\pi R^2 \). There are \( nl \) turns, and the flux passes through every one of them:
\[\Phi = (nl)\left( \mu_0 n I \pi R^2 \right) = \mu_0 n^2 l \pi R^2 I\] So
\[L = \frac{\Phi}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 \pi R^2 l\] It depends only on the geometry and how tightly it's wound, as it should.
Energy from the circuit:
\[W = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n^2\pi R^2 l I^2\] Energy from the field: the field fills the inside, volume \( \pi R^2 l \), and is uniform, so
\[W = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2\left( \pi R^2 l \right) = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}\left( \mu_0 n I \right)^2 \pi R^2 l = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n^2 \pi R^2 l I^2\] The two agree. ✓
Example# A short circular loop of radius \( a \) lies on the axis of a long solenoid of radius \( b \) with \( n \) turns per unit length, where \( a \ll b \). Find the mutual inductance.
The small loop sits in the uniform field inside the solenoid, so the flux through it is just B × its area. Solution triple-click to reveal The hard way: run current through the small loop and find the flux through the whole solenoid. The small loop's field is a messy dipole field, and you'd have to integrate it over every turn of the solenoid.
The easy way: use \( M_{12} = M_{21} \) and go the other way round. Run current \( I \) through the solenoid. Its field inside is uniform:
\[B = \mu_0 n I\] The small loop sits inside this uniform field, so the flux through it is just field × area:
\[\Phi_{\text{loop}} = \mu_0 n I \pi a^2\] So
\[M = \frac{\Phi_{\text{loop}}}{I} = \mu_0 n \pi a^2\] By reciprocity, that's also the flux through the solenoid per unit current in the small loop. We got it without ever touching the dipole field.
Notice that \( M \) depends on the small loop's radius but not the solenoid's, as long as the loop is inside where the field is uniform.
Full derivation: §7.2.

title: (7.3) Maxwell's Equations
content:
7.3 Maxwell's Equations# The problem before Maxwell# After Faraday, the four laws were
\[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \quad \div{\vec{B}} = 0, \quad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}, \quad \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J}\] and the last one contradicts itself. Take the divergence of both sides. The left side is always zero (the divergence of a curl is zero). The right side is \( \mu_0\div{\vec{J}} \), which by the continuity equation is \( -\mu_0\pdv{\rho}{t} \). That is only zero if charge isn't piling up anywhere, i.e. for steady currents.
You can see the problem with a charging capacitor. Ampère's law says: the line integral of \( \vec{B} \) round a loop is \( \mu_0 \) times the current through any surface with that loop as its edge. Put a loop round the wire leading to the capacitor.
Choose a flat surface that the wire passes through: the answer is \( \mu_0 I \). Choose a surface that bulges out like a bag and passes between the plates, where there is no wire: no current passes through it, so the answer is zero. Same loop, two different answers. Something is missing.
The same loop bounds two surfaces. The wire passes through surface 1. Nothing flows through surface 2, which passes between the plates, but the electric field there is changing. The displacement current# Maxwell's fix was to add a term involving the rate of change of the electric field:
\[\curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{\vec{E}}{t}\] The new piece, \( \vec{J}_d = \epsilon_0\pdv{\vec{E}}{t} \), is called the displacement current. No charge actually flows, so it isn't really a current, but it appears in the equation exactly as if it were one.
Now taking the divergence gives zero on both sides, because
\[\div{\vec{J}} + \epsilon_0\pdv{}{t}\left( \div{\vec{E}} \right) = \div{\vec{J}} + \pdv{\rho}{t} = 0\] by the continuity equation. The contradiction is gone. For the capacitor: between the plates, the electric field is growing as charge builds up, and its displacement current exactly makes up for the missing wire current. Both surfaces now give \( \mu_0 I \).
Maxwell saw the huge consequence straight away. With this new term, a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. So the two can keep creating each other, travelling through empty space with no charges or currents at all. That travelling disturbance is light. Chapter 9 works this out.
A changing E makes a circulating B; the changing B makes a circulating E; and so on. The chain carries itself along at c: light. Maxwell's equations# \[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\] \[\div{\vec{B}} = 0, \qquad \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{\vec{E}}{t}\] In words:
Electric field lines start and end on charges (Gauss). A changing magnetic field creates a swirling electric field (Faraday). There are no magnetic charges; magnetic field lines form closed loops. Currents and changing electric fields create swirling magnetic fields (Ampère–Maxwell). Together with the Lorentz force law \( \vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\cross\vec{B}) \) and the continuity equation, these contain all of classical electrodynamics.
Magnetic charge# The equations are lopsided: \( \vec{E} \) has a source (charge) and \( \vec{B} \) doesn't. If magnetic charge \( \rho_m \) and magnetic current \( \vec{J}_m \) existed, the equations would be symmetric:
\[\div{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\rho_m, \qquad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\mu_0\vec{J}_m - \pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\] But no magnetic monopole has ever been found, so as far as we know \( \rho_m = \vec{J}_m = 0 \). The lopsidedness is a fact of experiment; nothing in the theory forbids monopoles.
Maxwell's equations in matter# Split the charges and currents into free and bound parts, as in §4.3 and §6.3. (When the polarization changes with time, the moving bound charge makes a “polarization current”, which must be included too.) The result is
\[\div{\vec{D}} = \rho_f, \qquad \curl{\vec{H}} = \vec{J}_f + \pdv{\vec{D}}{t}\] with the other two equations unchanged. For linear materials, \( \vec{D} = \epsilon\vec{E} \) and \( \vec{H} = \vec{B}/\mu \), which completes the set.
Boundary conditions# At a boundary between two materials, with free surface charge \( \sigma_f \) and free surface current \( \vec{K}_f \):
\[D_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - D_{\text{below}}^{\perp} = \sigma_f, \qquad B_{\text{above}}^{\perp} - B_{\text{below}}^{\perp} = 0\] \[\vec{E}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{E}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel} = \vec{0}, \qquad \vec{H}_{\text{above}}^{\parallel} - \vec{H}_{\text{below}}^{\parallel} = \vec{K}_f\cross\vu{n}\] With no free charge or current on the boundary, all four right-hand sides are zero. These conditions are what give the laws of reflection and refraction in Chapter 9.
A thin pillbox across the boundary gives the conditions on the perpendicular parts (D and B); a thin loop gives those on the parallel parts (E and H). Example# A parallel-plate capacitor with circular plates of radius \( R \) is being charged by a steady current \( I \). Find the magnetic field between the plates at radius \( s < R \).
Solution triple-click to reveal No real current flows between the plates, so the magnetic field there comes entirely from the displacement current.
The field between the plates is \( E = \sigma/\epsilon_0 = Q/\epsilon_0\pi R^2 \), so
\[\pdv{E}{t} = \frac{1}{\epsilon_0 \pi R^2}\dv{Q}{t} = \frac{I}{\epsilon_0\pi R^2}\] Use the corrected Ampère's law on a circle of radius \( s \) between the plates. The displacement current through it is
\[I_d = \epsilon_0 \pdv{E}{t}\left( \pi s^2 \right) = I\frac{s^2}{R^2}\] so
\[B(s)\,2\pi s = \mu_0 I \frac{s^2}{R^2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I s}{2\pi R^2}\vu{\phi}\] This is exactly the field inside a thick wire of radius \( R \) carrying current \( I \) (§5.3). The displacement current is spread evenly across the gap, just as a real current would be across a wire. At \( s = R \) it joins smoothly onto the outside field \( \mu_0 I/2\pi R \).
End view while the capacitor charges. The growing E acts like a current spread over the plate, and B circles round it. Example# Show that Maxwell's equations in a region with no charges or currents admit solutions in which \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) satisfy a wave equation, and identify the propagation speed.
Solution triple-click to reveal With \( \rho = 0 \) and \( \vec{J} = \vec{0} \), take the curl of Faraday's law:
\[\curl{(\curl{\vec{E}})} = \curl{\left( -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t} \right)} = -\pdv{}{t}\left( \curl{\vec{B}} \right)\] On the right, use Ampère's law with the displacement term. On the left, use the identity \( \curl{(\curl{\vec{E}})} = \grad(\div{\vec{E}}) - \laplacian\vec{E} \), with \( \div{\vec{E}} = 0 \):
\[-\laplacian\vec{E} = -\mu_0\epsilon_0 \pdv{^2\vec{E}}{t^2}\] that is,
\[\laplacian\vec{E} = \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{^2\vec{E}}{t^2}\] This is the wave equation, with speed
\[v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = 3.00\times10^8\ \text{m/s}\] The same steps give the same equation for \( \vec{B} \).
This is remarkable. The speed comes entirely from two constants measured in experiments with charges, wires and magnets, which had nothing to do with light. Yet it equals the measured speed of light. That's how Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Chapter 9 develops this.
Notice the displacement term is essential. Without it the right-hand side would be zero and there would be no waves.
Full derivation: §7.3.

title: (7.4) The Field of a Rotating Magnet
content:
7.4 The Field of a Rotating Magnet# The question# Take a magnet that is symmetric about an axis (a cylindrical bar magnet, or the Earth) and spin it steadily about that axis. Does its magnetic field stay still, or does it spin round with the magnet? Are the field lines dragged round as it turns?
This section is about ideas only; there are no new calculations. It's here because students ask this question all the time, and the answer is subtler than it looks.
Faraday's experiments# Faraday tested this using the spinning disc of §7.1, with a magnet on the disc's axis, and tried every combination:
Configuration Result Magnet still, disc rotating current flows Magnet and disc rotating together current flows Disc still, magnet rotating no current Faraday's test: a disc above a magnet on the same axis, with a meter connected between the axle and the rim. Look at the pattern: only the disc's motion matters. Whether the magnet spins or not makes no difference. So Faraday concluded that a spinning magnet's field is exactly the same as a still magnet's: a magnet spinning about its symmetry axis does not drag its field round with it.
Not everyone agreed until 1912, when experiments by S. J. Barnett convinced people Faraday was right. In particular, the part of the Earth's magnetic field that is symmetric about its spin axis does not spin with the Earth.
Of course, a magnet spun about a different axis (say, end over end) certainly does carry its field round, because its north and south poles keep changing direction.
What the question actually means# The real trouble is that the question assumes something false. Faraday pictured field lines as actual physical things strung through space, like threads. If they were, asking whether they move would make sense. But in Maxwell's theory it's the field that is real. Field lines are just a drawing we make to picture it.
Think about the electric version. A point charge at rest has field lines like the spokes of a wheel. A second later the picture looks identical. Now ask: which line now is the same line as a particular one a second ago? There is no answer, because the lines have no labels. Someone who insists the spokes are rotating isn't wrong (the picture still shows the right field at every moment), just unhelpful.
The field of a charge at rest, now and a moment later. Which line is the one highlighted before? There is no answer: field lines carry no labels. Field lines tell you exactly two things: how closely packed they are gives the field's strength, and which way they point gives its direction. Once those are right, there is nothing more to know. “Which line is which” from one moment to the next is not a physics question, and it has no right answer.
Why the magnetic case is more troublesome# For electric fields that settles it. The magnetic case is trickier because of the \( \vec{v} \) in the Lorentz force law. Velocity measured relative to what?
The modern answer: relative to whatever (non-accelerating) frame you're working in, the same frame in which you measure \( \vec{B} \). But if you picture field lines as wires strung through space, it's easy to convince yourself (as 19th-century physicists did) that \( \vec{v} \) must mean velocity relative to the field lines. That way of talking survives in engineering, where people say a conductor “cuts” field lines.
If that idea were right, Faraday would have seen a current when only the magnet spun, and no current when magnet and disc spun together (no relative motion). He saw the exact opposite.
“Moving field lines” do not create electric fields. Fields that change with time do. These are not the same thing, and mixing them up causes the confusion. (A symmetric magnet spinning about its axis produces a field that doesn't change with time.)
The upshot# Whether you say field lines are “dragged round” or not is a choice of words, not something the laws of physics decide. It can be a helpful picture of how a field changes, which is why geophysicists, plasma physicists and astrophysicists use it a lot.
When you read such a statement, work out what the author actually means, and remember: field lines don't carry serial numbers, so you can't follow one particular line from one frame of the movie to the next.
