title: Intermission
content:
Intermission# Chapters 1 to 7 built up the laws. Everything after this uses them.
What has been established# The complete set of Maxwell's equations,
\[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\] \[\div{\vec{B}} = 0, \qquad \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{\vec{E}}{t}\] together with the Lorentz force law
\[\vec{F} = q\left( \vec{E} + \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \right)\] and the continuity equation \( \div{\vec{J}} = -\pdv{\rho}{t} \) (which actually follows from Maxwell's equations).
That is the whole theory. Nothing new will be added. Given the charges and currents, these equations tell you the fields. Given the fields, the force law tells you how charges move.
The route taken# We got here by starting with a simple special case and removing one restriction at a time:
Chapters Restriction Governing conditions 2-4 charges at rest \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) 5-6 steady currents \( \div{\vec{J}} = 0 \) 7 none full Maxwell equations Each stage brought its own helpful tools (the scalar potential, the vector potential, \( \vec{D} \) and \( \vec{H} \) for materials), but underneath it all are just the four equations above.
What follows# The rest of the course works out what these laws imply. There are no new laws.
Chapter 8 works out conservation of charge, energy, momentum and angular momentum, and shows that the fields themselves carry energy and momentum. Chapter 9 solves the equations in empty space, where they predict waves that keep themselves going, travelling at \( 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0} \) (light). It then follows those waves into materials and along waveguides. Chapter 10 rewrites the theory using potentials that change with time, including gauge freedom and “retarded” potentials (which account for the time light takes to travel). Chapter 11 is about radiation: the energy accelerating charges send out, and the recoil they feel from it. Chapter 12 shows the theory was consistent with relativity all along, and that electric and magnetic fields are two views of one field: what one observer calls electric, a moving observer sees as partly magnetic.

title: (8.1) Charge and Energy
content:
8.1 Charge and Energy# The continuity equation# Conservation of charge isn't an extra rule: it comes out of Maxwell's equations. Take the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law and use Gauss's law, and you get
\[\div{\vec{J}} = -\pdv{\rho}{t}\] This is local conservation, which says more than “the total charge stays the same”. Total conservation alone would allow charge to vanish here and instantly reappear on the Moon. The continuity equation forbids that: charge can only leave a region by flowing out through its boundary.
Charge inside a region can only change by current flowing through its boundary. Integrating over a volume and using the divergence theorem gives
\[\dv{Q_{\text{enc}}}{t} = -\oint \vec{J}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}}\] Every conservation law in this chapter has this same shape: the rate at which something increases inside a volume equals minus the rate at which it flows out through the surface. (Like a bank account: the balance changes only by money moving in or out.)
Poynting's theorem# From §2.4 and §7.2, electromagnetic fields store energy with density
\[u = \frac{1}{2}\left( \epsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2 \right)\] Work out the rate at which the fields do work on the charges in a volume (from the Lorentz force), and rearrange using Maxwell's equations. The result is Poynting's theorem:
\[\dv{W}{t} = -\dv{}{t}\int_V u \dd{\tau} - \oint_S \vec{S}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}}\] where
\[\vec{S} \equiv \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right)\] is the Poynting vector. It tells you which way energy is flowing and how much: energy per unit area per second (W/m²).
In words: the work done on the charges = the energy the field loses from inside the volume − the energy that flows out through the surface. Every joule is accounted for: it either goes into the charges or leaves through the boundary.
The energy budget: field energy inside a region goes either into the charges or out through the surface. In differential form,
\[\pdv{u}{t} = -\div{\vec{S}} - \vec{E}\cdot\vec{J}\] This has exactly the shape of the continuity equation, with \( \vec{S} \) in place of \( \vec{J} \), plus an extra term \( \vec{E}\cdot\vec{J} \) for energy handed over to the charges.
Notice \( \vec{B} \) isn't in that hand-over term, because magnetic forces do no work. But \( \vec{B} \) is in \( \vec{S} \): carrying energy from place to place is not the same as giving it to the charges.
Example# A current \( I \) flows down a cylindrical resistor of radius \( a \) and length \( L \), across which the potential difference is \( V \). Compute the Poynting vector at the surface and the total power flowing in.
E runs along the resistor and B circles it, so \( \vec{S} \) points into the wire from every side. Solution triple-click to reveal Inside a resistor carrying a current, the electric field isn't zero. It points along the axis and drives the current:
\[E = \frac{V}{L}\,\vu{z}\] At the surface, Ampère's law gives the magnetic field:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}\,\vu{\phi}\] So the Poynting vector at the surface is
\[\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right) = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\frac{V}{L}\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}\left( \vu{z}\cross\vu{\phi} \right) = -\frac{VI}{2\pi a L}\,\vu{s}\] pointing inward. Multiply by the curved surface area \( 2\pi a L \):
\[P = \left( \frac{VI}{2\pi a L} \right)\left( 2\pi a L \right) = VI\] which is exactly the Joule heating rate. ✓
This is a surprising picture. The energy that heats the resistor doesn't travel inside the wire along with the current. It flows in through the sides of the resistor, from the field in the space around it. The wire guides the energy, but the field carries it.
The same idea in a coaxial cable: the energy travels in the space between the conductors, from the battery to the resistor. Example# Find the Poynting vector for a plane electromagnetic wave with \( \vec{E} = E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\vu{x} \) and \( \vec{B} = (E_0/c)\cos(kz-\omega t)\vu{y} \), and its time average.
Solution triple-click to reveal The fields are perpendicular, so the cross product is easy:
\[\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right) = \frac{E_0^2}{\mu_0 c}\cos^2(kz-\omega t)\left( \vu{x}\cross\vu{y} \right) = \frac{E_0^2}{\mu_0 c}\cos^2(kz-\omega t)\,\vu{z}\] Energy flows along \( \vu{z} \), the way the wave is travelling, as it should.
In a wave \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) are at right angles, and \( \vec{S} \) points the way the wave travels. The average of \( \cos^2 \) over a cycle is \( 1/2 \), so
\[\langle \vec{S} \rangle = \frac{E_0^2}{2\mu_0 c}\vu{z} = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 c E_0^2 \,\vu{z}\] using \( c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0} \). This average power per unit area is the intensity of the wave (how bright the light is).
In a wave the electric and magnetic energies are equal, so \( u = \epsilon_0 E^2 \). Comparing,
\[\langle S \rangle = c \langle u \rangle\] This says: energy flow = energy density × speed \( c \). That's exactly what you'd expect for energy travelling along at the speed of light.
Full derivation: §8.1.

title: (8.2) Momentum
content:
8.2 Momentum# Newton's third law fails# Picture two charges, one moving along the \( x \)-axis and the other along the \( y \)-axis, both heading towards the origin. The electric forces between them are equal and opposite, as Newton's third law expects. The magnetic forces are not. Each charge's magnetic field pushes on the other, but the two pushes point in directions that don't cancel.
The electric forces (green) are equal and opposite. The magnetic forces (orange) are not, so Newton's third law fails. So Newton's third law fails for moving charges. Conservation of momentum is usually proved from the third law, so it looks as if momentum conservation fails too.
It doesn't. The missing momentum is carried by the fields.
The Maxwell stress tensor# The total electromagnetic force on all the charges inside a volume can be written using only the fields on the surface around it:
\[\vec{F} = \oint_S \overleftrightarrow{T}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} - \epsilon_0\mu_0\dv{}{t}\int_V \vec{S}\dd{\tau}\] where the Maxwell stress tensor is
\[T_{ij} \equiv \epsilon_0\left( E_i E_j - \frac{1}{2}\delta_{ij}E^2 \right) + \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left( B_i B_j - \frac{1}{2}\delta_{ij}B^2 \right)\] It has two indices because a force on a surface depends on two directions: \( T_{ij} \) is the force per unit area in direction \( i \) on a surface facing direction \( j \). The diagonal entries (\( i = j \)) are pushes or pulls straight through the surface (pressure or tension). The others are sideways (shear) forces.
A helpful picture (due to Faraday): field lines act like stretched rubber bands that also push sideways on their neighbours. They pull along their length and push apart across it.
Field lines behave like rubber bands. Between unlike charges they pull along their length; between like charges they push sideways on each other. What it's good for: you can find the force on a group of charges by integrating over any surface around them, without knowing what's going on inside.
Conservation of momentum# The fields carry momentum, with density
\[\vec{g} = \epsilon_0\mu_0 \vec{S} = \epsilon_0\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right)\] That's just the Poynting vector divided by \( c^2 \). Wherever energy flows, momentum flows with it.
Conservation of momentum then has the usual shape:
\[\pdv{}{t}\left( \vec{p}_{\text{mech}} + \vec{p}_{\text{em}} \right) = \oint_S \overleftrightarrow{T}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}}\] The total momentum (of the charges plus the fields) only changes by momentum flowing in or out through the surface. The stress tensor describes that flow.
So momentum conservation survives, as long as you count the momentum in the fields. This is the strongest reason to believe fields are real and not just a calculating device: they carry energy and momentum, and you need both to make the books balance.
An immediate consequence is radiation pressure. Light hitting a surface hands over momentum, so it pushes on it with pressure
\[P = \frac{I}{c}\] if the light is absorbed, and twice that if it's perfectly reflected.
Absorbed light hands over its momentum; reflected light hands over twice as much. Angular momentum# Since the fields carry momentum \( \vec{g} \), they also carry angular momentum, with density
\[\vec{\ell} = \vec{r}\cross\vec{g} = \epsilon_0\left[ \vec{r}\cross\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right) \right]\] Remarkably, fields that aren't changing at all can store angular momentum. An arrangement of electric and magnetic fields sitting perfectly still can hold angular momentum, which gets handed to the charges (making something start to spin) when the fields are switched off. This is the “Feynman disc paradox”.
Charges on a disc round a solenoid. Nothing moves; switch the current off and the disc starts to turn. The angular momentum was stored in the static fields. Example# Sunlight strikes the Earth with intensity about \( 1300\ \text{W/m}^2 \). Find the radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface, and compare with atmospheric pressure.
Solution triple-click to reveal For complete absorption, the momentum delivered per second per square metre is the energy flow divided by \( c \):
\[P = \frac{I}{c} = \frac{1300}{3.00\times10^8} \approx 4.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{Pa}\] Atmospheric pressure is about \( 1.0\times10^5 \) Pa, so sunlight pushes about \( 2\times10^{10} \) times more weakly.
That's why you never feel it. But where nothing else competes, it matters: it pushes comet tails away from the Sun, helps hold up the insides of stars, and drives solar sails, where a tiny push kept up for months gives a spacecraft real speed.
For a perfect mirror the push doubles, because the light bounces back instead of just stopping: \( P = 2I/c \). (Like a ball bouncing off a wall versus sticking to it.)
Example# Two point charges \( +q \) and \( -q \) are held a distance \( d \) apart. Use the stress tensor to find the force on the positive charge, integrating over the plane midway between them.
On the midplane the field points straight down. The outward normal of the region above the plane also points down. Solution triple-click to reveal Put \( +q \) at \( z = +d/2 \) and \( -q \) at \( z = -d/2 \). To find the force on \( +q \), use the region \( z > 0 \). Its boundary is the plane \( z = 0 \) (plus a surface at infinity, where the fields vanish). The outward normal from this region points down, \( -\vu{z} \), so only \( T_{zz} \) is needed, and there's no magnetic field:
\[F_z = -\int T_{zz}\, \dd{a}, \qquad T_{zz} = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\left( E_z^2 - E_x^2 - E_y^2 \right)\] The field on the midplane. At a point on the plane, the field from \( +q \) points away from \( +q \) (sideways and downward). The field from \( -q \) points towards \( -q \) (sideways back in, and downward). The sideways parts cancel and the downward parts add. So on the midplane the field points straight down, along \( -\vu{z} \): \( E_x = E_y = 0 \).
At distance \( s \) from the axis, each charge is \( \gr = \sqrt{s^2 + d^2/4} \) away, and each contributes a downward part with factor \( (d/2)/\gr \):
\[E_z = -2\left( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{\gr^2} \right)\frac{d/2}{\gr} = -\frac{q d}{4\pi\epsilon_0 (s^2+d^2/4)^{3/2}}\] So \( T_{zz} = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}E_z^2 \), which is positive: the field lines crossing the plane are “stretched rubber bands” pulling the two halves together.
Integrate over the plane, with \( \dd{a} = 2\pi s \dd{s} \):
\[F_z = -\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int_0^\infty \left( \frac{qd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2+d^2/4)^{3/2}} \right)^2 2\pi s\dd{s} = -\frac{q^2 d^2}{16\pi\epsilon_0}\int_0^\infty \frac{s \dd{s}}{(s^2+d^2/4)^3}\] Substituting \( u = s^2 + d^2/4 \), the integral is \( 1/[4(d^2/4)^2] = 4/d^4 \), so
\[F_z = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{d^2}\] That's Coulomb's law, with the minus sign meaning \( +q \) is pulled down towards \( -q \): attraction. ✓ We never needed the field at either charge, only on a surface between them. That's what the stress tensor is good for.
Full derivation: §8.2.

title: (8.3) Magnetic Forces Do No Work
content:
8.3 Magnetic Forces Do No Work# The paradox# Magnetic forces do no work: the force is always at right angles to the velocity, so \( \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0 \) (§5.1). Yet a magnetic crane in a scrapyard lifts a whole car. Something is doing work on that car. If not the magnetic field, then what?
The car is made of iron, a ferromagnet. In the crane's field it is full of lined-up atomic dipoles, and (§6.2) that magnetization acts like a current flowing round its surface. So we can model the car as a circular loop of current.
The crane as a big current loop and the car as a small one below it. The spreading field pulls the small loop up. Where the energy comes from# Here are three models. Each one answers the question in its own way.
1. A spinning charged ring. Model the loop as a ring of charge \( \lambda \), radius \( a \), spinning at angular speed \( \omega \), so it carries current \( I = \lambda\omega a \). In the magnet's uneven field it feels an upward force \( F = 2\pi I a B_s \), where \( B_s \) is the field's outward (radial) part. Lifting the ring by \( \dd{z} \) gains it energy
\[\dd{W} = 2\pi a^2 \lambda\omega B_s \dd{z}\] But as the ring rises, the magnetic force also has a sideways part that pushes back on the moving charges and slows the spinning. Work out the loss of spinning energy and you get exactly
\[\dd{W} = -2\pi a^2\lambda\omega B_s \dd{z}\] Equal and opposite. The spinning energy lost is exactly the height energy gained. The magnetic field just converted one kind of energy into another and supplied none. Loosely: the vertical part of the magnetic force does positive work, and the horizontal part does exactly the same amount of negative work.
One charge on the rising ring. The part \( q,\vec{w}\times\vec{B}_s \) lifts it; the part \( q,\vec{u}\times\vec{B}_s \) pushes against the spin. Their work cancels exactly. 2. Loops powered by batteries. Model the crane as a big loop with current \( I_b \) and the car as a small loop with current \( I_a \), each kept constant by its own power supply. As the small loop rises, an emf is induced in it, and its power supply has to work against that emf. That work equals the height energy gained. At the same time an emf appears in the crane's loop, and its power supply does the same amount of work again. The extra goes into the energy stored in the fields, \( U = \frac{1}{2}L_aI_a^2 + \frac{1}{2}L_bI_b^2 + MI_aI_b \). All four amounts turn out to be equal. The power supplies do the work, not the field.
3. The real crane. In a real crane the car stays stuck to the magnet, and a cable lifts the whole thing. The two induced emfs cancel exactly, so no power supply needs to do anything, and the field energy doesn't change. So who did the work? Whoever pulls the cable. The magnetic field just passed that energy on to the car, like a rope passing on a pull, without doing any work itself.
The general picture# “Magnetic forces do no work” follows directly from the Lorentz force law. Anyone claiming an exception is really claiming the force law is wrong.
The pattern is always the same: the magnetic force redirects energy but never supplies it. The real source is something else (the battery keeping the current going, the energy of a spinning ring, the person pulling the rope), and the magnetic force is the go-between.
One real loose end remains. The dipoles in a ferromagnet come mostly from electron spin, not from charges going round in circles. Spin is a quantum property: its angular momentum is fixed at \( \hbar/2 \), and no power supply keeps it going. Treating spins as little current loops is only a model, and the energy bookkeeping above doesn't carry over to them straightforwardly.
Example# A small current loop of magnetic moment \( m \) is raised a height \( h \) in a non-uniform field. Identify the energy source in the two cases: the current maintained by a battery, and the current circulating without resistance.
Solution triple-click to reveal The force on the dipole is \( \vec{F} = \grad(\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B}) \). As the loop moves up, it gains energy. Where does that energy come from?
With a battery. As the loop moves into a different field, the flux through it changes. That induces an emf that fights the current. To keep \( I \) fixed, the battery must push against this emf, supplying
\[\dd{W}_{\text{battery}} = -\mathcal{E}I\dd{t} = I \dd{\Phi}\] That's the energy source. The battery pays; the magnetic force delivers.
Without a battery (a superconducting loop), nothing holds the current fixed. The induced emf changes the current, and the energy stored in the loop, \( \frac{1}{2}LI^2 \), changes with it. The lifting energy comes out of that store.
Either way, the magnetic force does no work. It moves energy from the current into the loop's height energy. It is a converter, not a source.
Example# A charged particle enters a region of uniform magnetic field. Confirm that its kinetic energy is unchanged, and identify what the field does change.
Solution triple-click to reveal The rate of change of kinetic energy is the power, force · velocity:
\[\dv{}{t}\left( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \right) = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = q\left( \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \right)\cdot\vec{v} = 0\] because \( \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \) is always at right angles to \( \vec{v} \). So the speed and the kinetic energy never change, whatever the magnetic field looks like.
What the field changes is the direction of motion. The particle moves in a circle of radius \( R = mv/qB \), its momentum turning round at the cyclotron frequency \( \omega = qB/m \) while its size stays the same.
That's the simplest way to put it: a magnetic force only steers. It changes where a particle goes, never how much energy it has.
Compare an electric field, which does work at rate \( q\vec{E}\cdot\vec{v} \) and easily changes a particle's energy. That's why particle accelerators use electric fields to speed particles up and magnetic fields only to steer them round the ring.
