title: (9.1) Waves in One Dimension
content:
9.1 Waves in One Dimension# The wave equation# A wave is a disturbance that travels along while keeping its shape (think of a pulse sent down a rope). If a shape \( f(z,t) \) moves in the \( +z \) direction at speed \( v \) without changing, then at time \( t \) it's just the starting shape slid along by \( vt \):
\[f(z,t) = g(z - vt)\] The pulse keeps its shape and slides along a distance vt. Any function of \( z - vt \) is a wave moving right; any function of \( z + vt \) is a wave moving left. Differentiate twice and both satisfy
\[\pdv{^2 f}{z^2} = \frac{1}{v^2}\pdv{^2 f}{t^2}\] the wave equation. It's linear, so you can add solutions together. Its general solution is a right-moving wave plus a left-moving wave.
This is worth remembering: whenever a law of physics leads to this equation, there are waves, and you can read off their speed from the number in front of the time derivative.
Sinusoidal waves# The most important solution is
\[f(z,t) = A\cos\left( kz - \omega t + \delta \right)\] with amplitude \( A \) (height), wave number \( k \), angular frequency \( \omega \), and phase constant \( \delta \) (where in the cycle it starts). These are connected to the wavelength \( \lambda \), period \( T \) and speed:
\[\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}, \qquad v = \frac{\omega}{k}\] A sinusoidal wave: amplitude \( A \), wavelength \( \lambda \), moving at speed \( v \). Sine waves matter for more than being simple. By Fourier analysis, any wave shape can be built by adding sine waves. So if you can handle the sine wave, you can handle everything.
Complex notation# Working with sines and cosines is tedious, so we write waves as
\[\tilde{f}(z,t) = \tilde{A}e^{i(kz-\omega t)}, \qquad \tilde{A} = Ae^{i\delta}\] and agree that the real, physical wave is the real part. The complex amplitude \( \tilde{A} \) packs the height and the starting phase into one number.
Exponentials are much easier to differentiate and multiply than sines and cosines, and that's the only reason for doing this. It works because the wave equation is linear, so real and imaginary parts never mix. It fails for anything non-linear, such as squaring to get an intensity. Take the real part first in those cases.
Reflection and transmission# Where two different media join (say, a light rope tied to a heavy one), a wave is partly reflected and partly passed on. Requiring the rope to stay joined (the wave is continuous) and not kinked (its slope is continuous) at the knot gives:
\[\tilde{A}_R = \left( \frac{v_2 - v_1}{v_2 + v_1} \right)\tilde{A}_I, \qquad \tilde{A}_T = \left( \frac{2v_2}{v_2+v_1} \right)\tilde{A}_I\] (I = incident, R = reflected, T = transmitted.) The frequency is the same on both sides, because the knot can only wiggle at one rate. The speed and wavelength change.
Watch the sign. If \( v_2 < v_1 \) (the second medium is “heavier”), the reflected wave comes back upside down. In the extreme \( v_2 \to 0 \) (the end is tied to a wall), all of the wave reflects, upside down.
A pulse meets a knot joining a light string to a heavier one. Part goes on, narrower and slower; part comes back upside down. Polarization# A wave is transverse if the wiggle is at right angles to the direction of travel (a shaken rope), and longitudinal if it's along it (sound). Transverse waves have an extra choice: which way, within the perpendicular plane, the wiggle points. That direction is the polarization \( \vu{n} \).
Any polarization can be split into two independent directions, so a transverse wave has two possible polarizations; a longitudinal wave has one. Electromagnetic waves are transverse (§9.2). That's why polarizing sunglasses work.
A transverse wave can wiggle in a vertical plane or a horizontal one: two polarizations. Example# A wave travels along a string of mass density \( \mu_1 \) and meets a knot joining it to a heavier string of density \( \mu_2 = 4\mu_1 \), both under the same tension \( T \). Find the reflected and transmitted amplitudes.
Solution triple-click to reveal The wave speed on a string is \( v = \sqrt{T/\mu} \). With the same tension,
\[\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}\] so \( v_2 = v_1/2 \). Put this into the formulas:
\[\tilde{A}_R = \left( \frac{v_1/2 - v_1}{v_1/2 + v_1} \right)\tilde{A}_I = \left( \frac{-1/2}{3/2} \right)\tilde{A}_I = -\frac{1}{3}\tilde{A}_I\] \[\tilde{A}_T = \left( \frac{2(v_1/2)}{v_1/2 + v_1} \right)\tilde{A}_I = \frac{2}{3}\tilde{A}_I\] The reflected wave is a third as tall and upside down (the minus sign, which is the same as a phase shift of \( \pi \)). That always happens when reflecting off a heavier, slower medium.
The transmitted wave is upright and two-thirds as tall.
Check: at the knot, the string on the left (incident + reflected) must be at the same height as the string on the right (transmitted): \( 1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3} \). ✓ Note that amplitudes don't have to “add up” in any other sense. It's energy that must balance, and the energy carried also depends on the string's density and wave speed, not just the amplitude.
Example# Show that \( f(z,t) = A e^{-b(z-vt)^2} \) satisfies the wave equation, and describe the motion.
Solution triple-click to reveal The function only depends on \( z \) and \( t \) through the combination \( u \equiv z - vt \). By the chain rule, \( \pdv{}{z} = \dv{}{u} \) and \( \pdv{}{t} = -v\dv{}{u} \). Doing each twice,
\[\pdv{^2 f}{z^2} = \dv{^2 f}{u^2}, \qquad \pdv{^2 f}{t^2} = v^2 \dv{^2 f}{u^2}\] so
\[\pdv{^2 f}{z^2} = \frac{1}{v^2}\pdv{^2 f}{t^2}\] as required. ✓ We never used the actual shape of the function: any smooth function of \( z - vt \) satisfies the wave equation.
The motion: a bell-shaped (Gaussian) bump of height \( A \) and width about \( 1/\sqrt{b} \), sliding in the \( +z \) direction at speed \( v \) without changing shape. Keeping its shape means the medium is non-dispersive: all frequencies travel at the same speed. When that isn't true (e.g. waves in conductors, §9.4), a pulse spreads out as it goes.
Full derivation: §9.1.

title: (9.2) Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
content:
9.2 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum# The wave equation for E and B# In empty space (\( \rho = 0 \), \( \vec{J} = \vec{0} \)), Maxwell's equations link the two fields: a changing \( \vec{B} \) makes \( \vec{E} \), and a changing \( \vec{E} \) makes \( \vec{B} \). To separate them, take the curl of Faraday's law and put in Ampère's law (Example 7.3-b). The result:
\[\laplacian\vec{E} = \mu_0\epsilon_0 \pdv{^2\vec{E}}{t^2}, \qquad \laplacian\vec{B} = \mu_0\epsilon_0 \pdv{^2\vec{B}}{t^2}\] Every component obeys the wave equation of §9.1, with speed
\[c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = 3.00\times10^8\ \text{m/s}\] This speed comes purely from two constants measured with charges and currents sitting on a lab bench. It matches the measured speed of light. So light is an electromagnetic wave, arguably the most important conclusion in classical physics.
The displacement current is essential here. Without it, \( \vec{E} \) couldn't make \( \vec{B} \), and there'd be no wave.
Monochromatic plane waves# Take a wave of one frequency (“monochromatic”, one colour) travelling along \( \vu{z} \), with the fields the same everywhere on each flat plane of constant \( z \) (“plane wave”):
\[\tilde{\vec{E}}(z,t) = \tilde{\vec{E}}_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}, \qquad \tilde{\vec{B}}(z,t) = \tilde{\vec{B}}_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\] A plane wave: on each plane at right angles to the direction of travel, the field is the same everywhere. Maxwell's equations add three rules on top of the wave equation.
1. The wave is transverse. From \( \div{\vec{E}} = 0 \) and \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \),
\[(\tilde{E}_0)_z = (\tilde{B}_0)_z = 0\] Neither field points along the direction of travel. Both wiggle sideways.
2 and 3. \( \vec{B} \) is fixed by \( \vec{E} \). From Faraday's law,
\[\tilde{\vec{B}}_0 = \frac{k}{\omega}\left( \vu{z}\cross\tilde{\vec{E}}_0 \right) = \frac{1}{c}\left( \vu{z}\cross\tilde{\vec{E}}_0 \right)\] So:
\( \vec{E} \), \( \vec{B} \) and the direction of travel are all at right angles to each other (like the \( x \), \( y \), \( z \) axes); \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) are in step: they peak at the same place and time; their sizes are in a fixed ratio: \[E_0 = c B_0\] A plane wave. E and B are at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, and they peak together. (Drawn the same height for clarity; in SI units B is smaller by a factor of c.) In SI units \( B \) is smaller by a factor of \( c \). The magnetic force on a charge is \( qvB = (v/c),qE \), so for any charge moving much slower than light, the wave's electric force is far bigger than its magnetic force.
Energy and momentum# The energy density is
\[u = \frac{1}{2}\left( \epsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2 \right) = \epsilon_0 E^2\] using \( B = E/c \). The electric and magnetic parts carry exactly equal shares. The Poynting vector is
\[\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left( \vec{E}\cross\vec{B} \right) = c\epsilon_0 E^2\,\vu{z} = cu\,\vu{z}\] Energy density moving at speed \( c \), as expected. Averaging over a cycle (\( \langle\cos^2\rangle = 1/2 \)) gives the intensity:
\[I = \langle S \rangle = \frac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E_0^2\] In time \( dt \) the energy in a length \( c,dt \) of the tube crosses the end. That is why \( S = cu \). The momentum density is \( \vec{g} = \vec{S}/c^2 \). So a wave delivers momentum \( I/c \) per square metre per second: the radiation pressure of §8.2.
Polarization# The wave is transverse, so \( \tilde{\vec{E}}_0 \) lies in the \( xy \) plane. The direction it points in is the polarization. There are two independent directions (say \( x \) and \( y \)), and any wave is a mix of the two. If the two parts have equal size and are a quarter-cycle (\( 90^\circ \)) out of step, \( \vec{E} \) goes round in a circle: circular polarization. In general it traces an ellipse.
The field seen head-on as the wave comes towards you: back and forth along one line (linear), or round a circle (circular). Example# A monochromatic plane wave of intensity \( 1300\ \text{W/m}^2 \) — roughly sunlight at the Earth — travels along \( \vu{z} \). Find the amplitudes of \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \).
Solution triple-click to reveal Rearranging the intensity formula,
\[E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\epsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(1300)}{(3.00\times10^8)(8.85\times10^{-12})}}\] The bottom is \( c\epsilon_0 = 2.66\times10^{-3} \), so
\[E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2600}{2.66\times10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{9.79\times10^{5}} \approx 990\ \text{V/m}\] and
\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{990}{3.00\times10^8} \approx 3.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{T}\] The electric field is quite large by lab standards (about 1 kV/m). The magnetic field is about fifteen times weaker than the Earth's own field (roughly \( 5\times10^{-5} \) T). That difference is the factor of \( c \), and it's why light's effects on matter are almost always electric.
Example# A plane wave has \( \vec{E} = E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\vu{x} \). Find \( \vec{B} \), and verify that both satisfy Faraday's law.
Solution triple-click to reveal The wave travels along \( \vu{z} \), so
\[\vec{B} = \frac{1}{c}\left( \vu{z}\cross\vec{E} \right) = \frac{E_0}{c}\cos(kz-\omega t)\left( \vu{z}\cross\vu{x} \right) = \frac{E_0}{c}\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\vu{y}\] \( \vec{B} \) points along \( \vu{y} \): at right angles to \( \vec{E} \) and to the direction of travel, and in step with \( \vec{E} \).
Check with Faraday's law. \( \vec{E} \) only has an \( x \) component, which only depends on \( z \), so the curl has just one term:
\[\curl{\vec{E}} = \pdv{E_x}{z}\left( \vu{z}\cross\vu{x} \right) = -kE_0\sin(kz-\omega t)\,\vu{y}\] and
\[-\pdv{\vec{B}}{t} = -\frac{E_0}{c}\omega\sin(kz-\omega t)\,\vu{y}\] These match if \( k = \omega/c \), i.e. \( \omega = ck \). So Faraday's law holds exactly when the wave travels at speed \( c \). That's not an extra assumption; it comes out of the equations.
Full derivation: §9.2.

title: (9.3) Electromagnetic Waves in Matter
content:
9.3 Electromagnetic Waves in Matter# Waves in linear materials# Inside a linear material with no free charge or current, Maxwell's equations look just like the vacuum ones with \( \epsilon_0 \to \epsilon \) and \( \mu_0 \to \mu \). So everything in §9.2 carries over with that swap, and waves travel at
\[v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon\mu}} = \frac{c}{n}\] where the index of refraction is
\[n \equiv \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon\mu}{\epsilon_0\mu_0}} \approx \sqrt{\epsilon_r}\] The approximation works because most transparent materials are barely magnetic, \( \mu \approx \mu_0 \).
For ordinary materials \( n > 1 \), so light is slower in a material than in vacuum (in glass, about \( c/1.5 \)). The energy density and intensity become
\[u = \epsilon E^2, \qquad I = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon v E_0^2\] Reflection and transmission, straight on# When a wave hits a flat boundary between two materials head-on, part of it reflects and part goes through. Using the boundary conditions of §7.3 (the parallel parts of \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{H} \) don't jump) gives formulas just like those for waves on a string (§9.1):
\[\tilde{E}_{0_R} = \left( \frac{n_1 - n_2}{n_1 + n_2} \right)\tilde{E}_{0_I}, \qquad \tilde{E}_{0_T} = \left( \frac{2n_1}{n_1+n_2} \right)\tilde{E}_{0_I}\] If \( n_2 > n_1 \) the reflected amplitude is negative: the wave comes back upside down when it reflects off a “denser” material, just like reflection off a heavier string.
Head-on at a denser medium (\( n_2 = 1.5 n_1 \)): the transmitted wave has a shorter wavelength; the reflected wave is small and upside down. The fractions of energy reflected (\( R \)) and transmitted (\( T \)) are
\[R = \left( \frac{n_1-n_2}{n_1+n_2} \right)^2, \qquad T = \frac{4n_1n_2}{(n_1+n_2)^2}\] and \( R + T = 1 \): no energy goes missing.
Hitting at an angle# When a wave hits the boundary at an angle, three laws follow just from requiring that the incoming, reflected and transmitted waves stay in step with each other all along the boundary:
The three rays and the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface) all lie in one plane. Law of reflection: \( \theta_I = \theta_R \) (angle in = angle out). Snell's law: \( n_1\sin\theta_I = n_2\sin\theta_T \). Light bends towards the normal going into a denser material. Reflection at the same angle; the transmitted ray bends towards the normal (Snell's law). These only depend on the geometry of waves, not on what kind of wave it is. How much light reflects is a different question, which needs the boundary conditions and gives Fresnel's equations. For polarization in the plane of incidence,
\[\frac{E_{0_R}}{E_{0_I}} = \frac{\alpha - \beta}{\alpha + \beta}, \qquad \alpha \equiv \frac{\cos\theta_T}{\cos\theta_I}, \quad \beta \equiv \frac{n_2}{n_1}\] Two important results:
Brewster's angle. The reflected wave above disappears when \( \alpha = \beta \), at an angle with \( \tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1 \). At this angle only the other polarization reflects, so the reflected light is completely polarized. Glare off water or a road is mostly reflected light near this angle, polarized horizontally, which is why polarizing sunglasses (which block horizontal polarization) cut glare.
Fresnel's equations for \( n_2/n_1 = 1.5 \), polarization in the plane of incidence. The reflected wave vanishes at Brewster's angle. Total internal reflection. Going from a denser to a less dense material (\( n_1 > n_2 \)), Snell's law has no answer beyond the critical angle
\[\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\] and all the light reflects. This is how optical fibres trap light and carry internet signals under the ocean.
Rays from inside glass. Below the critical angle they escape; at it they skim the surface; beyond it they are totally reflected. Example# Light passes from air (\( n=1.0 \)) into glass (\( n=1.5 \)) at normal incidence. Find the fraction of energy reflected, and Brewster's angle for the interface.
Solution triple-click to reveal Reflection. Put the numbers into \( R \):
\[R = \left( \frac{1.0 - 1.5}{1.0 + 1.5} \right)^2 = \left( \frac{-0.5}{2.5} \right)^2 = (0.2)^2 = 0.04\] So 4% of the energy reflects and 96% goes into the glass. (That's the faint reflection you see in a shop window.) The amplitude ratio is negative, so the reflected wave is flipped, but you can't see that in the brightness.
Losing 4% at every glass surface adds up in a camera lens with many elements. That's why lenses have anti-reflection coatings.
Brewster's angle.
\[\tan\theta_B = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = 1.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_B = \arctan(1.5) = 56.3^\circ\] Light hitting the glass at \( 56.3^\circ \) from the normal reflects fully polarized, perpendicular to the plane of incidence. For flat horizontal surfaces like water and roads, that means horizontally polarized, which is exactly what polarizing sunglasses block.
Example# Find the critical angle for a glass-air interface with \( n_{\text{glass}} = 1.5 \), and explain why light escapes at all from a fibre bent too sharply.
Solution triple-click to reveal Total internal reflection only happens going from the denser material to the less dense one (glass to air). At the critical angle, the refracted ray would just skim along the surface, \( \theta_T = 90^\circ \):
\[\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1.0}{1.5} = 0.667 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_c = 41.8^\circ\] Light hitting the inside surface at more than \( 41.8^\circ \) from the normal is completely reflected.
In a straight fibre, light travels at a shallow slant and hits the walls at large angles (well past \( 41.8^\circ \)), so it bounces along forever. Bend the fibre sharply, and at the bend the light hits the outer wall more head-on. Once the angle drops below \( 41.8^\circ \), light leaks out. That's why optical fibres have a minimum bending radius.
“Total” reflection doesn't mean the field is exactly zero outside the glass. A weak evanescent wave pokes a tiny distance out (about a wavelength), dying away quickly and carrying no energy. But bring another piece of glass that close and energy can hop across the gap: this is “frustrated total internal reflection”, a light-wave version of quantum tunnelling.
Full derivation: §9.3.

title: (9.4) Absorption and Dispersion
content:
9.4 Absorption and Dispersion# Waves in conductors# In a conductor there are free charges, so a wave's electric field drives a current \( \vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E} \), and the current term in Ampère's law is no longer zero. (Any free charge put inside a conductor quickly spreads to the surface, dying away with time constant \( \epsilon/\sigma \). So we can take \( \rho_f = 0 \), but the current stays.)
The wave equation picks up an extra term with a first time derivative:
\[\laplacian\vec{E} = \mu\epsilon\pdv{^2\vec{E}}{t^2} + \mu\sigma\pdv{\vec{E}}{t}\] That extra term acts like friction. There are still plane-wave solutions, but the wave number becomes complex, \( \tilde{k} = k + i\kappa \):
\[\tilde{\vec{E}} = \tilde{\vec{E}}_0 e^{-\kappa z}e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\] The \( e^{-\kappa z} \) factor makes the wave die away as it goes in. The wave is absorbed (its energy heats the metal), and it only gets about
\[d \equiv \frac{1}{\kappa}\] into the material. This is the skin depth. For a good conductor, \( \kappa \approx \sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma/2} \), so the skin depth gets smaller at higher frequency. High-frequency currents only flow in a thin layer at the surface (“skin effect”), which is why radio-frequency parts are often just silver-plated.
In a conductor the wave dies away as \( e^{-z/d} \); \( d \) is the skin depth. Two other changes from vacuum: \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) are no longer in step (\( \vec{B} \) lags behind), and \( \vec{B} \) is relatively bigger than in vacuum.
Reflection from metals# For a perfect conductor (\( \sigma \to \infty \)) the skin depth is zero: nothing gets in, and all the wave reflects (upside down). That's why metals are shiny: visible light bounces off instead of being absorbed or passing through.
Real metals aren't perfect conductors, so a little light is absorbed. That's why even polished silver isn't a perfect mirror.
Dispersion# So far we treated \( \epsilon \) as a constant. In reality it depends on frequency, so the wave speed \( v = c/n(\omega) \) does too. A material in which different frequencies travel at different speeds is called dispersive. A pulse is made of many frequencies, so in such a material it spreads out as it travels.
To model this, treat the electrons bound in atoms as little masses on springs, with some friction, pushed back and forth by the wave's electric field. Solving that gives a complex permittivity, and its real part gives the index of refraction:
\[n(\omega) = 1 + \frac{Nq^2}{2\epsilon_0 m}\sum_j \frac{f_j\left( \omega_{0j}^2 - \omega^2 \right)}{\left( \omega_{0j}^2 - \omega^2 \right)^2 + \gamma_j^2\omega^2}\] where the \( \omega_{0j} \) are the natural frequencies (“resonances”) of the electrons in the material.
The model: each bound electron is a mass on a spring (with a little friction), shaken by the wave's electric field. Normal dispersion. Away from a resonance, \( n \) rises with frequency. So in glass, blue light (higher frequency) is slower than red. That's why a prism splits white light into colours, and why simple lenses have coloured fringes (chromatic aberration).
Normal dispersion: blue has a higher index than red, so it bends more at each face. Anomalous dispersion. Near a resonance it's the other way round: \( n \) falls as frequency rises. The imaginary part of the permittivity peaks there too, meaning the material absorbs strongly. The two go together: a material that disperses must absorb somewhere, and a material that absorbs at some frequency must disperse near it.
Near a resonance \( \omega_0 \): the index rises (normal dispersion), then falls steeply (anomalous dispersion) where the absorption peaks. Two different speeds now matter:
Phase velocity \( \omega/k \): how fast the crests of a single frequency move. It can be faster than \( c \), for instance near a resonance. Group velocity \( \dd{\omega}/\dd{k} \): how fast the overall shape of a pulse moves. In ordinary situations this is the speed at which energy and signals travel. Neither energy nor information ever travels faster than \( c \).
A wave packet. The ripples move at the phase velocity; the envelope, which carries the energy, moves at the group velocity. Example# Find the skin depth in copper (\( \sigma = 6\times10^7\ \text{S/m} \)) at 60 Hz and at 1 GHz, and comment on the implications.
Solution triple-click to reveal For a good conductor,
\[d = \frac{1}{\kappa} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega\mu\sigma}}\] with \( \mu \approx \mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7} \).
At 60 Hz (mains electricity), \( \omega = 2\pi(60) = 377\ \text{s}^{-1} \):
\[d = \sqrt{\frac{2}{(377)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(6\times10^7)}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{2.84\times10^4}} \approx 8.4\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}\] About 8 mm. A household wire is much thinner than that, so the current uses the whole wire. For very thick power-station bars, the effect starts to matter.
At 1 GHz (microwaves, mobile phones), \( \omega = 6.28\times10^9\ \text{s}^{-1} \), which is \( 1.67\times10^7 \) times bigger. Since \( d \propto 1/\sqrt{\omega} \), the skin depth is \( \sqrt{1.67\times10^7} \approx 4100 \) times smaller:
\[d \approx \frac{8.4\times10^{-3}}{4100} \approx 2.1\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}\] About two microns, much thinner than a human hair. At microwave frequencies the inside of a conductor carries no current and is wasted metal. That's why microwave parts can be made of cheap metal with a thin silver coating, and why hollow tubes work as well as solid rods.
Example# For a medium with a single resonance, determine whether the index of refraction rises or falls with frequency well below resonance, and relate this to the behaviour of a glass prism.
Solution triple-click to reveal Well below resonance (\( \omega \ll \omega_0 \)), the friction term is negligible, and the formula becomes
\[n(\omega) \approx 1 + \frac{Nq^2 f}{2\epsilon_0 m}\frac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\] As \( \omega \) goes up towards \( \omega_0 \), the bottom \( \omega_0^2 - \omega^2 \) gets smaller, so the fraction gets bigger and \( n \) increases with frequency. That's normal dispersion.
Glass has its resonances in the ultraviolet, so all visible light is below resonance and this applies. Blue light has a higher frequency than red, so a higher \( n \), so it travels more slowly.
By Snell's law, a higher \( n \) means more bending. So at each face of a prism, blue bends more than red, and the colours fan out with blue bent the most. Rainbows work the same way (with water drops instead of a prism).
This can't continue forever. Close to \( \omega_0 \), friction takes over, the material absorbs strongly, and \( n \) starts falling with frequency (anomalous dispersion). Glass is transparent to visible light precisely because its resonances are outside the visible range.
Full derivation: §9.4.

title: (9.5) Guided Waves
content:
9.5 Guided Waves# Wave guides# A wave guide is a hollow metal pipe that carries electromagnetic waves along it (used for microwaves in radar and satellite dishes). Treat the walls as perfect conductors. Then at the inside surface:
\[\vec{E}^{\parallel} = \vec{0}, \qquad B^{\perp} = 0\] (no electric field along the wall, no magnetic field into the wall).
A rectangular wave guide, \( a \times b \), running along \( z \). Trapping the wave in a pipe changes things. Inside a guide the fields are generally not purely transverse. Solving Maxwell's equations with these boundary conditions gives all the sideways field components in terms of the components along the pipe, \( E_z \) and \( B_z \), and these can't both be zero.
Modes are named by which one is zero:
Mode Condition TE (transverse electric) \( E_z = 0 \) TM (transverse magnetic) \( B_z = 0 \) TEM \( E_z = B_z = 0 \) A hollow pipe cannot carry a TEM wave. Here's why, using §3.1. If \( E_z = B_z = 0 \), the sideways electric field has no curl and no divergence across the pipe, so it comes from a potential obeying Laplace's equation in 2D. The pipe wall is a single conductor, so it's all at one potential. The uniqueness theorem then says the potential is constant inside, so the field is zero. So a hollow pipe carries only TE and TM waves.
TE waves in a rectangular guide# For a pipe with cross-section \( a \times b \) (with \( a > b \)), separation of variables gives modes labelled \( \text{TE}_{mn} \), with
\[k = \sqrt{\frac{\omega^2}{c^2} - \pi^2\left( \frac{m^2}{a^2} + \frac{n^2}{b^2} \right)}\] where \( m \) and \( n \) are whole numbers \( 0, 1, 2, \ldots \) (not both zero). They count the half-wavelengths across the width and height.
\( k \) is only a real number if \( \omega \) is above the cutoff frequency
\[\omega_{mn} = c\pi\sqrt{\frac{m^2}{a^2} + \frac{n^2}{b^2}}\] Below cutoff, \( k \) is imaginary, and the wave dies away instead of travelling. So a wave guide is a high-pass filter: each mode only carries frequencies above its cutoff. (Roughly: the wave must be short enough to fit across the pipe.)
The lowest cutoff is for \( \text{TE}{10} \), at \( \omega{10} = c\pi/a \). Between that and the next cutoff, only one mode can travel. Guides are normally used in this range, because different modes travel at different speeds and would smear a signal out.
The \( \text{TE}_{10} \) mode across the guide: E points across the short side, strongest in the middle and zero at the side walls. The phase and group velocities are
\[v_p = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{1 - (\omega_{mn}/\omega)^2}} > c, \qquad v_g = \dv{\omega}{k} = c\sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{\omega_{mn}}{\omega} \right)^2} < c\] and \( v_p v_g = c^2 \). The phase velocity is faster than light, but that's fine: nothing physical, and no information, travels at the phase velocity. The group velocity, which carries energy and signals, stays below \( c \).
A helpful picture: the wave in a guide is an ordinary plane wave bouncing back and forth between the walls at an angle. It travels at \( c \) along its zigzag path, so its progress along the pipe is slower than \( c \). That's the group velocity.
The wave bounces between the walls at c; its progress along the guide is slower. The coaxial cable# A hollow pipe can't carry TEM waves, but a guide with two separate conductors can. The uniqueness argument no longer works, because the inner wire and the outer tube can be at different potentials.
So a coaxial cable (like a TV aerial cable) carries a TEM wave:
\[\vec{E} = \frac{A\cos(kz-\omega t)}{s}\vu{s}, \qquad \vec{B} = \frac{A\cos(kz-\omega t)}{cs}\vu{\phi}\] This mode has no cutoff and travels at exactly \( c \) (in a vacuum-filled cable). \( \vec{E} \) points out from the centre wire and \( \vec{B} \) circles it, both at right angles to the cable, just like a wave in free space. That's why coax can carry signals at any frequency, right down to DC, while a hollow guide can't.
End view of a coaxial cable: E points straight out from the inner wire and B circles it, both at right angles to the cable. Example# A rectangular wave guide has dimensions \( a = 2.28\ \text{cm} \) and \( b = 1.01\ \text{cm} \). Find the cutoff frequency of the lowest mode and the range over which only that mode propagates.
Solution triple-click to reveal The lowest mode is \( \text{TE}_{10} \) (\( m=1 \), \( n=0 \)):
\[\nu_{10} = \frac{\omega_{10}}{2\pi} = \frac{c}{2a} = \frac{3.00\times10^8}{2(0.0228)} = 6.58\times10^9\ \text{Hz}\] About 6.6 GHz. Below this, nothing gets through.
The next cutoffs are \( \text{TE}{20} \) at \( c/a = 13.2\ \text{GHz} \) and \( \text{TE}{01} \) at \( c/2b = 14.9\ \text{GHz} \). The lower one is \( \text{TE}_{20} \), so only one mode travels for
\[6.6\ \text{GHz} < \nu < 13.2\ \text{GHz}\] That's a factor of exactly 2 in frequency (one octave), which always happens when \( a > 2b \). These are roughly the dimensions of standard “X-band” guide, used for radar.
Single-mode operation matters because different modes have different group velocities. Sending several at once would make a short pulse arrive smeared out.
Example# A signal at 10 GHz propagates in the guide above. Find the phase and group velocities, and confirm their product.
Solution triple-click to reveal In the \( \text{TE}{10} \) mode, \( \nu{10} = 6.58\ \text{GHz} \), so
\[\frac{\nu_{10}}{\nu} = \frac{6.58}{10} = 0.658, \qquad \sqrt{1 - (0.658)^2} = \sqrt{1 - 0.433} = 0.753\] So
\[v_g = c(0.753) = 2.26\times10^8\ \text{m/s}\] \[v_p = \frac{c}{0.753} = 3.98\times10^8\ \text{m/s}\] The phase velocity is a third faster than light. That's allowed, because it's just the speed of a pattern, not of anything physical. The group velocity, three-quarters of \( c \), is how fast a pulse actually travels.
Their product:
\[v_p v_g = (3.98\times10^8)(2.26\times10^8) = 8.99\times10^{16} \approx c^2\] ✓ Note that close to cutoff, \( v_g \) becomes very small and the guide becomes strongly dispersive. So in practice guides are run comfortably above cutoff.
Above cutoff \( v_p > c > v_g \) and \( v_p v_g = c^2 \). Close to cutoff the group velocity is small; far above it both approach \( c \). Full derivation: §9.5.
Chapter 9 recap# You have reached the end of Chapter 9. Dot Physics has no summary of this chapter, so to recap, watch a lecture on the heart of the chapter, electromagnetic waves in vacuum (§9.2), from the Electromagnetism Griffiths channel.

title: (10.1) The Potential Formulation
content:
10.1 The Potential Formulation# Scalar and vector potentials# In electrostatics, \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) let us write \( \vec{E} = -\grad V \). Once fields change with time that no longer works. But \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) is still always true, so we can still write
\[\vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}}\] Put this into Faraday's law:
\[\curl{\left( \vec{E} + \pdv{\vec{A}}{t} \right)} = \vec{0}\] So it's this combination, not \( \vec{E} \) on its own, that has zero curl, and it can be written as a gradient:
\[\vec{E} = -\grad V - \pdv{\vec{A}}{t}\] The first part is the familiar electrostatic piece. The second is the electric field made by a changing magnetic field (Faraday).
Written this way, two of Maxwell's equations (\( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) and Faraday's law) are automatically satisfied. The other two become equations for \( V \) and \( \vec{A} \):
\[\laplacian V + \pdv{}{t}\left( \div{\vec{A}} \right) = -\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}\] plus a messier one for \( \vec{A} \). We now have four unknown functions (\( V \) and three components of \( \vec{A} \)) instead of six (\( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \)), but the equations are tangled together.
Gauge transformations# The potentials are not unique. The fields don't change if you replace
\[\vec{A} \to \vec{A} + \grad\lambda, \qquad V \to V - \pdv{\lambda}{t}\] for any function \( \lambda(\vec{r},t) \). \( \vec{B} \) doesn't change because the curl of a gradient is zero. In \( \vec{E} \), the two changes cancel each other.
This is gauge freedom. It's not a flaw; it's a tool. You can choose \( \lambda \) to make the equations as simple as possible.
Coulomb and Lorenz gauges# Coulomb gauge: choose \( \div{\vec{A}} = 0 \). Then the equation for \( V \) becomes Poisson's equation, with solution
\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'},t)}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] That's easy, but strange: \( V \) here reacts instantly to charge moving anywhere in the universe. It doesn't actually break causality, because \( V \) can't be measured directly and the fields still travel at \( c \). But the equation for \( \vec{A} \) stays awkward.
Lorenz gauge: choose \( \div{\vec{A}} = -\mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{V}{t} \). This completely untangles the equations:
\[\laplacian V - \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{^2 V}{t^2} = -\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}\] \[\laplacian \vec{A} - \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{^2\vec{A}}{t^2} = -\mu_0\vec{J}\] Both are wave equations with a source on the right, and they have exactly the same form. Using the shorthand (“d'Alembertian”) \( \Box^2 \equiv \laplacian - \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{^2}{t^2} \),
\[\Box^2 V = -\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \Box^2 \vec{A} = -\mu_0\vec{J}\] This is electrodynamics in its neatest form, and it shows directly that effects spread out at speed \( c \). We use the Lorenz gauge from here on.
Ludvig Lorenz (Danish), not Hendrik Lorentz (Dutch, of the Lorentz force): two different physicists. Many books get this wrong.
The Lorentz force law using potentials# The force law can also be written with the potentials. Substitute them and use the identity \( \vec{v}\cross(\curl{\vec{A}}) = \grad(\vec{v}\cdot\vec{A}) - (\vec{v}\cdot\grad)\vec{A} \):
\[\vec{F} = q\left[ -\grad\left( V - \vec{v}\cdot\vec{A} \right) - \dv{\vec{A}}{t} \right]\] Careful: here \( \dd{\vec{A}}/\dd{t} = \pdv{\vec{A}}{t} + (\vec{v}\cdot\grad)\vec{A} \) is the rate of change of \( \vec{A} \) as seen by the moving particle, not at a fixed point.
The combination \( V - \vec{v}\cdot\vec{A} \) acts like a potential energy per unit charge that depends on velocity. It is the starting point for describing charged particles with Lagrangian mechanics.
Example# Show that the gauge transformation leaves both \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) unchanged.
Solution triple-click to reveal Magnetic field.
\[\vec{B}' = \curl{\vec{A}'} = \curl{\left( \vec{A} + \grad\lambda \right)} = \curl{\vec{A}} + \curl{(\grad\lambda)} = \curl{\vec{A}} = \vec{B}\] because the curl of a gradient is always zero (§1.2).
Electric field. Put in both changes:
\[\vec{E}' = -\grad V' - \pdv{\vec{A}'}{t} = -\grad\left( V - \pdv{\lambda}{t} \right) - \pdv{}{t}\left( \vec{A} + \grad\lambda \right)\] Multiply out:
\[\vec{E}' = -\grad V + \grad\pdv{\lambda}{t} - \pdv{\vec{A}}{t} - \pdv{}{t}\grad\lambda\] The second and fourth terms cancel, because it doesn't matter whether you differentiate by position or time first. So \( \vec{E}' = \vec{E} \). ✓
This is exactly why \( V \) must change by minus \( \partial\lambda/\partial t \): anything else would change \( \vec{E} \).
Example# A configuration has \( V = 0 \) and \( \vec{A} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{qt}{r^2}\vu{r} \). Find the fields, and identify the source.
Solution triple-click to reveal Electric field. \( V = 0 \), so only \( \vec{A} \) contributes:
\[\vec{E} = -\pdv{\vec{A}}{t} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}\vu{r}\] Magnetic field. \( \vec{A} \) points radially and depends only on \( r \), and any field like that has zero curl:
\[\vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}} = \vec{0}\] So this is just the steady field of a point charge \( q \) at the origin! Normally we'd describe it with \( V = q/4\pi\epsilon_0 r \) and \( \vec{A} = \vec{0} \).
You get from the potentials given here to the usual ones with the gauge function \( \lambda = -\frac{qt}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} \). This shows that wildly different potentials can describe exactly the same physics. It also shows that potentials that change with time don't mean the fields change: here \( \vec{A} \) grows forever, yet the field is completely steady.
Two very different sets of potentials, one field. Left: the usual \( V \). Right: \( V = 0 \) and an inward \( \vec{A} \) that grows steadily; \( -\partial\vec{A}/\partial t \) gives the same outward E. Full derivation: §10.1.

title: (10.2) Continuous Distributions
content:
10.2 Continuous Distributions# Retarded potentials# For steady sources, the potentials were integrals over the charges and currents. When things change with time, the same integrals work, with one change: each bit of source must be taken at an earlier time, to allow for the time the news takes to travel to you at speed \( c \):
\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}, \qquad \vec{A}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\] where the retarded time (“retarded” meaning delayed) is
\[t_r \equiv t - \frac{\gr}{c}\] These are the retarded potentials. They solve the wave equations of §10.1 (in the Lorenz gauge).
The idea is the same as looking at stars: you see a star as it was when the light left it, not as it is now. What matters here isn't where the charges are now, but where they were when the signal that is arriving now set off. Different parts of a large source are seen at different retarded times, because they're at different distances.
Each piece of the source is counted as it was when its signal set off: the farther piece is seen as it was longer ago. The same trick does not work for the fields. Putting \( t_r \) into Coulomb's law and the Biot-Savart law gives the wrong \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \). You have to differentiate the retarded potentials, and since \( t_r \) itself depends on position, that produces extra terms.
“Advanced” potentials, using \( t_a = t + \gr/c \), also solve the equations mathematically. We throw them out because they'd make the fields today depend on what the charges do in the future, which breaks cause and effect.
Jefimenko's equations# Differentiating the retarded potentials properly gives the fields directly from the sources:
\[\vec{E}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \left[ \frac{\rho(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr^2}\vu{\gr} + \frac{\dot{\rho}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{c\gr}\vu{\gr} - \frac{\dot{\vec{J}}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{c^2\gr} \right]\dd{\tau'}\] \[\vec{B}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \left[ \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr^2} + \frac{\dot{\vec{J}}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{c\gr} \right]\cross\vu{\gr}\,\dd{\tau'}\] (A dot means rate of change with time.) The first term in each is just Coulomb or Biot-Savart with the delay put in. The extra terms involve how fast the sources are changing, and they fall off only as \( 1/\gr \), not \( 1/\gr^2 \).
That difference is crucial. The area of a big sphere grows as \( \gr^2 \). Terms falling as \( 1/\gr^2 \) die off too fast to carry energy through a very distant sphere; terms falling as \( 1/\gr \) don't. So radiation comes entirely from the terms with time derivatives: only changing sources radiate. That's Chapter 11.
Power through a sphere of radius \( \mathscr{r} \): fields falling as \( 1/\mathscr{r}^2 \) carry nothing to infinity; fields falling as \( 1/\mathscr{r} \) do. If nothing changes with time, the extra terms vanish and Jefimenko's equations become Coulomb's law and the Biot-Savart law again, as they should.
Example# An infinite straight wire carries a current that is switched on at \( t=0 \): \( I(t) = 0 \) for \( t<0 \), \( I(t) = I_0 \) for \( t>0 \). Find the vector potential and the fields at distance \( s \).
Left: at time \( t \) only the part of the wire within \( ct \) of P has 'sent news'. Right: E is a brief pulse; B settles to its steady value \( \mu_0 I_0/2\pi s \). Solution triple-click to reveal The wire stays neutral, so \( V = 0 \) and we only need \( \vec{A} \). It points along the wire, the same way as the current.
For \( t < s/c \), no signal from any part of the wire has reached you yet. So \( \vec{A} = \vec{0} \) and both fields are zero. Nothing happens until the news arrives, and it arrives first from the nearest point of the wire.
For \( t > s/c \), only the part of the wire close enough to have “sent news” in time contributes. A point a distance \( z \) along the wire is \( \gr = \sqrt{s^2+z^2} \) away, and counts only if \( \gr < ct \), i.e. \( |z| < \sqrt{(ct)^2 - s^2} \). So
\[\vec{A}(s,t) = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{4\pi}\vu{z}\int_{-\sqrt{(ct)^2-s^2}}^{\sqrt{(ct)^2-s^2}}\frac{\dd{z}}{\sqrt{s^2+z^2}} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{2\pi}\ln\left( \frac{ct + \sqrt{(ct)^2-s^2}}{s} \right)\vu{z}\] Differentiate to get the fields:
\[\vec{E} = -\pdv{\vec{A}}{t} = -\frac{\mu_0 I_0 c}{2\pi\sqrt{(ct)^2-s^2}}\vu{z}, \qquad \vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{2\pi s}\frac{ct}{\sqrt{(ct)^2-s^2}}\vu{\phi}\] Check the long-time limit. As \( t \to \infty \), \( \vec{E} \) dies away and \( \vec{B} \) settles to \( \mu_0 I_0/2\pi s \), the steady result of §5.3. ✓ The temporary electric field, which only exists while the current is being switched on, is something a steady-state calculation would miss completely.
Example# Explain, using Jefimenko's equations, why a steady current produces no radiation however large it is, whereas a small oscillating current does.
Solution triple-click to reveal Radiation means energy that escapes to infinity. The power through a sphere of radius \( \gr \) is \( \oint \vec{S}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} \), and the sphere's area grows as \( \gr^2 \). The Poynting vector is (field)². So to get a power that doesn't shrink as the sphere grows, the fields must fall off as \( 1/\gr \), giving \( S \propto 1/\gr^2 \), which exactly cancels the growing area.
In Jefimenko's equations, the \( 1/\gr \) terms are exactly the ones with \( \dot{\rho} \) and \( \dot{\vec{J}} \). The terms with plain \( \rho \) and \( \vec{J} \) fall as \( 1/\gr^2 \) and carry nothing to infinity.
For a steady current, \( \dot{\vec{J}} = 0 \) and \( \dot{\rho} = 0 \), so those terms are all zero. No radiation, however large the current. Its field just falls off too fast to carry energy away.
For an oscillating current, \( \dot{\vec{J}} \neq 0 \), the \( 1/\gr \) terms are there, and energy escapes. What matters is how fast the current is changing, not simply how big it is. That's why radio antennas use rapidly oscillating currents.
This is the same conclusion as the Larmor formula in §11.2 (radiation needs acceleration), seen here from the point of view of the whole source rather than a single charge.
Full derivation: §10.2.

title: (10.3) Point Charges
content:
10.3 Point Charges# The Liénard-Wiechert potentials# For a single point charge \( q \) moving any way at all, the retarded potentials work out to
\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{qc}{\left( \gr c - \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{v} \right)}, \qquad \vec{A}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{\vec{v}}{c^2}V(\vec{r},t)\] Everything on the right is taken at the retarded time: the moment the charge sent out the signal that is arriving now. That time is found from
\[\left| \vec{r} - \vec{w}(t_r) \right| = c\left( t - t_r \right)\] where \( \vec{w}(t) \) is the charge's path. In words: the distance from where the charge was to where you are equals how far light travels in the time since. A point charge (moving slower than light) always has exactly one such moment.
The field at P now was sent from the retarded position \( \vec{w}(t_r) \); by now the charge has moved on. Compared with the static \( q/4\pi\epsilon_0\gr \), the new feature is the factor \( \left( \gr c - \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{v} \right)^{-1} \). It is not a relativity effect. It comes from timing: a charge coming towards you “stays in view” of the incoming signal for slightly longer than a still one would, so it counts for more. (It's the same effect as a Doppler shift.) So a charge heading towards you has a bigger potential than a still charge at the same retarded position.
The fields of a moving point charge# Differentiating the potentials (remembering that \( t_r \) depends on position and time too) gives
\[\vec{E}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\gr}{\left( \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{u} \right)^3}\left[ \left( c^2 - v^2 \right)\vec{u} + \vec{\gr}\cross\left( \vec{u}\cross\vec{a} \right) \right]\] with
\[\vec{u} \equiv c\vu{\gr} - \vec{v}\] and
\[\vec{B}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{c}\vu{\gr}\cross\vec{E}(\vec{r},t)\] So \( \vec{B} \) is always at right angles to \( \vec{E} \) and to the line from the retarded position.
The bracket has two parts:
The velocity field, with \( (c^2 - v^2)\vec{u} \). It doesn't depend on acceleration and falls as \( 1/\gr^2 \). This is Coulomb's law upgraded for a moving charge. It stays attached to the charge. The acceleration field, the triple cross product. It is proportional to the acceleration \( \vec{a} \) and falls only as \( 1/\gr \). This is the radiation field: it breaks away from the charge and travels off to infinity. Only the acceleration field radiates, for the reason in §10.2: a distant sphere's area grows as \( \gr^2 \), so only \( 1/\gr \) fields carry energy that far. No acceleration, no radiation. Chapter 11 follows this up.
A charge at rest is kicked and moves off. Outside the shell the news hasn't arrived: the old field. Inside, the field of the moving charge. The lines are joined by kinks across the shell, which moves out at c: that is the radiation. For a charge moving at constant velocity there's no acceleration field. The field then points away from where the charge is now (not where it was), and is squashed towards the plane perpendicular to the motion.
Example# Find the potentials and fields of a point charge moving with constant velocity \( \vec{v} \), and identify where the field appears to originate.
Solution triple-click to reveal Let the charge pass through the origin at \( t=0 \), so \( \vec{w}(t) = \vec{v}t \). Solving for the retarded time and putting it into the Liénard-Wiechert potential gives
\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{qc}{\sqrt{\left( c^2 t - \vec{r}\cdot\vec{v} \right)^2 + \left( c^2 - v^2 \right)\left( r^2 - c^2t^2 \right)}}\] With \( \vec{a} = \vec{0} \), only the velocity field is left:
\[\vec{E} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{1 - v^2/c^2}{\left( 1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\sin^2\theta \right)^{3/2}}\frac{\vu{R}}{R^2}\] Here \( \vec{R} \) is the vector from where the charge is now, and \( \theta \) is the angle between \( \vec{R} \) and \( \vec{v} \).
This is a surprising result. The potentials were built from where the charge was when the signal left. Yet the field points straight away from where the charge is now. It's as if the field “predicted” the charge's motion. The prediction works only because the velocity is constant. If the charge accelerates, the prediction goes wrong, and the error is exactly the radiation field.
The field isn't the same in all directions. The factor \( (1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\sin^2\theta)^{-3/2} \) makes it weaker in front of and behind the charge (\( \theta = 0, \pi \)) and stronger to the sides (\( \theta = \pi/2 \)). Near the speed of light the field is squashed into a flat pancake at right angles to the motion. Chapter 12 shows this is exactly what relativity predicts.
The field of a charge at constant velocity points away from where it is now, squashed towards the plane at right angles to the motion. B circles the line of motion. Example# A charge moves along the \( x \)-axis with \( w(t) = \sqrt{b^2 + c^2t^2} \), so-called hyperbolic motion. Find the retarded time for a field point on the \( x \)-axis with \( 0 < x < b \), and comment on the range of validity.
Solution triple-click to reveal The charge comes in from \( x = +\infty \) long ago, slows down, gets closest (\( x = b \)) at \( t = 0 \), and goes back out. Its speed gets closer and closer to \( c \) far in the past and future, but never reaches it.
The field point is at \( x < b \), so the charge is always to its right. The retarded-time condition is
\[w(t_r) - x = c(t - t_r) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 t_r^2} = x + c(t - t_r)\] Square both sides:
\[b^2 + c^2t_r^2 = \left( x + ct \right)^2 - 2c t_r\left( x + ct \right) + c^2t_r^2\] The \( c^2t_r^2 \) terms cancel, leaving a simple linear equation:
\[t_r = \frac{(x+ct)^2 - b^2}{2c(x+ct)}\] This only works if \( x + ct > 0 \), i.e. \( t > -x/c \). Before that time, no signal from the charge has ever reached the field point, so the fields there are zero.
This is real, not a maths glitch. Far in the past the charge was moving almost at the speed of light, travelling along with the light ray \( x = -ct \) and never quite catching up with it. Any signal it sends starts behind that ray, and nothing travels faster than light, so no signal can ever reach the region ahead of the ray. Examples like this are used to test the tricky ideas about radiation and radiation reaction in §11.3.
Hyperbolic motion on a spacetime diagram. The field point gets no signal until the light ray x = −ct passes it. Full derivation: §10.3.
Chapter 10 recap# You have reached the end of Chapter 10. Dot Physics has no summary of this chapter, so to recap, watch a video on the chapter's central ideas, retarded potentials and Jefimenko's equations (Reumi's world).

title: (11.1) Dipole Radiation
content:
11.1 Dipole Radiation# What radiation is# Radiation is energy that escapes to infinity and never comes back. The power passing through a sphere of radius \( r \) is \( \oint\vec{S}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} \). The sphere's area grows as \( r^2 \), so for the power not to shrink to zero at huge \( r \), the Poynting vector must fall no faster than \( 1/r^2 \). Since \( \vec{S} \) is (field)², the fields must fall as \( 1/r \).
Static fields, and the fields of steadily moving charges, fall as \( 1/r^2 \) or faster, so they carry no energy to infinity. Only terms involving how fast the sources change (equivalently, accelerating charges) give \( 1/r \) fields. So: radiation needs accelerating charge.
Radiation is the energy that still gets through a sphere of enormous radius. Electric dipole radiation# Take two small metal balls a distance \( d \) apart, joined by a wire, with charge sloshing back and forth between them:
\[q(t) = q_0\cos(\omega t), \qquad p(t) = p_0\cos(\omega t), \quad p_0 = q_0 d\] The oscillating dipole: charge sloshes between two balls a distance \( d \) apart. The field point is at distance \( r \), angle \( \theta \) from the axis. This is a simple model of a radio antenna. Far away (much further than both \( d \) and the wavelength \( c/\omega \)), the retarded potentials give
\[\vec{E} = -\frac{\mu_0 p_0\omega^2}{4\pi}\left( \frac{\sin\theta}{r} \right)\cos\left[ \omega(t - r/c) \right]\vu{\theta}\] \[\vec{B} = -\frac{\mu_0 p_0\omega^2}{4\pi c}\left( \frac{\sin\theta}{r} \right)\cos\left[ \omega(t - r/c) \right]\vu{\phi}\] They are in step, at right angles to each other and to the direction outwards, with \( E/B = c \). Far from the source, a small patch of this wave looks just like a plane wave.
The intensity is
\[\langle\vec{S}\rangle = \frac{\mu_0 p_0^2\omega^4}{32\pi^2 c}\left( \frac{\sin^2\theta}{r^2} \right)\vu{r}\] and adding it up over a sphere gives the total power radiated:
\[\langle P \rangle = \frac{\mu_0 p_0^2\omega^4}{12\pi c}\] Two things to notice:
The \( \sin^2\theta \) pattern is shaped like a doughnut around the dipole's axis. Nothing is sent out along the axis itself. (That's why a vertical radio mast sends signals out sideways, not up.) The \( \sin^2\theta \) pattern, cut through the doughnut: strongest sideways, nothing along the axis. 2. The power goes as \( \omega^4 \). Double the frequency and you get 16 times the power.
That \( \omega^4 \) is why the sky is blue. Sunlight makes air molecules oscillate like tiny dipoles, which re-radiate (scatter) the light. Violet-blue light has about 1.7 times the frequency of deep red light, so it is scattered roughly \( 1.7^4 \approx 9 \) times more strongly. Look at any part of the sky away from the Sun and you mostly see this scattered blue light. (At sunset, the sunlight reaching you has travelled through so much air that most of its blue has been scattered away, leaving red.)
At noon you see blue light scattered by the air all over the sky. At sunset the light crosses so much air that the blue has been scattered out of it, leaving red. Magnetic dipole radiation# A loop of area \( a \) with an oscillating current \( I(t) = I_0\cos(\omega t) \) has magnetic moment \( m_0 = I_0 a \) and radiates
\[\langle P \rangle = \frac{\mu_0 m_0^2 \omega^4}{12\pi c^3}\] It has the same doughnut pattern, with \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) swapping roles.
For sources of similar size \( b \),
\[\frac{P_{\text{magnetic}}}{P_{\text{electric}}} = \left( \frac{\omega b}{c} \right)^2\] \( \omega b/c \) is (source size)/(wavelength), which we already assumed is small, and here it's squared. So electric dipole radiation wins, unless the source has no electric dipole moment at all.
Radiation from any source# For a general small source, use the multipole expansion; the first term that isn't zero dominates. The monopole term can never radiate: total charge is conserved, so \( \dot{Q} = 0 \) always. A charged ball that pulsates in and out radiates nothing, however wildly it pulsates, because by Gauss's law its outside field only depends on its total charge.
So the electric dipole term is usually the main one. If that is zero, you go on to magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole radiation, and so on, each much weaker than the one before.
Example# Estimate the power radiated by an antenna of length \( d = 1\ \text{m} \) carrying charge amplitude \( q_0 = 1\ \text{nC} \) oscillating at 100 MHz.
Solution triple-click to reveal The dipole moment amplitude is
\[p_0 = q_0 d = (10^{-9})(1) = 10^{-9}\ \text{C}\cdot\text{m}\] and the angular frequency is
\[\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi(10^8) = 6.28\times10^8\ \text{s}^{-1}\] Put these in:
\[\langle P \rangle = \frac{\mu_0 p_0^2 \omega^4}{12\pi c} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10^{-9})^2(6.28\times10^8)^4}{12\pi(3.00\times10^8)}\] The top is \( (1.26\times10^{-6})(10^{-18})(1.56\times10^{35}) = 1.96\times10^{11} \) and the bottom is \( 1.13\times10^{10} \), so
\[\langle P \rangle \approx 17\ \text{W}\] That's a lot from a tiny charge, all thanks to the \( \omega^4 \). Drop the frequency by a factor of 10 and the power falls by 10,000. That's why radiating efficiently needs high frequencies, and why low-frequency antennas have to be huge.
Caution: the wavelength here is \( c/\nu = 3 \) m, only three times the antenna length. The formula assumes \( d \ll \lambda \), which is only roughly true, so treat 17 W as an estimate.
Example# Explain why a uniformly charged sphere whose radius oscillates emits no radiation, despite every part of its surface accelerating.
However the sphere swells or shrinks, the field outside depends only on the total charge, so it never changes. Solution triple-click to reveal Outside the sphere, Gauss's law gives
\[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2}\vu{r}\] at any \( r \) bigger than the sphere's largest radius. It doesn't matter how the charge is arranged inside, as long as it stays spherically symmetric. So the outside field never changes, and an unchanging field can't radiate.
In multipole terms: the monopole moment is \( Q \), which can't change because charge is conserved. The dipole and all higher moments are zero by symmetry. So every term that could radiate is either zero or constant.
Doesn't every accelerating charge radiate? That rule (the Larmor formula, §11.2) is for a single point charge. Here there are many charges, and their radiation fields add up as vectors. Power goes as (field)², so the total isn't simply the sum of each piece's power. For the pulsating sphere, the radiation from different parts cancels completely, in every direction.
The same reasoning explains why a uniformly charged ring spinning steadily doesn't radiate. It's a standard warning: don't apply the point-charge formula to spread-out charges without thinking.
Full derivation: §11.1.

title: (11.2) Power Radiated by a Point Charge
content:
11.2 Power Radiated by a Point Charge# The Larmor formula# The fields of a moving point charge (§10.3) have two parts: a velocity field falling as \( 1/\gr^2 \), and an acceleration field falling as \( 1/\gr \). Only the second radiates:
\[\vec{E}_{\text{rad}} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\gr}{\left( \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{u} \right)^3}\left[ \vec{\gr}\cross\left( \vec{u}\cross\vec{a} \right) \right]\] (The velocity field does hold energy, but that energy travels along with the particle rather than escaping to infinity.)
For a charge that is momentarily at rest, \( \vec{u} = c\vu{\gr} \), and this simplifies to
\[\vec{E}_{\text{rad}} = \frac{\mu_0 q}{4\pi\gr}\left[ \left( \vu{\gr}\cdot\vec{a} \right)\vu{\gr} - \vec{a} \right]\] with Poynting vector
\[\vec{S}_{\text{rad}} = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2}{16\pi^2 c}\left( \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\gr^2} \right)\vu{\gr}\] where \( \theta \) is measured from the direction of the acceleration. Again the doughnut shape: nothing goes out straight along the acceleration (forwards or backwards), and most goes out sideways.
A charge accelerating from rest radiates in a doughnut round the acceleration: none straight ahead or behind. Add it up over a sphere. The \( \gr^2 \) in the area cancels the \( 1/\gr^2 \) exactly (that's why a \( 1/\gr \) field counts as radiation), giving the Larmor formula:
\[P = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2}{6\pi c}\] Radiated power goes as acceleration squared. A charge at rest doesn't radiate. A charge moving at steady velocity doesn't radiate. An accelerating charge does. The formula is accurate whenever the speed is much less than \( c \).
The Larmor formula is for point charges. A uniformly charged ring spinning steadily has every piece accelerating, yet radiates nothing. For spread-out charges the radiation from different parts can cancel, so you can't just add up the powers.
The Liénard formula# When the charge is moving fast there's a new effect: the rate at which energy arrives at a distant sphere is not the same as the rate at which it left the charge. A charge moving towards you squeezes its emission into a shorter time, just like the Doppler effect. The squeeze factor is
\[\frac{\vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{u}}{\gr c} = 1 - \frac{\vu{\gr}\cdot\vec{v}}{c}\] Taking this into account and adding up over all directions gives the Liénard formula:
\[P = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 \gamma^6}{6\pi c}\left( a^2 - \left| \frac{\vec{v}\cross\vec{a}}{c} \right|^2 \right), \qquad \gamma \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\] At low speed this becomes Larmor's formula. The \( \gamma^6 \) means the radiated power shoots up as the particle nears the speed of light. That's the main headache in building circular particle accelerators.
The same radiation from a fast charge (\( v = 0.5c \), v along a): the pattern is swept forward. Two special cases have names:
Situation Power Name \( \vec{v}\parallel\vec{a} \) (speeding up or slowing down in a line) \( \mu_0 q^2 a^2\gamma^6/6\pi c \) bremsstrahlung (“braking radiation”) \( \vec{v}\perp\vec{a} \) (moving in a circle) \( \mu_0 q^2 a^2\gamma^4/6\pi c \) synchrotron radiation At speeds near \( c \), in both cases the radiation is thrown forward into a narrow cone around the direction of motion, like a searchlight. (Hospital X-ray tubes use bremsstrahlung; synchrotron light sources use the second.)
Synchrotron radiation: a fast charge going round a ring sends its radiation out in a narrow forward cone, like a searchlight. Example# In the Bohr model of hydrogen, an electron orbits at radius \( 5\times10^{-11}\ \text{m} \). Estimate the power radiated classically and the resulting lifetime of the atom.
Solution triple-click to reveal The electron's circular acceleration comes from the Coulomb pull of the proton:
\[a = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{m_e r^2} = \frac{(9\times10^9)(1.6\times10^{-19})^2}{(9.11\times10^{-31})(5\times10^{-11})^2}\] The top is \( 2.30\times10^{-28} \) and the bottom \( 2.28\times10^{-51} \), so \( a \approx 1.0\times10^{23}\ \text{m/s}^2 \).
By the Larmor formula,
\[P = \frac{\mu_0 e^2 a^2}{6\pi c} = \frac{(1.26\times10^{-6})(1.6\times10^{-19})^2(1.0\times10^{23})^2}{6\pi(3\times10^8)} \approx 5.7\times10^{-8}\ \text{W}\] The orbit's total energy is \( E = -e^2/8\pi\epsilon_0 r \approx -2.2\times10^{-18}\ \text{J} \), so a rough lifetime is
\[t \sim \frac{2.2\times10^{-18}}{5.7\times10^{-8}} \approx 4\times10^{-11}\ \text{s}\] So classical physics says every atom should collapse in about 40 picoseconds, with the electron spiralling into the nucleus. Atoms obviously don't do this. This failure is one of the clearest reasons we need quantum mechanics. Note that we haven't misused the theory: the electron's speed is much less than \( c \), so Larmor's formula should apply. The classical prediction is simply wrong.
Example# An electron is accelerated in a linear accelerator and, separately, held in a circular orbit at the same speed and acceleration magnitude. Compare the radiated power in the two cases at \( \gamma = 100 \).
Solution triple-click to reveal In a straight line, \( \vec{v} \) and \( \vec{a} \) point along the same line, so \( \vec{v}\cross\vec{a} = \vec{0} \) and the Liénard formula gives
\[P_{\text{lin}} = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2\gamma^6}{6\pi c}\] In a circle they're at right angles, so \( |\vec{v}\cross\vec{a}| = va \) and
\[P_{\text{circ}} = \frac{\mu_0 q^2\gamma^6}{6\pi c}\left( a^2 - \frac{v^2a^2}{c^2} \right) = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2 \gamma^6}{6\pi c}\left( 1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2} \right) = \frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2\gamma^4}{6\pi c}\] using \( 1 - v^2/c^2 = 1/\gamma^2 \). So
\[\frac{P_{\text{lin}}}{P_{\text{circ}}} = \gamma^2 = 10^4\] For the same acceleration, the straight-line case radiates 10,000 times more.
But that's misleading in practice, because real accelerations are nothing like equal. Steering a near-light-speed beam round a ring needs a huge sideways acceleration (\( a = v^2/R \)), while a linear accelerator speeds particles up quite gently. So in real machines it's the circular ones that lose enormous energy to radiation. That's why future high-energy electron colliders are planned as straight (linear) machines, and why the highest-energy ring, the LHC, uses protons: at the same energy a proton, about 2000 times heavier, has a far smaller \( \gamma \), and since the power goes as \( \gamma^4 \), it radiates vastly less.
Full derivation: the online full notes don't cover this section yet. See Griffiths §11.2.

title: (11.3) The Radiation Reaction
content:
11.3 The Radiation Reaction# The recoil# An accelerating charge radiates energy, and that energy has to come from somewhere. So a charged particle must respond to a push slightly differently from an uncharged particle of the same mass: its own fields push back on it. This push-back is the radiation reaction. (Think of the kick a gun gives when it fires.)
The Abraham-Lorentz formula# A first guess: set the work done by the reaction force equal to the radiated power. But that's not true moment by moment. The radiated power was worked out on a sphere at infinity, where the velocity field doesn't reach. Near the particle, though, the velocity field does hold energy, and that energy swaps back and forth between particle and field, separately from the radiation that escapes.
The fix is to average over a stretch of time that starts and ends with the particle in the same state, so the velocity-field energy is the same at both ends:
\[\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\vec{F}_{\text{rad}}\cdot\vec{v}\dd{t} = -\frac{\mu_0 q^2}{6\pi c}\int_{t_1}^{t_2}a^2\dd{t}\] Integrate the right side by parts. The boundary term vanishes (same state at both ends), and the equation is satisfied by
\[\vec{F}_{\text{rad}} = \frac{\mu_0 q^2}{6\pi c}\dot{\vec{a}}\] the Abraham-Lorentz formula. Strange feature: the force depends on how fast the acceleration is changing. So it can be non-zero when the particle isn't radiating, and zero when it is (e.g. constant acceleration). “Radiation reaction” is a misleading name; “field reaction” would be better.
This argument proves less than it seems. It only pins down the average of the force along the direction of motion, over special time intervals. It gives the simplest formula consistent with energy conservation, not the only possible one.
Two problems# Runaway motion. With no outside force, Newton's second law becomes \( \mu_0q^2\dot{a}/6\pi c = ma \), whose solution is
\[a(t) = a_0 e^{t/\tau}, \qquad \tau \equiv \frac{\mu_0 q^2}{6\pi m c}\] For an electron \( \tau \approx 6\times10^{-24} \) s. So a particle left completely alone could spontaneously accelerate faster and faster forever, out of nothing. Obviously absurd.
Pre-acceleration. You can rule out runaways by insisting \( a_0 = 0 \), but then something worse happens: the particle starts to move before the force is applied, by a time of about \( \tau \). Effect before cause.
Neither problem has been fully solved, more than a century later, and both are still there in the relativistic version.
Left: runaway motion, with no force yet the acceleration grows. Right: pre-acceleration, where the particle starts to accelerate about \( \tau \) before the force arrives. The self-force# What causes the reaction? The charge's own fields pushing on the charge itself. For a true point charge the fields are infinite at the particle, so instead we calculate for a small spread-out charge and then shrink it to zero size.
The key fact: when charges move, the force of one piece of the charge on another is not equal and opposite to the force back (Newton's third law fails for moving charges, §8.2). Add up all these mismatches over every pair of pieces, and there's a net force of the charge on itself.
The dumbbell model. Because each half feels the other's field as it was a moment ago, the two forces both lean backwards: a net force of the charge on itself. Take a simple “dumbbell”: total charge \( q \) split into two halves a distance \( d \) apart. Expanding for small \( d \) leaves two important terms:
\[\vec{F}_{\text{self}} = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[ -\frac{a}{4c^2 d} + \frac{\dot{a}}{3c^3} + O(d) \right]\vu{x}\] The first term is proportional to the acceleration. Move it to the other side of \( \vec{F} = m\vec{a} \) and it just adds to the mass. That makes sense: the electrostatic energy of the charge counts as mass through \( E = mc^2 \). Trouble is, it becomes infinite as \( d\to 0 \). The standard fix is to assume the particle's “bare” mass has a matching infinity the other way, so the measured mass is finite. This trick is called mass renormalization, and it's used in quantum electrodynamics too.
The second term is the radiation reaction. Once you also include each end's force on itself, it matches the Abraham-Lorentz formula exactly. That confirms the formula independently of the energy argument above.
Example# A charge is attached to a spring of natural frequency \( \omega_0 \) and oscillates at frequency \( \omega \). Find the damping constant produced by the radiation reaction.
Solution triple-click to reveal The equation of motion includes the spring, the radiation reaction, and whatever drives the oscillation:
\[m\ddot{x} = -m\omega_0^2 x + m\tau\dddot{x} + F_{\text{driving}}\] For oscillation at frequency \( \omega \), \( x = x_0\cos(\omega t + \delta) \). Differentiating twice just multiplies by \( -\omega^2 \), so
\[\dddot{x} = -\omega^2\dot{x}\] That turns the strange third-derivative term into an ordinary friction term proportional to velocity:
\[m\ddot{x} + m\gamma\dot{x} + m\omega_0^2 x = F_{\text{driving}}, \qquad \gamma = \omega^2\tau\] This is the standard damped, driven oscillator, with damping constant \( \gamma = \omega^2\tau \).
In §9.4 we simply assumed a friction force proportional to velocity when modelling dispersion. Now we see where (part of) it comes from: radiation damping. For sinusoidal motion it looks exactly like velocity-proportional friction, and now we even know its size.
Example# Estimate \( \tau \) for an electron and the distance light travels in that time. Comment on when the radiation reaction matters.
Solution triple-click to reveal \[\tau = \frac{\mu_0 q^2}{6\pi m c} = \frac{(1.26\times10^{-6})(1.6\times10^{-19})^2}{6\pi(9.11\times10^{-31})(3.00\times10^8)}\] The top is \( 3.22\times10^{-44} \) and the bottom \( 5.15\times10^{-21} \), so
\[\tau \approx 6\times10^{-24}\ \text{s}\] In that time light travels
\[c\tau \approx (3\times10^8)(6\times10^{-24}) \approx 2\times10^{-15}\ \text{m}\] That's about the “classical electron radius”, roughly the size of an atomic nucleus, and about 50,000 times smaller than an atom.
So the radiation reaction only matters if the motion changes noticeably within about \( 10^{-23} \) s, or over distances of about a femtometre. In almost every classical problem it is a tiny correction, which is why we could ignore it in Chapters 1–10.
It also explains why physicists live with the strange problems above. Pre-acceleration happens only about \( 10^{-23} \) s early, far too short to measure, and at scales where classical physics isn't expected to work anyway. That territory belongs to quantum electrodynamics.

title: (12.1) The Special Theory of Relativity
content:
12.1 The Special Theory of Relativity# Einstein's postulates# In ordinary mechanics, the laws are the same in every inertial frame (any frame moving at constant velocity): drop a ball on a smoothly moving train and it falls just as it does on the platform. Electrodynamics seemed to break this rule. Maxwell's equations predict one particular speed, \( c \), and people assumed that meant speed relative to some medium, the “ether”. But experiments could find no ether. Einstein's answer was to take both ideas as basic starting points:
The principle of relativity. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. The speed of light is universal. Light in vacuum travels at the same speed \( c \) for every inertial observer, however fast the source is moving. If Maxwell's equations count as laws of physics, the second actually follows from the first. What has to go is the everyday rule for adding velocities, and with it the idea that time is the same for everyone.
Three consequences# Simultaneity is relative. Two events that happen at the same time in one frame happen at different times in a frame moving relative to it. There's no universal “now”.
A flash in the middle of a moving carriage. On the train it reaches both ends at the same time; from the ground, the back end (moving towards the light) is lit first. Moving clocks run slow (time dilation):
\[\Delta t = \gamma \Delta \bar{t}, \qquad \gamma \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}\] A light clock. On the train the light goes straight up and down; from the ground it takes a longer, slanted path at the same speed c, so each tick takes longer. \( \Delta\bar{t} \) is the proper time: the time measured by a clock that is present at both events (so it sees them happen at the same place). Everyone else measures a longer time. \( \gamma \) is always at least 1, and is only noticeably bigger than 1 near light speed.
\( \gamma \) is barely above 1 until the speed is a good fraction of \( c \), then shoots up. Moving objects are shorter (Lorentz contraction) along their direction of motion:
\[\Delta x = \frac{\Delta\bar{x}}{\gamma}\] Sizes at right angles to the motion don't change.
A rod moving at \( 0.8c \) (\( \gamma = 5/3 \)) is shorter along its motion. Both effects work both ways: each observer finds the other's clocks slow and rulers short. That isn't a contradiction, because they disagree about which events are simultaneous, and comparing clocks or rulers depends on that.
The Lorentz transformations# For a frame moving at speed \( v \) along the shared \( x \)-axis:
\[\bar{x} = \gamma(x - vt), \qquad \bar{y} = y, \qquad \bar{z} = z, \qquad \bar{t} = \gamma\left( t - \frac{v}{c^2}x \right)\] When \( v \ll c \), \( \gamma \approx 1 \) and these become the everyday (Galilean) rules. So ordinary mechanics is still right at everyday speeds.
The rule for adding velocities becomes
\[\bar{u} = \frac{u - v}{1 - uv/c^2}\] This never gives a speed above \( c \) if neither input is above \( c \). Put in \( u = c \) and you get \( \bar{u} = c \): light has the same speed for everyone, as it should.
Spacetime# The interval between two events,
\[I \equiv -\left( c\Delta t \right)^2 + \left( \Delta x \right)^2 + \left( \Delta y \right)^2 + \left( \Delta z \right)^2\] is the same in every inertial frame, even though the time and distance separately aren't. (It's like how rotating your axes changes \( \Delta x \) and \( \Delta y \) but not the distance.) Its sign sorts pairs of events into three kinds:
Sign Name Meaning \( I < 0 \) timelike some observer sees both at the same place; one could cause the other \( I > 0 \) spacelike some observer sees them at the same time; neither can cause the other \( I = 0 \) lightlike a light signal could connect them exactly Everyone agrees which kind a pair is. That's what saves cause and effect: different observers can disagree about the order of two events only if they are spacelike, and then neither could have caused the other anyway.
A spacetime diagram. Light runs along the 45° lines. A particle's path stays inside the light cone. Events inside the cone are timelike from the origin, on it lightlike, outside it spacelike. Quantities that transform like \( (ct, x, y, z) \) are called four-vectors. For any two of them, \( -a^0b^0 + a^1b^1 + a^2b^2 + a^3b^3 \) is the same in every frame.
Example# Muons created in the upper atmosphere have a proper lifetime of \( 2.2\ \mu\text{s} \) and travel at \( 0.998c \). Show that they should not reach the ground classically, and resolve the discrepancy.
Solution triple-click to reveal Without relativity. In \( 2.2\ \mu\text{s} \) at \( 0.998c \), a muon travels
\[d = (0.998)(3\times10^8)(2.2\times10^{-6}) \approx 660\ \text{m}\] Muons are made about 10 km up, so hardly any should reach the ground. But detectors at sea level find lots of them.
With relativity. The Lorentz factor is
\[\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (0.998)^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{0.004}} \approx 15.8\] Seen from the ground, the muon's internal clock runs slow, so it lives longer:
\[\Delta t = \gamma\Delta\bar{t} = 15.8(2.2\times10^{-6}) = 3.5\times10^{-5}\ \text{s}\] In that time it travels about \( 10.4 \) km, enough to reach the ground. ✓
Seen by the muon, the story is different but gives the same result. Its lifetime is the normal \( 2.2\ \mu\text{s} \). What changes is the distance: the atmosphere rushing past at \( 0.998c \) is Lorentz-contracted to
\[\frac{10\ \text{km}}{15.8} \approx 630\ \text{m}\] which it covers easily. The two observers agree that the muon arrives, but disagree completely about why.
The same event from both sides, to scale. Ground: the muon's clock runs slow. Muon: the atmosphere is contracted to about 630 m. Example# A spaceship travelling at \( 0.8c \) fires a projectile forward at \( 0.8c \) relative to itself. Find the projectile's speed in the ground frame.
Solution triple-click to reveal Everyday addition would give \( 1.6c \), faster than light. Using the relativistic rule, with \( u' = 0.8c \) (projectile relative to ship) and \( v = 0.8c \) (ship):
\[u = \frac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2} = \frac{0.8c + 0.8c}{1 + (0.8)(0.8)} = \frac{1.6c}{1.64} \approx 0.976c\] Less than \( c \), as it must be.
The bottom line of the fraction is what keeps it below \( c \). For everyday speeds \( u'v/c^2 \) is incredibly tiny (for two jets it's about \( 10^{-12} \)), so the normal rule works perfectly well. That's why nobody noticed for centuries.
Check with light. If the ship shines a torch forward instead, \( u' = c \), and
\[u = \frac{c + v}{1 + v/c} = \frac{c(c+v)}{c+v} = c\] whatever \( v \) is. The light still travels at exactly \( c \) for the ground observer, just as the second postulate says.
